Coding track · Lesson C1

Variables: remembering facts

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • store a fact in a variable and use it again
  • tell text, numbers and true/false apart
  • print results and build a sentence from several facts

The idea

When you investigate a failing server you keep facts in your head: which server, which service, what state, how long it has been down. A program does the same with variables. A variable is a labelled box. You write the label on the left and the value on the right, joined by =. In Python = means "put this value into the box", not "is equal to".

Values come in a few basic kinds:

KindExampleUsed for
Text (a "string")"EV01"names, messages. Always inside quotes
Whole number42counts, minutes
Decimal number0.7measurements, averages
True or FalseTrueyes/no answers (a "boolean")

print(...) shows something on the screen. An f-string (text that starts with f") lets you drop variables into a sentence by putting their names in curly brackets. Lines that start with # are comments: notes for humans that Python ignores.

Watch it run

Press Next line and watch the Variables box fill up one box at a time.

Line by line

  • server = "EV01" creates a box labelled server holding the text EV01. The next three lines do the same for the service, its status and the minutes down.
  • print("Checking", server) prints the word Checking and then the value of server, separated by a space. Notice that "Checking" is in quotes (literal text) but server is not (a variable to look up).
  • message = f"{service} on {server} is {status}" builds one sentence from three variables and stores it in a new box.
  • hours_down = minutes_down / 60 does arithmetic: / divides. + adds, - subtracts, * multiplies.
  • round(hours_down, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places. 42 ÷ 60 is 0.7.
  • is_urgent = minutes_down > 30 asks a question: is 42 greater than 30? The answer, True, is stored. A variable can hold the answer to a yes/no question.
Why this matters for agents

An agent's state (Chapter 7) is nothing more than variables: the goal, the evidence so far, the current hypothesis. Everything in the later lessons is built from boxes like these.

Your turn

  1. Run it on your laptop. Then change minutes_down to 20 and run again. What happens to is_urgent? Predict first.
  2. Add a new variable severity = "High" and print a sentence that includes it.
  3. Make a mistake on purpose: delete one quote mark in a print line and read the error from the last line up.

Lesson C1 in plain words

  • A variable is a labelled box: label = value.
  • Basic kinds: text in quotes, whole numbers, decimals, True/False.
  • print shows output. f-strings put variables inside sentences. # starts a comment.
  • A comparison such as > produces True or False.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C2

Lists and dictionaries: holding many facts

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • keep many items in a list and pick one out
  • describe one thing with several labelled facts in a dictionary
  • recognise that a tool result is a dictionary, and a fleet is a list of them

The idea

One variable holds one fact. Real investigations have many facts. Python gives you two containers that cover most needs:

  • A list is a numbered shelf: ["EV01", "EV02", "SQL01"]. Order matters, and counting starts at 0, so the first item is servers[0]. Useful when you have a collection: servers, log lines, test cases.
  • A dictionary is a form with labelled fields: {"server": "EV01", "status": "Stopped"}. You look things up by label, not by position: record["status"]. Useful when you describe one thing in detail.

Put them together and you can describe a whole environment: a list of dictionaries, one per server. This is exactly the shape of the data that tools return and that language models read. When people say "JSON", they mean this notation (lists and dictionaries, written with quotes and braces). It is how programs pass structured information to each other.

Watch it run

Line by line

  • servers.append("EV03") adds an item at the end of the list. len(servers) counts the items. That is why it prints 4.
  • record = {...} creates a dictionary. None is Python's word for "nothing here", used for error when there is no error.
  • record["status"] looks up the value labelled status. record["checked_at"] = "09:14" adds a new field.
  • fleet is a list of three dictionaries. fleet spans several lines because brackets let Python continue on the next line.
  • stopped = [] creates an empty list. The for item in fleet: loop (more in C3) visits each server, and the if adds its name only when its status is Stopped.
  • The last print shows the finished dictionary. Notice it looks just like the structured tool results in Chapters 10 and 11.
Common mistake

Asking a dictionary for a label it does not have causes a KeyError. Asking a list for a position that does not exist causes an IndexError. Both mean "that is not in there". In an agent, a model sometimes asks a tool for something that does not exist, so tools must expect this (lesson C5).

Your turn

  1. Add a fourth server to fleet with status "Stopped". Predict the new stopped list.
  2. Print servers[1] and then servers[-1] (the last one). What do you learn about negative positions?
  3. Try print(record["owner"]). Read the error. Now try print(record.get("owner")), which returns None instead of failing. Why might a tool prefer that?

Lesson C2 in plain words

  • List = ordered collection, counted from 0. Dictionary = labelled fields.
  • A tool result is a dictionary. A fleet is a list of dictionaries. That is JSON.
  • Missing labels cause errors unless you handle them.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C3

Decisions and loops: the shape of an agent

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • make a program choose between paths with if, elif and else
  • repeat work with for and while
  • see why an agent is "a while loop with a model inside"

The idea

Two abilities turn a list of instructions into something that behaves intelligently:

  • Decisions. if some condition is true, do this. Otherwise (else), do that. You can add middle cases with elif ("else if").
  • Loops. A for loop does something for each item in a list. A while loop keeps going as long as a condition is true.

One Python rule matters here: the lines that belong inside an if or a loop are indented (pushed in by four spaces) and the line before ends in a colon. The indentation is how Python knows which lines are grouped together.

Think of an engineer reading an event log: look at every line, and if it says ERROR, note it and count it. That is a for loop containing an if. Then, if there are several errors, suspect a real fault. That is another decision. And "try connecting, and try again until it works or you give up" is a while loop.

Watch it run

Pay attention to how the highlight jumps back to the top of each loop, and how the Variables box changes.

Line by line

  • for line in events: means: take each item from events in turn, call it line, and run the indented block below.
  • if "ERROR" in line: asks whether the word ERROR appears inside this line. Only two of the four lines say it.
  • errors = errors + 1 adds one to the counter each time. A counter like this is a common pattern: start at 0, then add as you find things.
  • After the loop, if / elif / else picks exactly one of three messages. With two errors the first test, errors >= 2, is true.
  • The while loop repeats while attempts < 3 and not connected. Each pass adds 1 to attempts. When attempts reaches 3 the code sets connected = True and the loop stops. Without that update the loop would never end.
This is the agent loop

Look back at the loop from Chapter 11: ask the model what to do, run the tool, add the result, repeat until the model says it is done. It is a while loop with a decision inside it. And that is why every serious agent needs a step limit: a while loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever. Notice how the connection loop above has an exit (attempts < 3) so it cannot spin endlessly.

Your turn

  1. Delete one of the ERROR lines from events. Which message prints now? Predict first.
  2. Change the while loop to give up after 2 attempts. What does it print at the end? (It will still say "Connected". Why is that misleading? This kind of subtle wrongness is what your tests, in C8, must catch.)
  3. Add a WARN counter alongside the error counter.

Lesson C3 in plain words

  • if / elif / else chooses a path. Indented lines belong to the block above them.
  • for repeats once per item. while repeats until a condition is false.
  • A counter starts at zero and grows as you find things.
  • An agent is a while loop with a model's decision inside. Always give it an exit.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C4

Functions: the code behind a tool

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write a function with inputs and a returned result
  • explain the difference between return and print
  • see that an agent tool such as get_service_status is simply a function

The idea

A function is a named recipe. You define it once, give it inputs (called arguments), and it gives back a result. Then you can use it as often as you like. In Chapter 10 you designed tools with a name, a description, typed inputs and structured output. This lesson shows what that looks like in code: a tool is a function, and the "tool description" the model reads is just the function's name, inputs and short explanation.

  • def name(inputs): starts a definition. The indented lines below are the recipe.
  • return value hands a result back to whoever called the function and ends it.
  • The text in triple quotes right under the first line is a docstring: a description of what the function does. Frameworks (including MCP libraries) turn it into the tool description that the model reads.
Common mistake

print shows something to a human and the value is gone. return gives a value to the program so it can be used again. Tools must return their result, because the agent loop needs to pass it back to the model.

Watch it run

Notice how the highlight jumps up into the function when it is called, and how the Variables box then shows the function's own inputs under "in get_service_status()".

Line by line

  • def get_service_status(server, service): defines the tool. It takes two inputs. Defining a function does not run it. Python just remembers the recipe.
  • The dictionary known is a pretend lookup table (in real life this line would query Windows). known.get(service, "Unknown") looks up the service, and gives "Unknown" if it is not found, rather than crashing.
  • The function returns a dictionary with a fixed shape: server, service, status, error. A predictable shape makes a tool easy for a model to use and easy for you to test.
  • summarise(result) is a second function that turns a result into one readable line. Functions can use other functions' results.
  • The last three lines call the tool with different inputs. For "Search" the table has no entry, so the status is "Unknown". The tool handled it gracefully.
Design lessons you already know

Each tool has one job, typed inputs, structured output and an explicit way to report problems (here, "Unknown" and an error field). Those are the tool-design rules of Chapter 10, now visible as code. Notice also that this function only reads. Nothing about it changes any system.

Your turn

  1. Add a third entry to known, such as "Search": "Running". Call the tool for it. Predict, then run.
  2. Write a new function is_stopped(result) that returns True if the status is "Stopped". Test it on two results.
  3. Add a docstring to summarise. Why would a good docstring matter if a model were choosing between ten tools?

Lesson C4 in plain words

  • A function is a named recipe: def it once, call it many times.
  • return gives a value back. print only shows it.
  • A tool is a function with a clear job, predictable output and a docstring that describes it.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C5

Errors, validation and JSON

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • reject bad input on purpose, and catch the problem instead of crashing
  • turn a dictionary into JSON text, and back again
  • explain why "errors are data" in an agent

The idea

In Chapter 11 you saw a tool call fail because a model passed a value the API did not accept. Models make odd requests: a server that does not exist, a missing field, a typo. A good tool does not crash. It checks its input and returns a clear error that the model can read and adjust to.

  • raise ValueError("message") deliberately signals a problem.
  • try: ... except ValueError as problem: ... says "try this, and if that kind of problem happens, do this instead". The program carries on.

The second idea is JSON. Models and programs exchange text. json.dumps(result) turns a dictionary into JSON text. json.loads(text) turns that text back into a dictionary. That conversion is the bridge between your tool and the model: the tool's result becomes text that goes into the model's context.

Watch it run

Step to the third server, WEB9. Watch the program jump out of the function, land in except, and carry on instead of crashing.

Line by line

  • import json brings in a tool kit that Python ships with for reading and writing JSON.
  • In test_sql_connectivity, the first check rejects any server whose name does not start with "EV". It raises an error rather than guessing.
  • reachable = server != "EV03" pretends EV03's SQL link is down (!= means "is not equal to"). The result uses None if reachable else "timeout after 15s", a compact way to say "no error if reachable, otherwise this message".
  • The loop tries three names. try calls the tool. For WEB9 the tool raises ValueError, and except builds a result dictionary describing the problem. The error became data with the same shape as a normal result.
  • json.dumps(result) converts it to text. Notice Python's True, False and None become JSON's true, false and null.
  • Finally json.loads(text) proves the text can be read back into a dictionary.
Why this matters for agents

From Chapter 11: errors go back to the model as data so it can adjust, and arguments are validated before anything runs. It is also the structured-result rule from Chapter 10: put parsing and validation in code. And from Chapter 12: unknown or malformed requests should be refused, not guessed at.

Your turn

  1. Add a second validation: reject an empty string for the server name. Test with "".
  2. Remove the try/except and run again. Read the error. This is what an unhandled problem looks like, and the program stops.
  3. Print json.dumps(result, indent=2) to see the same JSON in a more readable layout.

Lesson C5 in plain words

  • Validate inputs and raise an error for bad ones. Catch errors with try / except.
  • Return errors as structured data so a model can react.
  • json.dumps makes text from a dictionary. json.loads reverses it.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C6

Classes: the state of an investigation

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read a simple class: attributes, methods, self
  • explain how a class can hold an agent's goal, evidence and hypothesis

The idea

So far, facts live in separate variables and actions live in separate functions. But an investigation is one thing: it has a goal, a growing list of evidence and a current hypothesis, and you do things to it (add evidence, print a report). A class bundles those together, like a case folder with a cover sheet and a set of standard procedures.

  • A class is a template. Writing Investigation("Why is indexing down?") makes one real folder from the template (an object).
  • __init__ runs once when the object is created and sets it up.
  • Variables that belong to the object are attributes, written self.goal. Functions that belong to it are methods.
  • self means "this particular object". It is always the first input of a method.

This is where agent state (Chapter 7) lives in real code. Frameworks do the same thing with larger state objects (for example, the LangGraph state in Chapter 13 that holds messages and the philosopher's context).

Watch it run

Look at the Variables box after the object is created: the whole object is shown with its attributes, and it changes as evidence is added.

Line by line

  • class Investigation: starts the template. Everything indented below belongs to it.
  • __init__(self, goal) stores the goal and starts an empty evidence list and a placeholder hypothesis.
  • add_evidence appends a fact and, if a new hypothesis is supplied, replaces the old one. The =None makes the hypothesis optional.
  • report builds lines of text. enumerate(..., start=1) counts the evidence from 1, and "\n".join(lines) glues the lines together with line breaks.
  • case = Investigation(...) creates the object. case.add_evidence(...) calls a method on it. Each call changes the object's own state.
Connect it to Chapter 7

Compare this output with the agent simulator: "Evidence so far" and "Working hypothesis" were exactly this object. The model decides the next action, and your code keeps the state. That is why Chapter 8 said you should be able to inspect what the agent knows at every step.

Your turn

  1. Add a third piece of evidence: "SQL connectivity test fails". Update the hypothesis. Predict the report.
  2. Add a method count_evidence(self) that returns how many facts there are.
  3. Create a second investigation for a different goal. Notice the two objects never interfere with each other.

Lesson C6 in plain words

  • A class is a template for bundling data (attributes) and actions (methods).
  • self means "this object". __init__ sets it up.
  • Agent state is a class holding the goal, evidence and hypothesis.

Coding track · Lesson C7

A pretend lab and a diagnosis loop

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read a complete mini agent made of tools, history and a loop
  • find the single function where an AI model would go
  • explain why building the rule-based version first is good engineering

The idea

Now combine everything: variables (C1), dictionaries (C2), loops and decisions (C3), functions as tools (C4). The result is a small Enterprise Vault diagnostic that behaves like the agent in Chapter 7, with one difference: its "brain" is a handful of rules, not an AI model. That is deliberate. You build the loop, the tools and the checks first, and make sure they work. Then replacing the rules with a model changes one function.

The pieces:

  • LAB is a dictionary that stands in for a real Enterprise Vault environment. It describes one failure: the service is stopped, the log shows a SQL timeout, SQL cannot be reached, DNS is fine.
  • Tools are four small functions that read from LAB. All read-only.
  • TOOLS is a dictionary mapping a tool's name to the function. This lets the loop call a tool by name, exactly as an agent does when a model says "call get_event_logs".
  • decide_next(history) looks at what has happened so far and picks the next tool, or returns None when it has seen enough.
  • history is a list recording each tool and its result.

Watch it run

This one is longer. Use Run to end if you want the overview first, then Restart and step through. Watch history grow and see which function the highlight visits at each turn.

Line by line

  • TOOLS = {"get_service_status": get_service_status, ...} stores the functions themselves (not the results of calling them) under their names.
  • decide_next reads the last tool and result. First time (history empty) it starts with the service status. If the status was Stopped it asks for the event logs. If the log mentions SQL it tests SQL. If SQL is unreachable it checks DNS. Otherwise it returns None.
  • while True: repeats forever, until break runs. The loop asks decide_next for a tool. If it is None, break leaves the loop.
  • result = TOOLS[tool]() looks up the function by name and calls it. The brackets at the end are what actually run it.
  • history.append((tool, result)) records the pair. A pair in round brackets is called a tuple: two things kept together.
An honest flaw to notice

The last line, print("Diagnosis: SQL server unreachable; DNS is fine."), is fixed text. It would print that even if the lab were different. The loop gathers evidence, but the conclusion is not computed from it. A tester would catch this at once: change LAB and the diagnosis is wrong. Lesson C8 teaches you to catch exactly this kind of bug, and the full starter agent in C11 fixes it by computing the answer.

Where the AI goes

Replace decide_next with a function that sends history to a language model and reads back which tool it wants. Nothing else changes: same tools, same loop, same history. That is the sentence "model proposes, software executes" in code. It is also why the step limit, the policy gate and the trace (C9) live in the loop and not in the model.

Your turn

  1. Change "sql_reachable": False to True. Predict which tools run, then run it. What diagnosis line prints? Is it right?
  2. Add a rule so that if DNS fails, decide_next returns nothing further, and fix the final line so it describes what happened. (Hint: look in history.)
  3. Add a fifth tool, check_disk_space, to LAB, to the functions and to TOOLS.

Lesson C7 in plain words

  • A mini agent is tools + history + a loop + a "decide next" function.
  • Calling a tool by name from a dictionary is how agent frameworks dispatch tool calls.
  • Build with rules first. Swap in a model later by replacing only decide_next.
  • A fixed conclusion that ignores the evidence is a bug that tests should catch.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C8

Tests and measuring: your QA skills in code

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write a small set of test scenarios with expected results
  • compute a pass rate and use assert as a regression alarm
  • explain how this becomes the evaluation harness for an agent

The idea

This is the lesson where you are already the expert. Chapter 9 said an agent needs a test set of reproducible failures with expected outcomes, a scorecard, and a regression suite. Testers do this every day. In code it is a list of cases, a loop that runs each one, and a comparison of actual to expected.

  • Each scenario is a dictionary: the conditions (service state, SQL, DNS) and the expected diagnosis.
  • The loop calls the function under test and compares its answer to the expectation: PASS or FAIL.
  • The task success rate is passes divided by total.
  • assert condition, "message" stops the program with an error if the condition is false. Put it at the end of a test run and any regression becomes impossible to miss.

Watch it run

Line by line

  • SCENARIOS is a list of three dictionaries. Each is a test case: the setup, plus "expect", the right answer.
  • diagnose(service, sql, dns) is the logic being tested. DNS failure first; then "stopped and SQL down"; otherwise it escalates to a human. (Note the third rule: it knows when to say I cannot tell. Chapter 9's "escalation rate" metric measures that.)
  • passed = passed + (1 if ok else 0) adds 1 for a pass. 1 if ok else 0 is a one-line decision.
  • {rate:.0%} inside an f-string formats a fraction as a percentage.
  • assert rate == 1.0, ... would crash the run with your message if any case failed. In a real project this runs every time you change anything.
From three cases to fifty

Your notes say to measure a diagnostic agent against 50 or more known failure scenarios, kept as a regression suite. This is the same program with more rows in SCENARIOS. The rows can come from your existing QA lab: every known failure mode you have reproduced becomes a case. Every time you improve the agent, you rerun the suite. If something that used to pass now fails, that is a regression.

Capability versus reliability

A rule-based diagnose gives the same answer every time, so a single run is enough. A language-model brain does not: run each scenario several times and report how often it succeeds every time (reliability, pass^k) as well as at least once (capability, pass@k). See reliability_demo.py in Chapter 9.

Your turn

  1. Break the code on purpose: change the third scenario's "expect" to "SQL unreachable". Run it. What is the success rate? What does the assert do?
  2. Add two scenarios of your own that reflect failures you have seen. Add the right expectation for each.
  3. Add a fourth tracked number, such as how many cases escalated to a human.

Lesson C8 in plain words

  • A test set is a list of cases with expected answers. Run, compare, count.
  • Success rate = passes ÷ total. assert turns a regression into an immediate failure.
  • Your QA experience maps directly onto evaluating agents.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C9

Traces and a policy gate

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • record a trace of what an agent did, one JSON line per step
  • write a gate that allows, denies or defers each tool call
  • explain "deny by default"

The idea

Two production habits from Chapters 12 and 13, in a few lines:

  • A policy gate. The model proposes a tool call; your code decides whether it may run. Read-only tools are allowed. Risky ones need human approval. Anything unknown is denied. Deny by default means a tool nobody thought about is blocked, not allowed.
  • A trace. A record of every proposal and decision, so when something goes wrong you can reconstruct what happened. We store each step as a small dictionary and print it as one line of JSON. Files of such lines are called JSON lines and are easy to search and replay.

Sets, written with curly brackets and no labels ({"a", "b"}), are handy for "is this tool in the allowed group?" checks.

Watch it run

Watch the trace list grow with each call, and see how verdict changes.

Line by line

  • READ_ONLY and NEEDS_APPROVAL are sets of tool names. They are the policy, kept in one visible place.
  • run_tool(name, human_ok=False) has a default for human_ok: if the caller does not say, it is False. A safe default.
  • The if / elif / else picks a verdict. The final else is the "deny by default" rule.
  • trace.append({...}) records the step number, the tool and the verdict. len(trace) + 1 numbers each entry.
  • The last two calls show the key behaviours. restart_service is denied without approval and allowed with it. delete_data is denied even with human_ok=True, because it is on no list at all. Some actions should never be available to an automated agent, whoever clicks approve.
  • The list comprehension [e["tool"] for e in trace if e["verdict"] == "deny"] is a short way to build a list: "the tool name of every entry whose verdict was deny".
Authorisation is policy

"The authorisation decision belongs to software policy, not model confidence." Notice that nothing in this code asks the model how sure it is. And because the gate sits in your loop, even a model that was tricked by prompt injection (Chapter 12) cannot call a tool the policy does not allow.

Your turn

  1. Add "check_dns" to READ_ONLY and call it. Check the trace.
  2. Make the trace record the time of each step (hint: import time and time.strftime("%H:%M:%S")).
  3. Make the program write the trace to a file, one line per entry, using open("trace.jsonl", "w"). Open it in Notepad. This is how you would keep an audit log.

Lesson C9 in plain words

  • A gate checks every proposed tool call against policy. Unknown means deny.
  • A trace records each step as a line of JSON so you can reconstruct what happened.
  • The model proposes. Your code decides. Neither the gate nor the trace asks the model for permission.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C10

Real models, secrets, an MCP server, and coding with AI

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • keep an API key out of your code and use it safely
  • describe a tool to a model with a JSON schema
  • read a small MCP server and know what to check before using one
  • use an AI assistant to help you code without losing control
What is tested and what is not

I ran the offline lessons (C1 to C9, C11) here. For this lesson: the environment-variable snippet and the JSON schema I ran. The MCP server snippet I installed and ran against the current library (to list its tool and its schema), but I did not connect a real client to it. The real model call (Chapter 11) needs a paid account that I do not have, so I checked only that the library accepts those parameters. Libraries change quickly, so treat every snippet here as a starting point and check the library's own documentation.

1. Secrets: API keys do not belong in code

To call a real language model you need an API key: a long secret string that identifies and bills your account. Anyone who has it can spend your money. So the first rule: never type a key into a file that you might share, upload or paste into a chat. Instead, store it in an environment variable, a named setting held by your computer, and have the program read it:

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")   # reads the setting; returns None if it is missing
if not api_key:
    print("Set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable first.")
else:
    print("Key found (not printing it).")

In Windows PowerShell you can set it for the current window only (it disappears when you close it):

$env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY = "paste-your-key-here"
python my_agent.py
  • Never paste the key into a chat, an issue, a screenshot or a Git repository.
  • If a key leaks, revoke it in your account and create a new one.
  • Use the narrowest permissions and spending limits your provider offers.

2. Describing a tool to a model

In Chapter 11 you saw that a model learns what tools exist from a description. That description is data, in JSON Schema form. For the C4 function it looks like this. It is the same information as the function's name, docstring and inputs, written for the model:

get_service_status_tool = {
    "name": "get_service_status",
    "description": "Return the state of one Windows service on one server. Read-only.",
    "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "server":  {"type": "string", "description": "Server name, for example EV01"},
            "service": {"type": "string", "description": "Service name, for example Indexing"},
        },
        "required": ["server", "service"],
    },
}

Good descriptions matter: they are the only thing the model knows about your tool. Write them for a stranger, then ask a model whether anything is ambiguous (Chapter 8).

3. Calling a real model

Chapter 11 shows the full loop. The shape is always: build the messages, send them with the tool descriptions, check whether the reply asks for a tool, run it yourself, send the result back, repeat. Your rule-based decide_next from C7 is replaced by that call. Everything else (tools, history, step limit, gate, trace) is the code you already have. Start with read-only tools and harmless data, and put a step limit and a cost limit in the loop before your first real run, because a loop that misbehaves spends real money.

4. Your tools as an MCP server

Chapter 10 explained MCP: write a server once and any compatible AI application can use it. With the official Python library the C4 function becomes a server almost unchanged. You add one line above the function (a "decorator", which registers it as a tool) and the library reads the name, the docstring and the typed inputs to build the schema for you:

# pip install mcp
from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer

mcp = MCPServer("ev-diagnostics")

@mcp.tool()
def get_service_status(server: str, service: str) -> dict:
    """Return the state of one Windows service on one server. Read-only."""
    fake = {"Indexing": "Stopped", "Storage": "Running"}
    return {"server": server, "service": service,
            "status": fake.get(service, "Unknown"), "error": None}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run()          # speaks MCP over standard input/output by default

I ran this against the current library (version 2.3.0 at the time of writing). The tool was listed with its description and a schema generated from the typed inputs. Two lessons from that test:

Lesson: the library changed under my feet

My first attempt used the import that older tutorials and my own memory had: from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP. It failed. Version 2 of the library renamed it to MCPServer and changed other things. This is exactly the warning in your study notes about MCP still changing. Always check the version you install and read its current documentation. When code from a tutorial fails with an import error, the first suspect is the version.

Before you use any MCP server (yours or someone else's), ask the four questions from Chapter 10: who can call its tools, what can they do, where can it act, and what gets logged. For an Enterprise Vault server: only read-only tools at first, credentials with minimal rights, and a trace of every call.

5. Coding with an AI assistant, and staying the engineer

AI assistants can write code quickly. For a learner that is a gift and a trap. The gift: you can get a working first draft of almost anything. The trap: you may end up running code you do not understand, with permissions it should not have. The habits that avoid the trap are the same habits as in the rest of this course:

HabitWhat it looks like
Ask for small piecesOne function at a time, with its inputs and output described. Not "build me an agent".
Ask it to explain"Explain this code line by line for a beginner." Then check the explanation against the step-through player idea: could you predict the output?
Tests firstWrite the expected results (C8) before asking for the code. Then you can tell whether the code is right.
Read before you runLook for anything that deletes, sends, installs or touches real systems. If you do not understand a line, ask.
Harmless data firstRun on fake data (like LAB). Never on production first.
Read-only firstNo write actions until diagnosis is measured and trusted (Chapter 14).
Paste the whole errorCopy the entire traceback, not a paraphrase, when asking for help. Never paste a secret.
Check versionsSay which library version you use. Libraries move (see above).

Lesson C10 in plain words

  • Keep keys in environment variables, never in files or chats. Revoke leaked keys.
  • A tool is described to the model as a JSON schema. Descriptions are all the model knows.
  • A real model replaces only decide_next. Add a step limit, a cost limit and a gate first.
  • An MCP server can be your functions plus a decorator. Check the library version and the four security questions.
  • With AI help: small pieces, tests first, read before running, harmless and read-only first.

Check yourself

Coding track · Lesson C11

The complete starter agent

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read a complete agent program and name which course idea each part implements
  • run it, evaluate it, and watch the gate block a badly behaved brain
  • list the next upgrades, from easy to advanced

This is the capstone in code. Every part comes from something you have learned. It is one file, about a hundred and twenty lines, and it runs on any computer with Python and nothing installed. (Saved as course/examples/ev_agent.py.) Read the code first, then the map below it.

"""Enterprise Vault diagnostic agent: a runnable starter (standard library only).

Parts, matching the course:
  Lab        a pretend environment with four failure scenarios (Chapter 9: a test set)
  tools      read-only functions (Chapters 6 and 10)
  gate       policy check before any tool runs (Chapter 12)
  brain      decides the next step. Rules today; swap in an LLM later (Chapters 7, 11)
  run_agent  the loop with a step limit and a trace (Chapters 7, 11, 13)
  evaluate   runs every scenario and scores the agent (Chapter 9)
"""
import json

SCENARIOS = {
    "sql_down": {"service": "Stopped", "events": ["09:12 ERROR SQL connection timeout"],
                 "sql": False, "dns": True, "root_cause": "SQL server unreachable"},
    "dns_broken": {"service": "Running", "events": ["10:40 WARN Name resolution failed for sql01"],
                   "sql": True, "dns": False, "root_cause": "DNS record for SQL host failing"},
    "stopped_unknown": {"service": "Stopped", "events": [],
                        "sql": True, "dns": True, "root_cause": "cause unclear: escalate to a human"},
    "all_good": {"service": "Running", "events": [],
                 "sql": True, "dns": True, "root_cause": "no fault found"},
}

class Lab:
    """A pretend environment. Each method is a read-only tool."""
    def __init__(self, scenario):
        self.s = scenario

    def get_service_status(self):
        return {"status": self.s["service"]}

    def get_event_logs(self):
        return {"lines": list(self.s["events"])}

    def test_sql_connectivity(self):
        return {"reachable": self.s["sql"]}

    def check_dns(self):
        return {"resolved": self.s["dns"]}

    def restart_service(self):                  # a WRITE tool: the gate must block it
        return {"restarted": True}

READ_ONLY = {"get_service_status", "get_event_logs", "test_sql_connectivity", "check_dns"}

def gate(tool):
    """Allow read-only tools. Everything else is denied (add human approval later)."""
    return "allow" if tool in READ_ONLY else "deny"

def brain(history):
    """Decide the next step from what has been seen so far. Returns (kind, value)."""
    seen = {tool: result for tool, result in history}
    if "get_service_status" not in seen:
        return "tool", "get_service_status"
    if "get_event_logs" not in seen:
        return "tool", "get_event_logs"
    service = seen["get_service_status"]["status"]
    lines = seen["get_event_logs"]["lines"]
    if any("Name resolution" in line for line in lines) and "check_dns" not in seen:
        return "tool", "check_dns"
    if any("SQL" in line for line in lines) and "test_sql_connectivity" not in seen:
        return "tool", "test_sql_connectivity"
    if "check_dns" in seen and not seen["check_dns"]["resolved"]:
        return "final", "DNS record for SQL host failing"
    if "test_sql_connectivity" in seen and not seen["test_sql_connectivity"]["reachable"]:
        return "final", "SQL server unreachable"
    if service == "Stopped":
        return "final", "cause unclear: escalate to a human"
    return "final", "no fault found"

def eager_brain(history):
    """A badly behaved brain: after diagnosing it tries to restart the service on its own."""
    kind, value = brain(history)
    if kind == "final" and not any(tool == "restart_service" for tool, _ in history):
        return "tool", "restart_service"
    return kind, value

def run_agent(lab, brain_fn=brain, max_steps=8):
    history, trace, denied = [], [], 0
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        kind, value = brain_fn(history)
        if kind == "final":
            trace.append({"step": step, "final": value})
            return value, trace, denied
        verdict = gate(value)
        trace.append({"step": step, "tool": value, "verdict": verdict})
        if verdict == "allow":
            history.append((value, getattr(lab, value)()))
        else:
            denied += 1
            history.append((value, {"error": "blocked by policy"}))
    return "step limit reached", trace, denied

def evaluate(brain_fn=brain):
    passed, total_steps, blocked = 0, 0, 0
    for name, scenario in SCENARIOS.items():
        answer, trace, denied = run_agent(Lab(scenario), brain_fn)
        ok = answer == scenario["root_cause"]
        passed += ok
        total_steps += len(trace)
        blocked += denied
        print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {name:<16} steps={len(trace)}  answer={answer}")
    n = len(SCENARIOS)
    print(f"success {passed}/{n}  avg steps {total_steps / n:.1f}  blocked write attempts {blocked}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- one run, with its trace ---")
    answer, trace, _ = run_agent(Lab(SCENARIOS["sql_down"]))
    for entry in trace:
        print(json.dumps(entry))
    print("Answer:", answer)
    print("\n--- evaluation: careful brain ---")
    evaluate(brain)
    print("\n--- evaluation: eager brain (tries to restart on its own) ---")
    evaluate(eager_brain)

What it prints

This is the actual output when I ran it:

--- one run, with its trace ---
{"step": 1, "tool": "get_service_status", "verdict": "allow"}
{"step": 2, "tool": "get_event_logs", "verdict": "allow"}
{"step": 3, "tool": "test_sql_connectivity", "verdict": "allow"}
{"step": 4, "final": "SQL server unreachable"}
Answer: SQL server unreachable

--- evaluation: careful brain ---
PASS  sql_down         steps=4  answer=SQL server unreachable
PASS  dns_broken       steps=4  answer=DNS record for SQL host failing
PASS  stopped_unknown  steps=3  answer=cause unclear: escalate to a human
PASS  all_good         steps=3  answer=no fault found
success 4/4  avg steps 3.5  blocked write attempts 0

--- evaluation: eager brain (tries to restart on its own) ---
PASS  sql_down         steps=5  answer=SQL server unreachable
PASS  dns_broken       steps=5  answer=DNS record for SQL host failing
PASS  stopped_unknown  steps=4  answer=cause unclear: escalate to a human
PASS  all_good         steps=4  answer=no fault found
success 4/4  avg steps 4.5  blocked write attempts 4

How the parts map to the course

In the codeWhat it isCourse idea
SCENARIOSfour controlled failures with the correct root causea test set (Ch 9, C8)
class Laba pretend environment whose methods are toolsenvironment and tools (Ch 7, 8, C4)
READ_ONLY, gate()deny by default; only read-only tools runleast privilege, policy (Ch 12, C9)
brain()chooses the next step from history, or concludesthe decision step; where an LLM goes (Ch 7, 11, C7)
run_agent()the loop, with a step limit and a tracethe agent loop (Ch 7, 11, C3)
evaluate()runs every scenario, reports success and cost-like numbersscorecard, regression (Ch 9, C8)
eager_brain()a brain that tries to restart the service itselfwhy the gate must not trust the model (Ch 12)
The most important thing in the output

Look at the last line: the badly behaved brain made four attempts to restart a production service, and the gate blocked every one, while the diagnoses stayed correct. Nothing in the gate needed to know the brain was misbehaving. That is the point of putting authority in software policy, and you can verify it in thirty seconds by running the file.

Fixes since C7

  • The conclusion is now computed from the evidence (the return "final", ... lines), not printed as fixed text.
  • There are scenarios where the right answer is "cause unclear: escalate to a human" and "no fault found". A good agent knows when to stop and when to ask.
  • Results are scored against known answers, so a regression shows up as FAIL.

Upgrades, from easy to advanced

Each one maps to a skill level and a chapter. Do them in order, and run the evaluation after every change.

#UpgradeWhat you learn
1Add a fifth scenario from a real failure you have seenbuilding a test set from your QA lab
2Add a tool, check_disk_space, to Lab and READ_ONLYtool design and permissions
3Write the trace to trace.jsonl with timestampsobservability (C9)
4Move SCENARIOS into a JSON file and load itfiles and JSON (C5)
5Add human approval: for restart_service, ask input("Approve? y/n ") instead of always denyingan approval boundary (Ch 12)
6Count tool calls per run as "cost", and add a hard limitbudgets (Ch 8, 9)
7Replace brain() with a real model call (Chapter 11), keeping everything elsereal model, same loop
8Run each scenario ten times and report pass@k and pass^kcapability versus reliability (Ch 9)
9Expose the tools through an MCP server (C10)MCP (Ch 10)
10Connect to a real lab, read-only, with minimal credentialsproduction thinking (Ch 12, 13)
Honest checkpoint

If you can read this file and say what every part does, and you have done upgrades 1 to 3 yourself, you are at skill level 4 (Implement). With 5 to 8 you are into levels 5 and 6 (Debug and Evaluate). Upgrades 9 and 10 take you toward 7 and 8. That is the realistic path the capstone chapter describes, and now it is a list of steps you can actually take.

Where to go from here

  • Do the "Your turn" tasks you skipped in C1 to C9. They are the real learning.
  • Revisit Chapter 14's design workbook and compare its brief with this program. Which of your choices are not yet in the code?
  • Look at the PhiloAgents repository (Chapter 13) and find the same parts: tools, graph, state, tracing, evaluation, in a bigger form.

Lesson C11 in plain words

  • A complete agent is a few simple parts: scenarios, tools, a gate, a brain, a loop, an evaluation.
  • The gate protected the system from a misbehaving brain without needing to know it was misbehaving.
  • You improve it in small steps, measuring after each. Replace the brain last.

Linux · Lesson 1

Meet the shell

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what Linux, a distribution, a terminal and a shell are
  • get a Linux prompt on your own computer
  • run your first commands and read their output
  • find help when you are stuck

What is Linux, really?

Almost every server in a data centre, every cloud virtual machine and every container runs Linux. Even if your Enterprise Vault servers run Windows, the tools around them (containers, pipelines, automation, monitoring) mostly run on Linux. Learning it is the best single investment you can make as an infrastructure engineer.

Four words get mixed up, so let us separate them:

WordWhat it isEveryday comparison
Kernelthe core of the operating system: it talks to the hardware and decides which program gets the processor, memory and diskthe engine
Distribution ("distro")a kernel plus a collection of programs, packaged and supported by someone (Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat, Alpine)a complete car model built around an engine
Terminalthe window where you type commandsthe dashboard
Shellthe program inside the terminal that reads your commands and runs them (usually bash)the driver who understands your instructions

In this course the examples run on Ubuntu, a very common distribution. The commands work almost identically on Debian, Red Hat and others.

Getting a Linux prompt

You are on Windows, so the easiest route is WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), which runs real Ubuntu inside Windows. In PowerShell, run as administrator:

Example output (not run here)
$ wsl --install
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
wsl

What it does: Windows Subsystem for Linux: runs a real Linux distribution inside Windows.

When to use it: Getting a Linux terminal on a Windows laptop: wsl --install.

Open the full command reference

Restart when asked, then open "Ubuntu" from the Start menu and create a username and password. You now have a Linux terminal. Alternatives: a virtual machine (VirtualBox or Hyper-V) running Ubuntu, a free cloud virtual machine, or a spare computer. A phone is fine for reading these lessons, but typing commands is best on a laptop.

Tip

Everything in the terminal boxes below is a command you can type yourself. Boxes marked Real output show exactly what happened when I ran the commands on a Linux machine while building this page. Your output will be the same or very close.

Reading a prompt

When the terminal is ready for a command it shows a prompt, something like student@lab:~$. It tells you who you are (student), which machine (lab), where you are (~ means your home directory) and that you are an ordinary user ($, while # means the all-powerful administrator, root). In the examples below, a line starting with $ is what you type. Do not type the $ itself.

Your first commands

The commands below run in a small pretend Enterprise Vault server folder, so there is something to look at.

Real output
$ whoami
student
$ pwd
/home/student/lab
$ echo "Hello from Linux"
Hello from Linux
$ uname -s
Linux
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
whoami

What it does: Prints the name of the user you are currently logged in as.

When to use it: After switching accounts or using sudo, to confirm who you are before changing anything.

pwd

What it does: Prints the full path of the folder you are in ("print working directory").

When to use it: When you are lost, or before running something destructive, to be sure where you are.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

uname

What it does: Prints information about the operating system and kernel.

When to use it: Checking which OS or kernel version a server runs.

-s kernel name-r kernel release-m hardware architecture-a everything

Open the full command reference

What each one did:

  • whoami prints your username.
  • pwd ("print working directory") prints where you are in the file system. Everything in Linux is a file in one big tree that starts at /. Here you are in /home/student/lab.
  • echo prints whatever you give it.
  • uname -s prints the name of the kernel. It says Linux.

Which distribution is this?

Real output
$ cat /etc/os-release | head -3
PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS"
NAME="Ubuntu"
VERSION_ID="24.04"
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

The shape of every command

Nearly every Linux command follows one pattern:

command  -options  arguments
   ls      -l       docs
  • The command is the program to run.
  • Options (also called flags) change how it behaves. A single dash and a letter (-l), or two dashes and a word (--help).
  • Arguments say what to act on: a file, a folder, some text.

Try the same command with and without an option:

Real output
$ ls
docs
ev
$ ls -l --time-style=long-iso
total 8
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 docs
drwxr-xr-x 6 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 ev
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

Short options can be combined: ls -la means ls -l -a. Options are case-sensitive: -r and -R are different. And Linux file names are case-sensitive too, so Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files.

Getting help

Nobody memorises every option. Skilled engineers look things up constantly. Three ways:

Real output
$ ls --help | head -8
Usage: ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...
List information about the FILEs (the current directory by default).
Sort entries alphabetically if none of -cftuvSUX nor --sort is specified.

Mandatory arguments to long options are mandatory for short options too.
  -a, --all                  do not ignore entries starting with .
  -A, --almost-all           do not list implied . and ..
      --author               with -l, print the author of each file
$ help cd | head -3
cd: cd [-L|[-P [-e]] [-@]] [dir]
    Change the shell working directory.
    
$ type cd
cd is a shell builtin
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
help

What it does: Shows built-in help for shell builtins such as cd or export.

When to use it: A shell builtin has no man page; use help cd instead.

type

What it does: Tells you what a command name really is: a builtin, an alias, a function or a program (and where).

When to use it: Working out why a command behaves oddly, for example whether ls is an alias.

Open the full command reference

  • command --help prints a short summary (pipe it into head as above to see only the top).
  • man command opens the full manual page. Press q to leave, /word to search, and the space bar to page down. (Very minimal systems, such as small container images, leave the manuals out, which is why this page uses --help and help in its examples.)
  • help cd explains a shell builtin (a command built into bash itself). type cd tells you what kind of thing a command is: cd is a builtin, not a separate program.

Four tricks that save hours

  1. Tab completion. Type the first letters of a command or file name and press Tab. The shell finishes it or shows the choices. It is faster and avoids typos.
  2. Up arrow. Recall the previous command. history lists earlier ones, and Ctrl+R searches them.
  3. Ctrl+C stops a running command. Ctrl+L (or clear) clears the screen.
  4. Copy and paste. In most terminals, paste is Ctrl+Shift+V (or right-click).
Careful

The shell does exactly what you say, immediately, with no "are you sure". Commands such as rm (delete) have no recycle bin. Develop the habit now: read a command through before pressing Enter, and practise in a throwaway folder.

Enterprise Vault connection

When an Enterprise Vault server misbehaves, people often ask you to "send me the log file" or "check the service". If those servers or their monitoring run on Linux, every one of those requests is a few of the commands you are about to learn.

Your turn
  1. Open a terminal and run whoami and pwd. What is your home directory?
  2. Run ls -la ~ (the ~ means your home). Which files start with a dot? (Files that start with a dot are hidden.)
  3. Run man ls and find the option that sorts by size. Press q to leave.

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers

Check yourself against real output. Task 1 and 2 (we make a hidden file ourselves so the result is predictable):

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "my home directory is: $HOME"
my home directory is: /home/student
$ touch .hidden-example
$ echo "--- ls (hidden files not shown):"; ls
--- ls (hidden files not shown):
docs
ev
$ echo "--- ls -a (the dot files appear):"; ls -a | grep '^\.' | grep -v '^\.\.\?$'
--- ls -a (the dot files appear):
.hidden-example
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Task 3: man is not installed in this lab, but the same information is in --help. Find the "sort by size" option:

Real output
$ ls --help | grep -i "sort by" | head -3
  -c                         with -lt: sort by, and show, ctime (time of last
                             with -l: show ctime and sort by name;
                             otherwise: sort by ctime, newest first

-S sorts by file size, largest first. Try ls -lS and add -r to reverse it.

Common mistakes
  • Typing the $ from the examples. It is part of the prompt, not the command.
  • Forgetting that Linux is case-sensitive. Notes.txt and notes.txt are different files, and LS is not a command.
  • Copy-pasting commands you do not understand into a server. Read each one first; use the command guide boxes and --help.
  • Looking for an "Undo". The shell has no recycle bin. Practise in a throwaway folder.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Linux is a kernel. A distribution packages it. The shell reads your commands in a terminal.
  • On Windows, WSL gives you a real Linux prompt.
  • Commands look like command -options arguments. pwd, ls, whoami and echo are your first four.
  • Use --help, man, Tab and the up arrow constantly.

Check yourself

Linux · Lesson 2

Files and directories

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • picture the Linux directory tree and name the important folders
  • tell absolute paths from relative paths and move around with cd
  • create, copy, move and delete files and folders
  • use wildcards to act on many files at once

One tree, no drive letters

Windows has C: and D:. Linux has a single tree that starts at the root, written /. Other disks are attached ("mounted") onto folders in that tree. Everything, including devices and running programs, appears as a file or folder somewhere in it. The standard layout is the same on almost every distribution, so learn it once:

FolderWhat lives thereEnterprise Vault connection
/homeeach user's personal files (/home/student)your scripts and notes
/etcsystem and application configuration fileswhere settings of Linux services live
/var/loglog filesthe first place to look when something breaks
/var/libprograms' saved data (databases and so on)where a database keeps its files
/tmptemporary files, cleared oftenscratch space
/usrinstalled programs and libraries
/bin, /usr/binthe commands you run
/optoptional add-on softwarevendor products often install here
/proc, /sys, /devlive views of the kernel, hardware and devices
/rootthe home of the administrator account

Your home directory is written ~. This lesson works in a small pretend server folder:

Real output
$ pwd
/home/student/lab
$ ls
docs
ev
$ ls ev
archive
config
logs
scripts
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
pwd

What it does: Prints the full path of the folder you are in ("print working directory").

When to use it: When you are lost, or before running something destructive, to be sure where you are.

ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

Paths: where is it?

A path is the address of a file or folder.

  • An absolute path starts with / and works from anywhere: /home/student/lab/ev/logs/indexing.log.
  • A relative path does not start with /. It is measured from where you are now: ev/logs/indexing.log.

Three special names help: . is "here", .. is "the parent folder", and ~ is your home. cd ("change directory") moves you around:

Real output
$ cd ev/logs
$ pwd
/home/student/lab/ev/logs
$ cd ..
$ pwd
/home/student/lab/ev
$ cd ../docs
$ pwd
/home/student/lab/docs
$ cd -
/home/student/lab/ev
$ pwd
/home/student/lab/ev
$ cd ~
$ pwd
/home/student
$ cd ~/lab
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

Open the full command reference

cd - jumps back to where you just were. cd with no argument goes home.

Tip

Quote or escape file names that contain spaces: cd "My Documents". Better still, avoid spaces in names you create. Use - or _.

Looking around

Real output
$ ls -l --time-style=long-iso ev
total 16
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 archive
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 config
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 logs
drwxr-xr-x 2 student student 4096 2026-01-15 09:00 scripts
$ ls -a
.
..
docs
ev
$ ls -R docs ev/config
docs:
notes.txt
readme.txt

ev/config:
evault.conf
$ ls -lh --time-style=long-iso ev/logs
total 8.0K
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 716 2026-01-15 09:00 indexing.log
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 297 2026-01-15 09:00 storage.log
  • -l long format: permissions, owner, size, date, name.
  • -a all files, including hidden ones that start with a dot.
  • -h human-readable sizes (K, M, G), used with -l.
  • -R recursive: go into sub-folders.

file tells you what kind of file something is, and stat shows everything the system knows about it:

Real output
$ file ev/config/evault.conf ev/scripts/check.sh
ev/config/evault.conf: ASCII text
ev/scripts/check.sh:   Bourne-Again shell script, ASCII text executable
$ stat -c '%n  size=%s bytes  owner=%U' ev/config/evault.conf
ev/config/evault.conf  size=146 bytes  owner=student
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
file

What it does: Guesses what kind of data a file contains (text, script, image, executable).

When to use it: Identifying an unknown file that has no useful extension.

stat

What it does: Shows detailed information about a file: size, permissions, owner, times, inode.

When to use it: Checking exact permissions in octal, or the last modification time.

-c '%a %U %n' custom format (octal permissions, owner, name)

Open the full command reference

Creating things

Real output
$ mkdir reports
$ mkdir -p reports/2026/september
$ touch reports/2026/september/summary.txt
$ ls -R reports
reports:
2026

reports/2026:
september

reports/2026/september:
summary.txt
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

Open the full command reference

  • mkdir makes a folder. mkdir -p also makes any missing parent folders, and does not complain if the folder already exists.
  • touch creates an empty file (or updates the timestamp of an existing one).

Copying, moving, renaming

Real output
$ cp docs/notes.txt docs/notes-backup.txt
$ cp -r ev/config reports/config-copy
$ mv docs/notes-backup.txt reports/
$ mv reports/notes-backup.txt reports/backup-notes.txt
$ ls docs reports
docs:
notes.txt
readme.txt

reports:
2026
backup-notes.txt
config-copy
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
cp

What it does: Copies files or folders.

When to use it: Making a backup copy before you edit a file.

-r copy folders recursively-a preserve permissions, owners and times-i ask before overwriting-v show what was copied
mv

What it does: Moves or renames files and folders.

When to use it: Renaming a file, or moving it to another folder (the same command does both).

-i ask before overwriting-n never overwrite

Open the full command reference

  • cp source destination copies. Use -r (recursive) for folders.
  • mv source destination moves, and renaming is just moving to a new name.

Deleting (carefully)

Real output
$ rm reports/backup-notes.txt
$ rm -r reports/config-copy
$ rmdir reports/2026/september 2>&1 | head -1
rmdir: failed to remove 'reports/2026/september': Directory not empty
$ ls -R reports
reports:
2026

reports/2026:
september

reports/2026/september:
summary.txt
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

rmdir

What it does: Removes an empty folder.

When to use it: Safe clean-up: it refuses to delete a folder that still has files.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

  • rm removes files, rm -r removes a folder and everything in it, and rmdir only removes empty folders (it refused above because the folder still has summary.txt).
  • There is no undo and no recycle bin.
The most dangerous habit

Never run rm -rf with a path you have not looked at, and never paste a delete command you do not understand. A stray space, as in rm -rf / home/student, deletes the whole system. Before deleting with a wildcard, run the same command with ls first to see exactly what it matches. Use rm -i to be asked before each deletion.

Wildcards: acting on many files

The shell expands patterns before running the command:

PatternMatches
*any run of characters (including none)
?exactly one character
[abc]one character from the list
{a,b}either word (brace expansion)
Real output
$ ls ev/logs/*.log
ev/logs/indexing.log
ev/logs/storage.log
$ ls docs/n*
docs/notes.txt
$ ls docs/?otes.txt
docs/notes.txt
$ ls ev/{logs,config}
ev/config:
evault.conf

ev/logs:
indexing.log
storage.log
$ echo ev/logs/*.log
ev/logs/indexing.log ev/logs/storage.log
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

The last line shows what really happens: echo receives the already-expanded list of file names. The command never sees the *.

Finding a file you cannot remember

Real output
$ find . -name "*.log"
./ev/logs/storage.log
./ev/logs/indexing.log
$ find . -type d
.
./ev
./ev/config
./ev/scripts
./ev/logs
./ev/archive
./reports
./reports/2026
./reports/2026/september
./docs
$ find . -name "*.conf" -o -name "*.sh"
./ev/config/evault.conf
./ev/scripts/check.sh
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
find

What it does: Searches a folder tree for files by name, type, size, age and more, and can run a command on each match.

When to use it: Locating a file, finding large or old files, cleaning up logs older than N days.

-name "*.log" match by name-type f/d files or directories-mtime +7 modified more than 7 days ago-size +100M bigger than 100 MB-exec CMD {} \ run a command on every match

Open the full command reference

find where -name pattern searches the folder and everything below it. -type d finds only directories, -type f only files.

  2. Copy ev/logs into practice/ and rename the copy logs-old.
  3. Use find to list every file whose name ends in .log. How many are there?
  4. Before deleting practice, list what is inside with ls -R practice. Then remove it.
