Worked answers and common mistakes

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ rm -rf practice
$ mkdir practice
$ touch practice/{a,b,c}.txt
$ ls practice
a.txt
b.txt
c.txt
$ echo "--- 2: copy a folder and rename the copy"
--- 2: copy a folder and rename the copy
$ cp -r ev/logs practice/
$ mv practice/logs practice/logs-old
$ ls practice
a.txt
b.txt
c.txt
logs-old
$ echo "--- 3: how many .log files exist under ev?"
--- 3: how many .log files exist under ev?
$ find ev -name "*.log" | wc -l
2
$ echo "--- 4: look before you delete"
--- 4: look before you delete
$ ls -R practice
practice:
a.txt
b.txt
c.txt
logs-old

practice/logs-old:
indexing.log
storage.log
$ rm -r practice
$ ls practice 2>&1 | head -1
ls: cannot access 'practice': No such file or directory
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

cp -r is needed to copy a folder (recursive). {a,b,c} is brace expansion: the shell turns it into three names before touch runs. ls -R before rm -r is the habit that prevents disasters.

Common mistakes
  • rm -rf with a typo or an empty variable. rm -rf $DIR/ with DIR unset becomes rm -rf /. Always ls first; quote variables.
  • cp without -r on a folder ("omitting directory").
  • Unquoted file names with spaces. rm my file.txt tries to delete two files called my and file.txt. Quote: rm "my file.txt".
  • Using mv to "copy". It removes the original.
  • Wildcard surprises. rm *.log deletes in the current folder only; check what ls *.log matches first.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • One tree starting at /. /etc is configuration, /var/log is logs, /home is people's files.
  • Absolute paths start with /. Relative paths do not. . is here, .. is the parent, ~ is home.
  • mkdir -p, touch, cp -r, mv (also renames), rm -r (permanent!).
  • Wildcards * ? [] {} are expanded by the shell before the command runs. Use find to search.

Check yourself

Linux · Lesson 3

Reading files, redirection and pipes

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read files of any size with cat, less, head and tail
  • watch a log grow with tail -f
  • send output to files with > and >>, and separate errors from output
  • connect commands with pipes

Seeing what is inside a file

Real output
$ cat docs/readme.txt
Welcome to the EV01 lab
$ cat ev/config/evault.conf
# Enterprise Vault server settings (pretend)
server_name = EV01
sql_server = SQL01
indexing_enabled = true
max_index_threads = 4
log_level = info
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

Open the full command reference

cat prints a whole file. For a big file that scrolls past too fast, use something smarter:

CommandUse
head -n 5 filethe first 5 lines (default 10)
tail -n 5 filethe last 5 lines
less filepage through a file. Space = next page, b = back, /word = search, q = quit
wc -l filecount lines (-w words, -c bytes)
nl fileprint with line numbers
Real output
$ head -n 3 ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:10:02 INFO  Indexing service started
2026-09-30 09:10:05 INFO  Connected to SQL01
2026-09-30 09:11:40 INFO  Indexed 1200 items
$ tail -n 3 ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
$ wc -l ev/logs/indexing.log ev/logs/storage.log
  14 ev/logs/indexing.log
   5 ev/logs/storage.log
  19 total
$ nl -ba ev/config/evault.conf | head -4
     1	# Enterprise Vault server settings (pretend)
     2	server_name = EV01
     3	sql_server = SQL01
     4	indexing_enabled = true
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes
nl

What it does: Prints a file with line numbers.

When to use it: Referring to specific lines of a file.

Open the full command reference

Logs are written at the end of a file, so tail is the engineer's most-used reading command.

Watching a log live

tail -f file shows the last lines and then keeps waiting, printing new lines as they arrive. Stop it with Ctrl+C. Here is a controlled demonstration: a background job appends two lines to a log while tail -f watches (the timeout stops it after three seconds):

Real output
$ touch live.log
$ (sleep 1; echo "09:30 INFO service ready" >> live.log; sleep 1; echo "09:31 ERROR disk full" >> live.log) &
$ timeout 3 tail -f live.log
09:30 INFO service ready
09:31 ERROR disk full
$ wait
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

wait

What it does: Waits for background jobs to finish.

When to use it: In scripts, after starting several jobs with &.

Open the full command reference

In real work: tail -f /var/log/something.log while you reproduce a problem is the fastest way to see what the system says at the moment it fails. tail -F also copes with logs that are rotated (replaced by a new file).

Redirection: sending output somewhere else

Every command has three standard streams:

StreamNumberDefault destinationMeaning
stdin0keyboardinput
stdout1screennormal output
stderr2screenerror messages

Redirection changes where they go:

SyntaxMeaning
cmd > filesend stdout to a file, overwriting it
cmd >> fileappend stdout to a file
cmd 2> filesend stderr to a file
cmd > file 2>&1send both to the same file
cmd < fileread stdin from a file
cmd > /dev/nullthrow output away
Real output
$ echo "first line" > notes.txt
$ echo "second line" >> notes.txt
$ cat notes.txt
first line
second line
$ echo "this overwrites" > notes.txt
$ cat notes.txt
this overwrites

Stdout and stderr are different streams, which is why errors still appear on screen when you redirect normal output:

Real output
$ ls docs nosuchfolder > out.txt
ls: cannot access 'nosuchfolder': No such file or directory
$ echo "---- out.txt contains:"
---- out.txt contains:
$ cat out.txt
docs:
notes.txt
readme.txt
$ ls docs nosuchfolder > out.txt 2> err.txt
$ echo "---- err.txt contains:"
---- err.txt contains:
$ cat err.txt
ls: cannot access 'nosuchfolder': No such file or directory
$ ls nosuchfolder 2>/dev/null; echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 2
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

Notice $?: the exit code of the last command. 0 means success, anything else means failure. Scripts and pipelines rely on it.

Careful

> silently destroys the old contents of the target file. sort data.txt > data.txt empties your file before sort reads it. When unsure, write to a new file, or use >>.

Pipes: the idea that makes Linux powerful

A pipe | connects the output of one command to the input of the next. Each command does one small job, and you build bigger jobs by chaining them:

Real output
$ cat ev/logs/indexing.log | grep ERROR
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
$ cat ev/logs/indexing.log | grep ERROR | wc -l
5
$ tail -n 4 ev/logs/indexing.log | head -n 2
2026-09-30 11:05:00 INFO  Indexed 3400 items
2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
$ ls ev/logs | wc -l
2
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Read the second line left to right: take the log, keep only the lines containing ERROR, count them. You will use this pattern all the time (grep gets its own lesson next).

You can send the result of a pipeline to a file at the end, and tee lets you see the output and save it at the same time:

Real output
$ grep ERROR ev/logs/indexing.log | tee errors.txt | wc -l
5
$ cat errors.txt
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
tee

What it does: Copies its input to both the screen and a file.

When to use it: Saving output while still watching it; with sudo it lets you write to a protected file (echo x | sudo tee file).

-a append instead of overwrite

Open the full command reference

A small editor, so you are never stuck

You will eventually need to edit a config file in the terminal. Two editors are everywhere:

  • nano: easy. It lists its commands at the bottom (^O = write out/save with Ctrl+O, ^X = exit).
  • vi / vim: powerful and always installed, but confusing at first. The survival kit: press i to start typing, press Esc when finished, then type :wq and Enter to save and quit, or :q! and Enter to quit without saving.
Example output (not run here)
$ nano ev/config/evault.conf
(an editor opens; edit, then Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X)
$ vi ev/config/evault.conf
(press i to insert, Esc, then :wq to save and quit)
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
nano

What it does: A simple terminal text editor.

When to use it: Editing a file on a server. Ctrl+O saves, Ctrl+X exits.

vi

What it does: A powerful terminal text editor found on every Linux server.

When to use it: Editing files when nothing else is installed. Press i to type, Esc then :wq to save and quit, :q! to quit without saving.

Open the full command reference

Enterprise Vault connection

"Send me the last 200 lines of the log, with just the errors" becomes tail -n 200 indexing.log | grep ERROR > errors.txt. Three small tools, one pipe, one redirect.

Your turn
  1. Show lines 5 to 8 of ev/logs/indexing.log using only head and tail and a pipe. (Hint: the first 8 lines, then the last 4 of those.)
  2. Count how many lines in storage.log contain the word WARN.
  3. Run a command that produces an error and write only the error to a file called problems.txt.

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "--- 1: lines 5 to 8 (first 8 lines, then the last 4 of those)"
--- 1: lines 5 to 8 (first 8 lines, then the last 4 of those)
$ head -n 8 ev/logs/indexing.log | tail -n 4
2026-09-30 09:12:19 WARN  Retrying connection, attempt 1
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 09:13:01 INFO  Indexing service stopped
$ echo "--- 2: WARN lines in storage.log"
--- 2: WARN lines in storage.log
$ grep -c WARN ev/logs/storage.log
1
$ echo "--- 3: send only the error output to a file"
--- 3: send only the error output to a file
$ ls /nonexistent 2> problems.txt
$ cat problems.txt
ls: cannot access '/nonexistent': No such file or directory
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

Open the full command reference

Redirection summary: > writes standard output to a file (overwriting), >> appends, 2> writes error output (stream 2), and 2>&1 merges errors into the normal output. In command1 | command2 only the standard output flows through the pipe; errors still go to the screen unless you add 2>&1.

Common mistakes
  • > instead of >>. echo x > log.txt erases the file first. Use >> to add.
  • Reading and writing the same file in one command. sort file > file empties it before sort reads it. Write to a new file, then move it.
  • Expecting errors to go through a pipe. Add 2>&1 if you want them captured.
  • cat file | grep x works, but grep x file is simpler and faster (no useless cat).
  • Using tail -f on a log inside a script and wondering why it never finishes: it follows forever by design.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • cat (all), head (start), tail (end), less (page), wc (count). tail -f follows a live log.
  • Redirection: > overwrite, >> append, 2> errors, /dev/null bin. Exit code 0 means success.
  • A pipe | feeds one command's output into the next. Small tools plus pipes beat big programs.
  • Know one editor: nano for ease, vi for survival.

Check yourself

Linux · Lesson 4

Searching and processing text

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • find lines with grep, including patterns, context and counts
  • summarise data with sort, uniq, cut and awk
  • change text with sed and tr
  • build a real log-analysis pipeline for Enterprise Vault logs

Why text tools matter

Almost everything on Linux is plain text: logs, configuration, command output. So a toolbox of small text programs, chained with pipes (last lesson), solves a surprising range of problems. Our sample log has this shape (date, time, level, message):

Real output
$ head -n 4 ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:10:02 INFO  Indexing service started
2026-09-30 09:10:05 INFO  Connected to SQL01
2026-09-30 09:11:40 INFO  Indexed 1200 items
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

grep: find lines

grep pattern file prints lines that contain the pattern.

Real output
$ grep ERROR ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
$ grep -c ERROR ev/logs/indexing.log
5
$ grep -n "SQL01" ev/logs/indexing.log
2:2026-09-30 09:10:05 INFO  Connected to SQL01
4:2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
6:2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
10:2026-09-30 11:02:14 INFO  Connected to SQL01
12:2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
13:2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
$ grep -i "warn" ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:12:19 WARN  Retrying connection, attempt 1
2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
$ grep -v INFO ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:19 WARN  Retrying connection, attempt 1
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

OptionMeaning
-iignore case
-nshow line numbers
-ccount matching lines
-vinvert: show lines that do not match
-rsearch folders recursively
-wmatch whole words only
-Eextended patterns (`a\b, +, ?`)
-A n / -B nalso show n lines After / Before each match
Real output
$ grep -A1 "connection timeout" ev/logs/indexing.log
2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:19 WARN  Retrying connection, attempt 1
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
$ grep -E "WARN|ERROR" ev/logs/storage.log
2026-09-30 10:15:44 WARN  Vault store 1 is 91 percent full
2026-09-30 11:20:09 ERROR Vault store 1 write failed: disk full
$ grep -r "SQL01" ev/
ev/config/evault.conf:sql_server = SQL01
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 09:10:05 INFO  Connected to SQL01
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 11:02:14 INFO  Connected to SQL01
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
ev/logs/indexing.log:2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
$ grep -l "disk full" ev/logs/*
ev/logs/storage.log

-A/-B (context) are gold when diagnosing: the line after an error often says what the system did next. -l lists only the names of files that contain a match.

sort, uniq and counting

sort orders lines, and uniq -c counts adjacent repeated lines, which is why you sort first. The classic pattern sort | uniq -c | sort -rn means "count how often each distinct line occurs, most frequent first".

Real output
$ cut -d' ' -f3 ev/logs/indexing.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      7 INFO
      5 ERROR
      2 WARN
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
uniq

What it does: Collapses repeated adjacent lines; with -c it counts them.

When to use it: Counting how often something occurs: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn.

-c prefix lines with counts-d show only duplicated lines

Open the full command reference

Here cut -d' ' -f3 takes the third space-separated column (the level). Counting what happens most often is the first step in understanding any log.

sort options: -n numeric, -r reverse, -k2 sort by the 2nd column, -u unique.

cut and awk: pick columns

cut is simple. awk is a tiny programming language for columns. It splits each line into fields $1, $2, ... ($0 is the whole line):

Real output
$ awk '{print $3, $4}' ev/logs/storage.log
INFO Storage
INFO Archived
WARN Vault
INFO Archived
ERROR Vault
$ awk '$3 == "ERROR" {print $2, $5}' ev/logs/indexing.log
09:12:18 connection
09:12:34 connection
09:12:35 task
12:15:41 resolution
12:15:42 task
$ awk '{count[$3]++} END {for (l in count) print l, count[l]}' ev/logs/indexing.log | sort
ERROR 5
INFO 7
WARN 2
$ awk '/Indexed/ {sum += $5} END {print "items indexed:", sum}' ev/logs/indexing.log
items indexed: 4600
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
for

What it does: A loop that repeats commands once for each item in a list.

When to use it: Doing the same thing to several files, servers or numbers: for h in ev01 sql01; do ...; done.

Open the full command reference

Read the third example: for every line add one to a counter keyed by the level, and at the end print the counters. The fourth adds up the numbers on lines mentioning "Indexed". awk is worth learning slowly, because it replaces many small scripts.

sed and tr: change text

sed edits text as it flows past. The most useful form is substitution, s/old/new/:

Real output
$ sed 's/SQL01/SQL-PRIMARY/' ev/config/evault.conf
# Enterprise Vault server settings (pretend)
server_name = EV01
sql_server = SQL-PRIMARY
indexing_enabled = true
max_index_threads = 4
log_level = info
$ sed -n '2,4p' ev/config/evault.conf
server_name = EV01
sql_server = SQL01
indexing_enabled = true
$ sed '/^#/d' ev/config/evault.conf
server_name = EV01
sql_server = SQL01
indexing_enabled = true
max_index_threads = 4
log_level = info
$ echo "ev01 is up" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
EV01 IS UP
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

tr

What it does: Translates or deletes single characters.

When to use it: Converting case (tr a-z A-Z), squeezing spaces, or turning separators into newlines.

-d delete the characters-s squeeze repeats into one

Open the full command reference

  • sed 's/old/new/' replaces the first match on each line (s/old/new/g replaces all).
  • sed -n '2,4p' prints only lines 2 to 4.
  • sed '/^#/d' deletes lines that start with # (comments).
  • tr translates characters.

By default sed prints the result and leaves the file alone. sed -i edits the file in place. Take a backup first (sed -i.bak ...).

find: search by properties

grep searches inside files. find searches for the files themselves, by name, type, size or age, and can act on them:

Real output
$ find ev -name "*.log"
ev/logs/storage.log
ev/logs/indexing.log
$ find ev -type f -size -300c
ev/config/evault.conf
ev/scripts/check.sh
ev/logs/storage.log
$ find ev -name "*.log" -exec wc -l {} \;
5 ev/logs/storage.log
14 ev/logs/indexing.log
$ find ev -type f -newermt "2026-01-01" | sort
ev/config/evault.conf
ev/logs/indexing.log
ev/logs/storage.log
ev/scripts/check.sh
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
find

What it does: Searches a folder tree for files by name, type, size, age and more, and can run a command on each match.

When to use it: Locating a file, finding large or old files, cleaning up logs older than N days.

-name "*.log" match by name-type f/d files or directories-mtime +7 modified more than 7 days ago-size +100M bigger than 100 MB-exec CMD {} \ run a command on every match

Open the full command reference

-exec command {} \; runs the command on each match ({} stands for the file). A tidier alternative for many files is xargs, which turns lines into arguments:

Real output
$ find ev -name "*.log" | sort | xargs grep -c ERROR
ev/logs/indexing.log:5
ev/logs/storage.log:1

A real analysis: what went wrong, and when?

Put the tools together to answer questions about the Enterprise Vault logs.

Q1. What are the distinct error messages, and how often does each occur?

Real output
$ grep ERROR ev/logs/indexing.log | cut -d' ' -f4- | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      2 SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
      2 Indexing task aborted
      1 Name resolution failed for SQL01

Q2. At which hours did errors occur? (cut -c12-13 takes characters 12 to 13 of each line, the hour.)

Real output
$ grep ERROR ev/logs/*.log | cut -d: -f2,3 | cut -c12-13 | sort | uniq -c
      3 09
      1 11
      2 12

Q3. Which problems repeat across services?

Real output
$ grep -h ERROR ev/logs/*.log | awk '{print $5, $6}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
      2 task aborted
      2 connection timeout
      1 store 1
      1 resolution failed

Within a minute you can tell the story: SQL connection timeouts first, then a name-resolution failure, and a full storage volume at another time. These are the same three causes the AI agent in the earlier chapters investigated.

Enterprise Vault connection

The diagnostic agent you designed gathers evidence with read-only tools such as get_event_logs. On a Linux-hosted component, that tool is this pipeline: grep, cut, sort, uniq. Knowing the commands means you can check the agent's evidence yourself.

Your turn
  1. Count how many lines in indexing.log do not contain INFO.
  2. Print only the times (second column) of the Indexing service started events.
  3. Replace max_index_threads = 4 with max_index_threads = 8 in a copy of the config using sed, and show the result.
  4. Find the five longest lines in a file: awk '{print length, $0}' file | sort -rn | head -5.

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "--- 1: lines without INFO"
--- 1: lines without INFO
$ grep -vc INFO ev/logs/indexing.log
7
$ echo "--- 2: the times of the 'started' events"
--- 2: the times of the 'started' events
$ grep "service started" ev/logs/indexing.log | awk '{print $2}'
09:10:02
11:02:10
$ echo "--- 3: edit a COPY of the config with sed"
--- 3: edit a COPY of the config with sed
$ cp ev/config/evault.conf /tmp/evault-copy.conf
$ sed 's/max_index_threads = 4/max_index_threads = 8/' /tmp/evault-copy.conf | grep max_index
max_index_threads = 8
$ diff ev/config/evault.conf /tmp/evault-copy.conf && echo "(the copy is unchanged because we did not use -i)"
(the copy is unchanged because we did not use -i)
$ echo "--- 4: the five longest lines"
--- 4: the five longest lines
$ awk '{print length, $0}' ev/logs/indexing.log | sort -rn | head -5 | cut -c1-70
58 2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
56 2026-09-30 11:40:22 WARN  Name resolution slow for SQL01
56 2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
56 2026-09-30 09:12:19 WARN  Retrying connection, attempt 1
56 2026-09-30 09:12:18 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cp

What it does: Copies files or folders.

When to use it: Making a backup copy before you edit a file.

-r copy folders recursively-a preserve permissions, owners and times-i ask before overwriting-v show what was copied
diff

What it does: Compares two files (or folders with -r) and shows the differences.

When to use it: Checking what changed between two versions of a config, or confirming a restored copy is identical.

-r compare folders-u unified format (the same used by git diff)

Open the full command reference

Notice that sed without -i only prints the edited text; the file is untouched. That is the safe way to rehearse an edit. When you are happy, add -i (and keep a backup with -i.bak).

Common mistakes
  • grep pattern treated as a regular expression. grep 1.5 file also matches 105. Use grep -F for literal text or escape the dot.
  • uniq without sort. uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates. Always sort | uniq -c.
  • Quoting. Single quotes '...' stop the shell touching $ and *; awk programs and regexes usually need them.
  • sed -i on the only copy of a file. Test without -i, or keep a backup.
  • Counting fields wrongly in awk. $1 is the first field; $0 is the whole line; the default separator is any run of spaces, so -F matters for CSV.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • grep finds lines (-i -n -c -v -r -E -A -B -l). find finds files.
  • sort | uniq -c | sort -rn counts and ranks. cut and awk select columns. sed and tr change text.
  • Chain small tools with pipes to answer questions about logs.

Check yourself

Linux · Lesson 5

Users, groups and permissions

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read the permission string in ls -l
  • change permissions with chmod (symbolic and octal) and ownership with chown
  • explain users, groups, root and sudo
  • set up a shared folder for a team

Who are you?

Every process and every file belongs to a user and a group. Users have a numeric user ID (UID); groups have a GID. The special user root (UID 0) can do anything, so people use it as rarely as possible.

Real output
$ id
uid=30033(student) gid=30033(student) groups=30033(student),996(docker)
$ whoami
student
$ groups
student docker
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
id

What it does: Shows your numeric user ID (uid), primary group ID (gid) and all groups you belong to.

When to use it: Diagnosing "permission denied" problems: check whether the user is in the group that owns the file.

-un only the user name-gn only the primary group name-G all group IDs
whoami

What it does: Prints the name of the user you are currently logged in as.

When to use it: After switching accounts or using sudo, to confirm who you are before changing anything.

groups

What it does: Lists the groups a user belongs to.

When to use it: Quick check of group membership, for example before using a shared folder or the docker group.

Open the full command reference

User accounts live in /etc/passwd, groups in /etc/group. (Despite the name, passwords are not in /etc/passwd; hashed passwords are in /etc/shadow, readable only by root.)

Real output
$ grep '^student' /etc/passwd
student:x:30033:30033::/home/student:/bin/bash
$ stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' /etc/shadow /etc/passwd
-rw-r----- root:shadow /etc/shadow
-rw-r--r-- root:root /etc/passwd
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

stat

What it does: Shows detailed information about a file: size, permissions, owner, times, inode.

When to use it: Checking exact permissions in octal, or the last modification time.

-c '%a %U %n' custom format (octal permissions, owner, name)

Open the full command reference

Reading permissions

The first column of ls -l is the permission string:

Real output
$ ls -l --time-style=long-iso ev/config/evault.conf ev/scripts/check.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 146 2026-01-15 09:00 ev/config/evault.conf
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student  33 2026-01-15 09:00 ev/scripts/check.sh
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

Take -rw-r--r-- apart, ten characters:

PositionMeaning
1type: - file, d directory, l link
2 to 4owner permissions: rw-
5 to 7group permissions: r--
8 to 10others (everyone else): r--

And the three letters:

LetterOn a fileOn a directory
r readview contentslist names inside
w writechange contentscreate, rename and delete files inside
x executerun as a programenter it (cd) and reach what is inside

So -rw-r--r-- means: the owner can read and write, the group can only read, everyone else can only read.

chmod: change permissions

Two notations. Symbolic: who (u owner, g group, o others, a all), an operator (+ add, - remove, = set), and the permissions.

Real output
$ ls -l ev/scripts/check.sh
-rw-r--r-- 1 student student 33 Jan 15  2026 ev/scripts/check.sh
$ ./ev/scripts/check.sh 2>&1 | head -1
bash: line 69: ./ev/scripts/check.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod u+x ev/scripts/check.sh
$ ls -l ev/scripts/check.sh
-rwxr--r-- 1 student student 33 Jan 15  2026 ev/scripts/check.sh
$ ./ev/scripts/check.sh
checking EV01
$ chmod go-r ev/config/evault.conf
$ ls -l ev/config/evault.conf
-rw------- 1 student student 146 Jan 15  2026 ev/config/evault.conf
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

Open the full command reference

The first attempt failed with "Permission denied" because the script had no x. After chmod u+x it ran.

Octal notation writes each trio as one digit, adding r=4, w=2, x=1:

DigitMeaningDigitMeaning
7rwx (4+2+1)3-wx (2+1)
6rw- (4+2)2-w-
5r-x (4+1)1--x
4r--0---

So 755 is rwxr-xr-x (a typical program), 644 is rw-r--r-- (a typical file), and 600 is rw------- (private).

Real output
$ chmod 644 ev/config/evault.conf
$ stat -c '%a %A %n' ev/config/evault.conf
644 -rw-r--r-- ev/config/evault.conf
$ chmod 600 ev/config/evault.conf
$ stat -c '%a %A %n' ev/config/evault.conf
600 -rw------- ev/config/evault.conf
$ chmod -R 750 ev/scripts
$ stat -c '%a %A %n' ev/scripts ev/scripts/check.sh
750 drwxr-x--- ev/scripts
750 -rwxr-x--- ev/scripts/check.sh

Try the calculator to build permission strings both ways:

Ownership: chown and chgrp

chown user:group file changes who owns a file. Only root can give files away, so you normally use sudo.

Real output
$ sudo chown root:root ev/config/evault.conf
$ ls -l ev/config/evault.conf
-rw------- 1 root root 146 Jan 15  2026 ev/config/evault.conf
$ sudo chown student:student ev/config/evault.conf
$ ls -l ev/config/evault.conf
-rw------- 1 student student 146 Jan 15  2026 ev/config/evault.conf
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
chown

What it does: Changes the owner (and optionally the group) of files.

When to use it: A service cannot write to its folder because it belongs to another user.

user:group set both-R recursive

Open the full command reference

sudo: borrowing root, briefly

sudo command runs one command with administrator rights, after checking that you are allowed (it is configured in /etc/sudoers). It is better than logging in as root, because only the commands you choose get the power, and each use is logged.

Real output
$ whoami
student
$ sudo whoami
root
$ sudo cat /etc/shadow | head -c 0; echo "(read a root-only file: allowed with sudo)"
(read a root-only file: allowed with sudo)
$ cat /etc/shadow
cat: /etc/shadow: Permission denied
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

read

What it does: Reads a line of input into a variable.

When to use it: Asking the user for input in a script, or processing a file line by line (while read line).

Open the full command reference

Careful

Run only commands you understand with sudo. Never paste sudo commands from the internet that you cannot read. A mistake with root rights can break the whole machine.

Groups and shared folders

Suppose two engineers, alice and bob, must both work in an evteam shared folder, while nobody else may enter. The recipe: create a group, add the users, give the folder to the group, and set permissions.

Real output
$ sudo userdel -r alice 2>/dev/null; sudo userdel -r bob 2>/dev/null; sudo groupdel evteam 2>/dev/null || true
$ sudo groupadd evteam
$ sudo useradd -m -G evteam alice
$ sudo useradd -m -G evteam bob
$ sudo mkdir /srv/evshared
$ sudo chgrp evteam /srv/evshared
$ sudo chmod 2770 /srv/evshared
$ stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' /srv/evshared
drwxrws--- root:evteam /srv/evshared
$ sudo -u alice bash -c 'echo "from alice" > /srv/evshared/a.txt'
$ sudo -u bob bash -c 'cat /srv/evshared/a.txt'
from alice
$ sudo -u bob stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' /srv/evshared/a.txt
-rw-rw-r-- alice:evteam /srv/evshared/a.txt
$ echo "--- and you (not in evteam):"
--- and you (not in evteam):
$ cat /srv/evshared/a.txt
cat: /srv/evshared/a.txt: Permission denied
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
userdel

What it does: Deletes a user account.

When to use it: Removing an account that is no longer needed.

-r also remove the home folder
groupdel

What it does: Deletes a group.

When to use it: Cleaning up a group you no longer use.

groupadd

What it does: Creates a new group.

When to use it: Setting up a group for shared access before adding users.

useradd

What it does: Creates a new user account.

When to use it: Adding a person or service account to a server.

-m create a home folder-G group add to extra groups-s SHELL login shell-r system account
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
chgrp

What it does: Changes the group that owns a file or folder.

When to use it: Setting up a shared folder for a team.

Open the full command reference

Why 2770? The leading 2 is the setgid bit: new files created inside inherit the folder's group (evteam), so teammates can always work on each other's files. The 770 gives the owner and group full access and everyone else nothing. Other special bits: setuid (4, run as the file's owner, as passwd does) and the sticky bit (1, in folders like /tmp, so users can delete only their own files).

Real output
$ stat -c '%A %n' /tmp
drwxrwxrwt /tmp
$ sudo rm -rf /srv/evshared
$ sudo userdel -r alice 2>/dev/null; sudo userdel -r bob 2>/dev/null; sudo groupdel evteam
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

(The last line tidies up the demonstration accounts.) The t at the end of /tmp's permissions is the sticky bit.

umask: the default permissions

New files do not start at 777. A umask removes permissions from the defaults (666 for files, 777 for folders). A umask of 022 removes write from group and others, giving 644 files and 755 folders.

Real output
$ umask
0022
$ touch f1 && mkdir d1 && stat -c '%a %n' f1 d1
644 f1
755 d1
$ umask 077
$ touch f2 && mkdir d2 && stat -c '%a %n' f2 d2
600 f2
700 d2
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
umask

What it does: Shows or sets the default permissions removed from newly created files.

When to use it: Making sure new files are private (umask 077) or group-writable (umask 002).

touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

Open the full command reference

Enterprise Vault connection

Two classic causes of "it works for me but not for the service": the service account lacks read access to a config file or write access to a log folder. ls -l and id service-account tell you in seconds. On Windows the same ideas appear as NTFS permissions and service accounts, so the thinking transfers.

Your turn
  1. Create a file secret.txt. Make it readable and writable only by you. Check with stat.
  2. Make a script that prints a message, make it executable, and run it.
  3. What octal mode is rwxr-x---? What is rw-rw-r--?
  4. Look at ls -l /usr/bin/passwd. Which special character appears in the owner's execute position, and why does passwd need it?

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "--- 1: a private file"
--- 1: a private file
$ echo "top secret" > secret.txt
$ chmod 600 secret.txt
$ stat -c '%a %A %n' secret.txt
600 -rw------- secret.txt
$ echo "--- 2: make a script executable and run it"
--- 2: make a script executable and run it
$ printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "hello from my script"\n' > hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh 2>&1 | head -1
bash: line 210: ./hello.sh: Permission denied
$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh
hello from my script
$ echo "--- 3: octal values (r=4, w=2, x=1)"
--- 3: octal values (r=4, w=2, x=1)
$ python3 -c "
> def octal(s): return ''.join(str(sum(v for c, v in zip(s[i:i+3], (4,2,1)) if c != '-')) for i in (0,3,6))
> for s in ('rwxr-x---', 'rw-rw-r--'): print(s, '=', octal(s))"
rwxr-x--- = 750
rw-rw-r-- = 664
$ echo "--- 4: the special character on passwd"
--- 4: the special character on passwd
$ ls -l /usr/bin/passwd | cut -c1-10
-rwsr-xr-x
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

Answers: rwxr-x--- is 750; rw-rw-r-- is 664. The first attempt to run hello.sh failed ("Permission denied") until chmod +x. In task 4 the owner's execute position shows s: the setuid bit. passwd must edit /etc/shadow, which only root may write, so the program runs as its owner (root) whoever starts it; that is a controlled, deliberate exception.

Common mistakes
  • chmod 777 to "fix" a permission error. It lets everyone modify the file. Find who needs what and grant exactly that (a group, or 750/640).
  • Forgetting that folders need x. To enter a folder you need execute permission on it.
  • Running everything with sudo. Files created as root later cannot be edited by your user; use sudo only for the one command.
  • Secrets world-readable. Private keys and password files should be 600; SSH refuses keys that are not.
  • Confusing user, group and others in chmod g+w versus chmod o+w.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Every file has an owner, a group and permissions for owner, group, others: read 4, write 2, execute 1.
  • chmod changes permissions (u+x, 755). chown changes owner. sudo runs one command as root.
  • Shared team folders: a group, chgrp, and 2770 (setgid keeps the group).
  • umask decides the default permissions of new files.

Linux · Lesson 6

Processes, jobs and signals

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a process is and read ps and top
  • run commands in the background and manage jobs
  • stop programs with signals: kill, SIGTERM, SIGKILL
  • write a script that cleans up when it is stopped

What is a process?

A program is a file on disk. A process is a program that is running: it has a process ID (PID), an owner, memory and open files. A process is always started by another process (its parent, PPID), so processes form a family tree that begins at PID 1.

Real output
$ ps -o pid,ppid,user,comm -p $$,$PPID
  PID  PPID USER     COMMAND
 6374  5423 root     runuser
 6375  6374 student  bash
$ echo "(PIDs differ on every machine)"
(PIDs differ on every machine)
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ps

What it does: Shows a snapshot of running processes.

When to use it: Checking whether a program is running, or finding its process ID (PID).

aux every process with CPU/memory-ef full listing with parent PID-o pid,comm choose columns-p PID just that process
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

Process listings: ps shows a snapshot, top is a live view.

CommandShows
ps auxevery process, all users, with CPU and memory
ps -efevery process in full format, with parent PID
ps -o pid,stat,comm -p PIDchosen columns for one process
pgrep namePIDs of processes whose name matches
top / htoplive view. In top: q quit, M sort by memory, P by CPU, k kill

Foreground, background and jobs

By default a command runs in the foreground: the shell waits, and you cannot type until it finishes. Add & to start it in the background and get the prompt back:

Real output
$ sleep 120 &
$ sleep 130 &
$ jobs
[1]-  Running                 sleep 120 &
[2]+  Running                 sleep 130 &
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

jobs

What it does: Lists the background jobs started from this shell.

When to use it: Seeing what you have running with & or paused with Ctrl+Z.

Open the full command reference

jobs lists the shell's background jobs by job number. Useful controls: Ctrl+Z pauses the foreground job, bg resumes it in the background, fg brings it back, and kill %1 stops job 1.

Real output
$ pid=$!
$ ps -o stat,comm -p $pid
STAT COMMAND
S    sleep
$ kill %1
$ sleep 0.2
$ jobs
[2]+  Running                 sleep 130 &
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
kill

What it does: Sends a signal to a process (by default asks it to stop politely, SIGTERM).

When to use it: Stopping a process or job: kill PID. Use kill -9 PID only if it ignores the polite request.

-15 (default) please terminate-9 force kill, no cleanup-0 only check the process exists-l list signals

Open the full command reference

The STAT letter says what the process is doing: S sleeping (waiting for something), R running, T stopped (paused), Z zombie (finished, waiting for its parent to notice), D waiting on disk or network (cannot be interrupted).

Signals: how to talk to a process

kill does not only kill: it sends a signal, a small message. The programs decide how to react.

SignalNumberMeaning
SIGTERM15"Please shut down." The polite default. The program can clean up first
SIGKILL9"Die now." Cannot be caught or ignored. No cleanup, so a last resort
SIGINT2what Ctrl+C sends
SIGHUP1"hang up". Many services reload their configuration on it
SIGSTOP/SIGCONT19 / 18pause and resume
Real output
$ kill -l TERM; kill -l KILL; kill -l HUP
15
9
1
Rule of thumb

Always try kill PID (SIGTERM) first and wait a few seconds. Use kill -9 PID only if the process ignores it. A process killed with -9 cannot flush its buffers or remove its lock files, which can leave a database or a service in a bad state.

Programs that handle signals

A well-behaved program cleans up when told to stop. Here is a script that traps SIGTERM, and what happens when it is stopped:

Real output
$ cat > worker.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> cleanup() { echo "worker: received stop signal, cleaning up"; exit 0; }
> trap cleanup TERM
> echo "worker: started"
> while true; do sleep 0.2; done
> EOF
$ chmod +x worker.sh
$ ./worker.sh > worker.out &
$ wpid=$!
$ sleep 0.5
$ kill $wpid
$ wait $wpid
$ echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 0
$ cat worker.out
worker: started
worker: received stop signal, cleaning up
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

wait

What it does: Waits for background jobs to finish.

When to use it: In scripts, after starting several jobs with &.

Open the full command reference

The script printed its goodbye message because kill sent SIGTERM and the trap caught it. Now the opposite: a script that ignores SIGTERM, so only kill -9 works.

Real output
$ cat > stubborn.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> trap '' TERM
> while true; do sleep 0.2; done
> EOF
$ chmod +x stubborn.sh
$ ./stubborn.sh &
$ spid=$!
$ sleep 0.5
$ kill $spid
$ sleep 0.5
$ echo "after SIGTERM, still running?"; kill -0 $spid 2>/dev/null && echo yes || echo no
after SIGTERM, still running?
yes
$ kill -9 $spid
$ wait $spid 2>/dev/null
$ echo "after SIGKILL, still running?"; kill -0 $spid 2>/dev/null && echo yes || echo no
after SIGKILL, still running?
no

kill -0 PID sends no signal at all. It only checks whether the process exists, which is a handy test in scripts.

Staying alive after you log out

A background job started from a terminal gets a SIGHUP when the terminal closes. To keep it running, start it with nohup (ignores SIGHUP) or, for real services, use a service manager such as systemd (the next lesson).

Real output
$ nohup sleep 300 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ pid=$!
$ pgrep -f "sleep 300" > /dev/null && echo "nohup job is running"
nohup job is running
$ kill $pid
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
pgrep

What it does: Finds process IDs by name.

When to use it: Is the service running? Which PIDs belong to it?

-f match against the full command line-a show the command too

Open the full command reference

Looking inside a process: /proc

Linux shows every process as a folder in /proc. This is where ps and top get their data.

Real output
$ sleep 100 &
$ pid=$!
$ ls /proc/$pid | head -8
arch_status
attr
autogroup
auxv
cgroup
clear_refs
cmdline
comm
$ echo "---"
---
$ head -3 /proc/$pid/status | sed 's/\t/ /'
Name: sleep
Umask: 0022
State: S (sleeping)
$ echo "---"
---
$ readlink /proc/$pid/cwd | sed "s#$HOME#~#"
~/lab
$ kill $pid
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

readlink

What it does: Prints where a symbolic link points.

When to use it: Finding the real file behind a link; -f resolves the full path.

Open the full command reference

Process priority

nice starts a process with lower priority (a higher "niceness" up to 19 means "be nice, let others go first"). renice changes it for a running process.

Real output
$ nice -n 10 sleep 60 &
$ pid=$!
$ ps -o ni,comm -p $pid
 NI COMMAND
 10 sleep
$ kill $pid
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
nice

What it does: Starts a program with lower (or higher) scheduling priority.

When to use it: Running a heavy job without slowing other things.

Open the full command reference

<!-- deeper -->

Practice with worked answers

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "--- start a long job, find it, stop it politely, confirm"
--- start a long job, find it, stop it politely, confirm
$ sleep 300 &
$ pid=$!
$ ps -o pid,stat,comm -p $pid | tail -1 | awk '{print "running:", $3, "state", $2}'
running: sleep state S
$ kill $pid
$ sleep 0.3
$ kill -0 $pid 2>/dev/null && echo "still alive" || echo "stopped by SIGTERM"
stopped by SIGTERM
$ echo "--- pgrep finds by name"
--- pgrep finds by name
$ sleep 301 &
$ pgrep -f "sleep 301" > /dev/null && echo "found it by name"
found it by name
$ pkill -f "sleep 301"
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
pkill

What it does: Sends a signal to processes selected by name.

When to use it: Stopping all processes of a program.

-f match full command line-9 force kill

Careful: A loose pattern can kill things you did not intend. Check first with pgrep -a.

Open the full command reference

Common mistakes
  • Jumping straight to kill -9. It gives the program no chance to clean up (lock files, buffers, child processes). Try plain kill and wait first.
  • pkill name too broadly. It kills every match. Check with pgrep -a name first.
  • Forgetting that closing the terminal can stop background jobs. Use nohup, tmux/screen, or a systemd service for anything long-running.
  • Treating "zombie" processes as running. A Z state process has already finished; the fix is its parent, not kill.
  • Reading top memory wrongly. Linux uses spare memory as cache; look at "available", not "free".

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • A process is a running program with a PID and a parent. ps snapshots, top is live.
  • & starts a job in the background; jobs, fg, bg manage it.
  • kill sends signals. SIGTERM (15) asks nicely, SIGKILL (9) cannot be refused. Try 15 first.
  • trap lets a script clean up when it is stopped.
  • nohup or a service manager keeps programs alive after logout.
Your turn

The EV indexing service hangs and kill PID does nothing. Walk through what you would try, in order, and say why kill -9 is the last resort.

Linux · Lesson 7

Packages and services

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a package manager does and use apt and dnf/yum
  • inspect what a package installed
  • manage services with systemctl and read their logs with journalctl
  • read and write a systemd unit file

Packages, not downloads

On Windows you usually download an installer. On Linux you ask a package manager to fetch, verify, install and later update software from a trusted repository. It also installs dependencies (other packages the software needs) for you.

FamilyDistrosToolPackage file
DebianDebian, Ubuntuapt (and dpkg underneath).deb
Red HatRHEL, Rocky, Alma, Fedora, CentOSdnf (older: yum; rpm underneath).rpm
TaskDebian/UbuntuRed Hat family
refresh the list of available packagessudo apt update(automatic) sudo dnf check-update
installsudo apt install nginxsudo dnf install nginx
upgrade everythingsudo apt upgradesudo dnf upgrade
removesudo apt remove nginxsudo dnf remove nginx
searchapt search worddnf search word
which package owns a filedpkg -S /pathrpm -qf /path
list files of a packagedpkg -L pkgrpm -ql pkg
Update vs upgrade

apt update only refreshes the catalogue ("what is available"). apt upgrade actually installs newer versions. Run both, in that order.

Looking at a package

This lab runs Ubuntu, so we use the Debian tools. Ask about the bash package that is already installed:

Real output
$ dpkg -s bash | grep -E '^(Package|Status|Priority)'
Package: bash
Status: install ok installed
Priority: required
$ dpkg -S "$(readlink -f /bin/bash)"
bash: /usr/bin/bash
$ dpkg -L bash | grep -E '/bin/' | head -3
/usr/bin/bash
/usr/bin/bashbug
/usr/bin/clear_console
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
dpkg

What it does: Low-level Debian/Ubuntu package tool: lists and inspects installed packages.

When to use it: Which package owns this file (dpkg -S)? What files does a package install (dpkg -L)? Is it installed (dpkg -s)?

-s PKG status-L PKG files installed-S PATH which package owns the file-l list all installed
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

readlink

What it does: Prints where a symbolic link points.

When to use it: Finding the real file behind a link; -f resolves the full path.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Install and use a small package for real:

Real output
$ sudo apt-get install -y -q cowsay > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo "installed"
installed
$ dpkg -s cowsay | grep -E '^(Package|Status)'
Package: cowsay
Status: install ok installed
$ /usr/games/cowsay "packages are easy"
 ___________________
< packages are easy >
 -------------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
$ sudo apt-get remove -y -q cowsay > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo "removed"
removed
$ dpkg -s cowsay > /dev/null 2>&1 || echo "cowsay is no longer installed"
cowsay is no longer installed
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
apt-get

What it does: Installs, removes and updates software on Debian and Ubuntu.

When to use it: apt-get install -y PKG to add software; apt-get update to refresh the package list.

-y answer yes automaticallyinstall / remove / update / upgrade
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

cowsay

What it does: Prints a text message spoken by an ASCII-art cow.

When to use it: A harmless package to practise installing and removing software.

Open the full command reference

(If you see a different message the first time, it is because the package catalogue needed refreshing with sudo apt update first.)

Services and systemd

A service (a "daemon" in Linux slang) is a program that runs in the background without a terminal: a web server, a database, an SSH server. Modern Linux uses systemd to start services at boot, restart them if they crash, and log their output.

The tool is systemctl. This sandbox container has no systemd, so the transcripts below are examples of what you will see on a real server:

Example output (not run here)
$ systemctl status nginx
● nginx.service - A high performance web server
     Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/nginx.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Mon 2026-09-28 08:14:02 UTC; 2 days ago
   Main PID: 1042 (nginx)
$ sudo systemctl restart nginx
$ sudo systemctl enable --now nginx
Created symlink /etc/systemd/system/multi-user.target.wants/nginx.service
$ systemctl is-active nginx
active
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
systemctl

What it does: Controls services managed by systemd: start, stop, restart, enable at boot, show status.

When to use it: Managing a service on a modern Linux server.

status X is it running and its recent logrestart X enable --now X start now and at every bootlist-units --failed what is broken

Open the full command reference

CommandMeaning
systemctl status Xis it running? last log lines
systemctl start X / stop X / restart Xact now
systemctl reload Xre-read the config without dropping connections (if supported)
systemctl enable X / disable Xstart (or not) at boot
systemctl enable --now Xenable and start in one go
systemctl list-units --failedwhat is broken right now
systemctl daemon-reloadafter editing a unit file

Start vs enable trips up every beginner. start = run it now. enable = run it at every boot. They are independent.

Logs with journalctl

systemd collects service output in the journal:

Example output (not run here)
$ journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
$ journalctl -u nginx -f            # follow, like tail -f
$ journalctl -p err -b              # only errors since this boot
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
journalctl

What it does: Reads the systemd journal (the logs of services and the system).

When to use it: Why did the service fail? journalctl -u NAME shows its log.

-u NAME one service-f follow live--since "1 hour ago" time filter-p err only errors

Open the full command reference

Classic text logs also live under /var/log (for example /var/log/syslog or /var/log/messages, /var/log/auth.log). Your EV analogy: systemctl is like the Services console on a Windows EV server, and journalctl is like the Event Viewer.

Writing your own service

A unit file describes a service. Here is a complete one for a small script. Compare with what you learned earlier: it names the user to run as, the command, and what to do on failure.

/etc/systemd/system/evcheck.service
[Unit]
Description=EV health check loop
After=network.target

[Service]
User=evadmin
ExecStart=/opt/ev/check.sh
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then: sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl enable --now evcheck. Restart=on-failure is the self-healing part: if the script crashes, systemd restarts it five seconds later.

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

The two problems are separate: the service is stopped now, and it is not enabled at boot. On a real server:

Example output (not run here)
$ sudo systemctl start ev-indexing        # fixes "stopped now"
$ sudo systemctl enable ev-indexing       # fixes "will not come back after a reboot"
$ sudo systemctl enable --now ev-indexing # both in one command
$ systemctl status ev-indexing            # verify: "Active: active (running)" and "enabled"

(Example commands: the lab has no systemd. The service name ev-indexing is made up.) If it fails to start, read why: journalctl -u ev-indexing -n 50 --no-pager.

Common mistakes
  • Starting a service but never enabling it, so it dies at the next reboot (or enabling but never starting it).
  • Editing a unit file and forgetting systemctl daemon-reload.
  • apt install without apt update first, so the package list is stale and the install fails or installs an old version.
  • Mixing package managers (installing the same software by apt and by a downloaded installer) and then not knowing which copy runs; which -a and dpkg -S tell you.
  • Not reading the log. systemctl status shows only the last lines; journalctl -u NAME shows the story.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Package managers install, update and remove software and its dependencies from repositories.
  • apt/dpkg for Debian and Ubuntu; dnf/rpm for the Red Hat family.
  • systemd runs services. systemctl start/stop/restart/status, and enable for boot.
  • journalctl -u name shows a service's logs.
  • A unit file defines a service; daemon-reload after changing it.
Your turn

The EV indexing service is stopped and will not come back after a reboot. Which two systemctl commands fix both problems? Which one command does both?
