Linux · Lesson 8

Disks, links and archives

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read df, du and lsblk
  • explain mounting, filesystems and /etc/fstab
  • understand hard links and symbolic links
  • create and unpack tar archives
  • diagnose and fix a full disk

One tree, many disks

Windows gives each disk a letter (C:, D:). Linux has one tree starting at /. A disk or partition is mounted onto a folder, called a mount point, and its contents appear there. Everything under /var/log might be on a different physical disk from /, and you cannot tell by the path alone.

CommandUse
lsblklist block devices (disks, partitions)
df -hfree space per mounted filesystem (-h = human sizes)
du -sh folderhow much space a folder uses
mount / findmntwhat is mounted where
/etc/fstabthe file listing what to mount at boot
Real output
$ df -h / | head -1
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
$ findmnt -n -o TARGET,FSTYPE /
/      ext4
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
findmnt

What it does: Shows the mounted file systems as a tree, or details for one path.

When to use it: Seeing which file system a folder lives on and its type.

Open the full command reference

A full disk, safely

A full disk is one of the most common real incidents (EV storage, logs, SQL). Rather than just read about it, we build a tiny 8 MB disk image, format it with a filesystem (ext4), mount it and fill it.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=tiny.img bs=1M count=8 status=none
$ mkfs.ext4 -q tiny.img
$ mkdir -p mnt
$ sudo mount -o loop tiny.img mnt
$ sudo chown student mnt
$ findmnt -n -o TARGET,FSTYPE mnt
/home/student/lab/mnt ext4
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

dd

What it does: Copies raw data block by block, often used to create files of an exact size or copy disk images.

When to use it: Making a test file or disk image (dd if=/dev/zero of=file bs=1M count=10).

Careful: dd writes wherever you point it, including whole disks. Double-check the of= target.

mkfs.ext4

What it does: Creates an ext4 file system on a disk, partition or image file.

When to use it: Preparing new storage for use. It erases what was there.

mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
mount

What it does: Attaches a disk or file system to a folder (or lists what is mounted).

When to use it: Using a new disk, a network share or a disk image.

chown

What it does: Changes the owner (and optionally the group) of files.

When to use it: A service cannot write to its folder because it belongs to another user.

user:group set both-R recursive

Open the full command reference

Now fill it and watch it break:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ dd if=/dev/zero of=mnt/big.dat bs=1M count=100 2>&1 | grep -i "no space"
dd: error writing 'mnt/big.dat': No space left on device
$ df -h mnt | awk 'NR==2{print "use%:", $5}'
use%: 70%
$ echo "try to write a new file:"
try to write a new file:
$ echo hello > mnt/new.txt
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

No space left on device. First instinct: find what is big.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ ls -lh mnt | awk 'NR>1{print $5, $9}'
2.0M big.dat
16K lost+found
6 new.txt
$ ls -lh mnt/big.dat | awk '{print $5, $9}'
2.0M mnt/big.dat
$ rm mnt/big.dat
$ df -h mnt | awk 'NR==2{print "use%:", $5}'
use%: 1%
$ echo hello > mnt/new.txt && echo "writing works again"
writing works again
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

A related trap: inodes. A filesystem has a limited number of file entries (inodes). Millions of tiny files can exhaust inodes while df -h still shows free space. Check with df -i.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ df -i mnt | awk 'NR==2{print "inode use%:", $5}'
inode use%: 1%
$ sudo umount mnt
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
umount

What it does: Detaches a mounted file system.

When to use it: Before removing a disk, or to clean up a test image. It fails if something is still using it.

Open the full command reference

Find the space hog

du -ah /var | sort -rh | head -20 lists the 20 biggest items under /var. Also check for deleted files still held open by a running program: lsof +L1. The space is freed only when the program closes the file or restarts.

Links: two ways to have another name

Real output
$ cd ~/lab && rm -f orig.txt hard.txt soft.txt
$ echo "version 1" > orig.txt
$ ln orig.txt hard.txt        # hard link
$ ln -s orig.txt soft.txt     # symbolic link (shortcut)
$ ls -li orig.txt hard.txt soft.txt | awk '{print $1, $2, $10, $11, $12}'
794704 -rw-r--r-- hard.txt  
794704 -rw-r--r-- orig.txt  
794717 lrwxrwxrwx soft.txt -> orig.txt
$ cat soft.txt
version 1
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ln

What it does: Creates links between files: hard links, or symbolic links with -s (shortcuts).

When to use it: Pointing a stable name (current) to a changing target (release-42), or sharing one file under two names.

-s symbolic link-f replace an existing link
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

Open the full command reference

  • A hard link is a second name for the same data (same inode number, first column). Deleting one name leaves the other working.
  • A symbolic link (symlink) is a small file that holds a path, like a Windows shortcut. If the target is deleted, the link dangles.
Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ rm orig.txt
$ cat hard.txt
version 1
$ cat soft.txt
cat: soft.txt: No such file or directory

The hard link still holds the data; the symlink is broken. Symlinks are used everywhere: /etc/alternatives, release folders (current -> release-42), systemd's enabled services.

Archives and compression

tar bundles many files into one; gzip compresses. They are usually combined as .tar.gz.

CommandMeaning
tar -czf out.tar.gz folder/create, gzip, file
tar -tzf out.tar.gztest: list contents
tar -xzf out.tar.gzextract
tar -xzf out.tar.gz -C /destextract into /dest
gzip file / gunzip file.gzcompress or expand one file
zip -r / unzipWindows-friendly zip
Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ tar -czf ev-backup.tar.gz ev/config ev/scripts
$ tar -tzf ev-backup.tar.gz
ev/config/
ev/config/evault.conf
ev/scripts/
ev/scripts/check.sh
$ mkdir -p restore && tar -xzf ev-backup.tar.gz -C restore
$ diff -r ev/config restore/ev/config && echo "restored copy is identical"
restored copy is identical
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
tar

What it does: Bundles many files into one archive, optionally compressed.

When to use it: Backups and moving a folder as one file.

-c create-x extract-t list contents-z gzip compression-f FILE archive file name-C DIR change folder first
diff

What it does: Compares two files (or folders with -r) and shows the differences.

When to use it: Checking what changed between two versions of a config, or confirming a restored copy is identical.

-r compare folders-u unified format (the same used by git diff)

Open the full command reference

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

The order to work in when a file system is full:

Example output (not run here)
$ df -h /var                                  # 1. confirm which file system is full
$ df -i /var                                  # 2. check inodes too (many tiny files can fill it)
$ sudo du -xh /var --max-depth=2 | sort -rh | head -15      # 3. find the biggest folders
$ sudo find /var/log -type f -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \; # 4. find the large files
$ sudo lsof +L1                               # 5. files that are deleted but still held open
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
df

What it does: Shows free and used space for each mounted file system.

When to use it: First check when a disk is full; df -i shows inodes (number of files) instead.

-h human-readable sizes-i inode usage
du

What it does: Shows how much disk space files and folders use.

When to use it: Finding what is filling a disk.

-s one total per argument-h human-readable--max-depth=1 only one level deep
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
find

What it does: Searches a folder tree for files by name, type, size, age and more, and can run a command on each match.

When to use it: Locating a file, finding large or old files, cleaning up logs older than N days.

-name "*.log" match by name-type f/d files or directories-mtime +7 modified more than 7 days ago-size +100M bigger than 100 MB-exec CMD {} \ run a command on every match
lsof

What it does: Lists open files, including network connections, and which process owns them.

When to use it: Which process has this file or port open? Why is the disk still full after deleting a file (lsof +L1)?

-i :80 who uses port 80+L1 deleted files still open

Open the full command reference

Why deleting a huge log may not free space: a running program still has the file open. The name is gone, but the data stays on disk until the program closes it. lsof +L1 shows it. Fix: restart the service (or truncate the file instead of deleting it: : > /var/log/big.log). Then add log rotation so it does not recur.

Try the truncate-versus-delete idea safely:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ ( exec 3> held.log; dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=3 >&3 2>/dev/null; rm held.log
>   echo "file deleted, but this shell still holds it open:"; ls -l /proc/$$/fd/3 | awk '{print $NF, $(NF-1), $(NF-2)}' | sed 's#/home/student/lab/##' ; exec 3>&- )
file deleted, but this shell still holds it open:
ls: cannot access '/proc/6507/fd/3': No such file or directory
Common mistakes
  • Deleting random files in /var to free space. Find what is big and why first; some files (databases, journals) are vital.
  • Forgetting inodes. df -h looks fine but "No space left on device" appears: df -i.
  • Deleting a log a service is writing instead of truncating or rotating it.
  • rm -rf on a mount point that is actually another disk.
  • No monitoring. Alert at 80% so it never reaches 100%.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • One directory tree; disks are mounted onto folders. df -h, du -sh, lsblk, findmnt.
  • Full disk: df -h to find the full filesystem, du to find the hog, remove or move, check df -i and lsof +L1.
  • Hard link = another name for the same data. Symlink = a path shortcut that can dangle.
  • tar -czf to create, -tzf to list, -xzf to extract.
Your turn

df -h says /var is 100% full. List, in order, the commands you would run to find what to clear. Then say why deleting a huge log file might not free space immediately.

Shell scripting

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write and run a bash script
  • use variables, arguments and exit codes
  • use if, for, while and case
  • write functions and make a script fail safely

Your first script

A script is a text file of commands. The first line, the shebang #!/bin/bash, says which program should run it.

Real output
$ cat > hello.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> echo "Hello from a script"
> echo "Today the lab folder has $(ls | wc -l) entries"
> EOF
$ chmod +x hello.sh
$ ./hello.sh | head -1
Hello from a script
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Two steps every time: make the file executable (chmod +x), then run it with a path (./hello.sh).

Variables and arguments

No spaces around =. Use $name or ${name} to read. Always quote variables: "$name".

Real output
$ cat > greet.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> name="${1:-world}"
> echo "Hello, $name"
> echo "I was given $# argument(s)"
> EOF
$ chmod +x greet.sh
$ ./greet.sh
Hello, world
I was given 0 argument(s)
$ ./greet.sh Rohan
Hello, Rohan
I was given 1 argument(s)
$ ./greet.sh "two words"
Hello, two words
I was given 1 argument(s)
SpecialMeaning
$1 $2 ...arguments
$#number of arguments
$@all arguments
$?exit code of the last command (0 = success)
$$this script's PID

${1:-world} means "use the first argument, or world if it is empty".

Conditions

Real output
$ cat > check_file.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> f="$1"
> if [ -z "$f" ]; then
>   echo "usage: $0 file"; exit 2
> elif [ -d "$f" ]; then
>   echo "$f is a directory"
> elif [ -f "$f" ]; then
>   echo "$f is a file with $(wc -l < "$f") lines"
> else
>   echo "$f does not exist"; exit 1
> fi
> EOF
$ chmod +x check_file.sh
$ ./check_file.sh ev/logs/indexing.log
ev/logs/indexing.log is a file with 14 lines
$ ./check_file.sh ev
ev is a directory
$ ./check_file.sh nothing; echo "exit code: $?"
nothing does not exist
exit code: 1
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

Common tests: -f file exists, -d folder, -z string empty, -n not empty, -eq -ne -lt -gt numbers, == != strings, -r -w -x permissions.

Loops

Real output
$ for f in ev/logs/*.log; do
>   errors=$(grep -c ERROR "$f")
>   echo "$f: $errors errors"
> done
ev/logs/indexing.log: 5 errors
ev/logs/storage.log: 1 errors
$ n=3
$ while [ $n -gt 0 ]; do echo "countdown $n"; n=$((n-1)); done
countdown 3
countdown 2
countdown 1
$ for host in EV01 SQL01 FS01; do echo "would ping $host"; done
would ping EV01
would ping SQL01
would ping FS01
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
for

What it does: A loop that repeats commands once for each item in a list.

When to use it: Doing the same thing to several files, servers or numbers: for h in ev01 sql01; do ...; done.

Open the full command reference

Functions and case

Real output
$ cat > svc.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> say() { echo "[$(basename "$0")] $*"; }
> case "$1" in
>   start) say "starting EV services" ;;
>   stop)  say "stopping EV services" ;;
>   *)     say "usage: start|stop"; exit 1 ;;
> esac
> EOF
$ chmod +x svc.sh
$ ./svc.sh start
[svc.sh] starting EV services
$ ./svc.sh stop
[svc.sh] stopping EV services
$ ./svc.sh oops; echo "exit code: $?"
[svc.sh] usage: start|stop
exit code: 1

Writing safe scripts

Scripts keep going after an error unless told otherwise, which can do damage (for example, cd fails and then rm -rf * runs in the wrong folder). A strong starting line:

safe-header.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
  • -e stop on the first failing command
  • -u error on an unset variable
  • -o pipefail a pipeline fails if any stage fails
Real output
$ cat > unsafe.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> set -euo pipefail
> echo "step 1"
> false
> echo "step 2 (never printed)"
> EOF
$ bash unsafe.sh; echo "exit code: $?"
step 1
exit code: 1
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
bash

What it does: Runs the Bash shell: a script file, or one command with -c.

When to use it: Running a script without making it executable, or running a command string in a fresh shell.

-c 'cmd' run a command string-n check syntax only

Open the full command reference

A practical script: a mini health report for the pretend EV server.

Real output
$ cat > report.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> set -euo pipefail
> log="${1:?usage: report.sh logfile}"
> errors=$(grep -c ERROR "$log" || true)
> warns=$(grep -c WARN "$log" || true)
> echo "file: $(basename "$log")"
> echo "errors: $errors  warnings: $warns"
> if [ "$errors" -gt 0 ]; then
>   echo "last error:"; grep ERROR "$log" | tail -1
>   exit 1
> fi
> EOF
$ chmod +x report.sh
$ ./report.sh ev/logs/indexing.log; echo "exit code: $?"
file: indexing.log
errors: 5  warnings: 2
last error:
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
exit code: 1

Exit code 1 is how a script tells another program (a scheduler, Jenkins, Ansible) that something failed. This simple idea underlies all automation.

<!-- deeper -->

A worked solution

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ cat > disk_check.sh <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> set -euo pipefail
> dir="${1:?usage: disk_check.sh FOLDER LIMIT_KB}"
> limit="${2:?usage: disk_check.sh FOLDER LIMIT_KB}"
> used=$(du -sk "$dir" | cut -f1)
> if [ "$used" -gt "$limit" ]; then
>   echo "WARNING: $dir uses ${used} KB, above the limit of ${limit} KB" >&2
>   exit 1
> fi
> echo "ok: $dir uses ${used} KB (limit ${limit} KB)"
> EOF
$ chmod +x disk_check.sh
$ ./disk_check.sh ev 100000; echo "exit code: $?"
ok: ev uses 36 KB (limit 100000 KB)
exit code: 0
$ ./disk_check.sh ev 1; echo "exit code: $?"
WARNING: ev uses 36 KB, above the limit of 1 KB
exit code: 1
$ ./disk_check.sh 2>&1 | head -1; echo "exit code: ${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
./disk_check.sh: line 3: 1: usage: disk_check.sh FOLDER LIMIT_KB
exit code: 1
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

Open the full command reference

The three runs show the three outcomes: under the limit (exit 0), over the limit (exit 1, message on stderr), and missing arguments (${1:?...} stops the script with a usage message).

Common mistakes
  • Unquoted variables (rm $dir/* when dir has a space or is empty). Always "$dir".
  • No set -euo pipefail, so a failed step is ignored and later steps do damage.
  • Spaces around = in assignments (x = 5 is an error; write x=5).
  • [ $a = $b ] with an empty variable. Quote: [ "$a" = "$b" ].
  • Using == in plain sh; = is portable, == is a bash extension.
  • Printing errors to standard output. Send diagnostics to stderr (>&2) and use meaningful exit codes.
  • Parsing ls output. Use globs (for f in *.log) or find.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • A script is a file with a shebang and executable permission.
  • $1, $#, $?, quoting, ${var:-default}.
  • if, for, while, case, functions.
  • set -euo pipefail and meaningful exit codes make scripts safe and automatable.
Your turn

Write disk_check.sh that takes a folder, and exits 1 with a message if du -s of that folder exceeds a limit you pass as the second argument. Test it with ev and a tiny limit.

Linux · Lesson 10

Scheduling, SSH and environment

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read and write cron schedules
  • explain SSH keys and use ssh, scp and ~/.ssh/config
  • understand environment variables and PATH

Environment variables and PATH

An environment variable is a named value that programs inherit from the shell that started them.

Real output
$ export EV_SERVER=EV01
$ echo "server is $EV_SERVER"
server is EV01
$ env | grep '^EV_'
EV_SERVER=EV01
$ bash -c 'echo "child sees: $EV_SERVER"'
child sees: EV01
$ unset EV_SERVER
$ bash -c 'echo "after unset: [$EV_SERVER]"'
after unset: []
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
export

What it does: Sets an environment variable that child programs also receive.

When to use it: Passing settings (like a server name or a PATH change) to programs you start from this shell.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

bash

What it does: Runs the Bash shell: a script file, or one command with -c.

When to use it: Running a script without making it executable, or running a command string in a fresh shell.

-c 'cmd' run a command string-n check syntax only
unset

What it does: Removes a shell variable.

When to use it: Clearing a variable you no longer want programs to see.

Open the full command reference

Without export, a variable is private to the current shell. The most important variable is PATH, the list of folders searched when you type a command name:

Real output
$ echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | head -3
/usr/local/sbin
/usr/local/bin
/usr/sbin
$ which ls
/usr/bin/ls
$ type cd
cd is a shell builtin
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
tr

What it does: Translates or deletes single characters.

When to use it: Converting case (tr a-z A-Z), squeezing spaces, or turning separators into newlines.

-d delete the characters-s squeeze repeats into one
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
which

What it does: Shows the full path of the program that would run for a command name.

When to use it: Checking which copy of a tool is used, or whether it is installed at all.

type

What it does: Tells you what a command name really is: a builtin, an alias, a function or a program (and where).

When to use it: Working out why a command behaves oddly, for example whether ls is an alias.

Open the full command reference

"command not found" usually means the program is not in any PATH folder. You can run it with its full path, or add its folder:

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/bin
$ printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "my own tool"\n' > ~/bin/mytool && chmod +x ~/bin/mytool
$ mytool 2>&1 | head -1
bash: line 39: mytool: command not found
$ export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
$ mytool
my own tool
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

Open the full command reference

To make a variable permanent, put the export line in ~/.bashrc (for you) or /etc/environment (for everyone).

Scheduling with cron

cron runs commands on a schedule. Each line of a crontab has five time fields and a command:

┌ minute (0-59)
│ ┌ hour (0-23)
│ │ ┌ day of month (1-31)
│ │ │ ┌ month (1-12)
│ │ │ │ ┌ day of week (0-7, Sun = 0 or 7)
* * * * *  command

Common patterns: */5 * * * * every five minutes, 0 2 * * * daily at 2am, 30 6 * * 1-5 weekdays at 06:30, 0 0 1 * * first of each month.

Example output (not run here)
$ crontab -e                    # edit your schedule
$ crontab -l                    # list it
0 2 * * * /opt/ev/backup.sh >> /var/log/ev-backup.log 2>&1
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
crontab

What it does: Edits or lists a user's scheduled jobs.

When to use it: Running a backup or report on a schedule: crontab -e to edit, crontab -l to list.

Open the full command reference

Cron's environment is tiny

Cron runs with a minimal PATH and no profile. Use full paths to commands and scripts, and redirect output to a log (>> file 2>&1) so you can see failures. "Works in my terminal but not in cron" is nearly always this. systemd timers are a modern alternative with better logging.

SSH: logging in to other machines

SSH (Secure Shell) gives you a terminal on a remote machine over an encrypted connection (port 22). It replaces Telnet and, for Linux servers, RDP.

Example output (not run here)
$ ssh evadmin@ev01.example.com
$ ssh -p 2222 evadmin@ev01.example.com
$ ssh evadmin@ev01 'df -h /'          # run one command and return
$ scp backup.tar.gz evadmin@ev01:/tmp/   # copy a file
$ rsync -av ev/ evadmin@ev01:/srv/ev/    # copy only what changed
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
ssh

What it does: Opens a secure shell on another machine, or runs one command there.

When to use it: Administering remote servers.

-p PORT port-i KEY private key filessh host 'command' run one command and return
scp

What it does: Copies files over SSH.

When to use it: Sending a file to or fetching one from another server.

rsync

What it does: Copies only what changed between two folders, locally or over SSH.

When to use it: Backups and deployments; much faster than copying everything each time.

-a archive mode (keeps permissions and times)-v verbose--delete remove files that no longer exist at the source

Open the full command reference

Keys instead of passwords

Passwords can be guessed. SSH can use a key pair: a private key (secret, stays with you) and a public key (safe to share, placed on servers). The server challenges you and only the private key can answer it.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab && rm -f demo_key demo_key.pub
$ ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N "" -C "rohan@laptop" -f demo_key
$ ls demo_key demo_key.pub
demo_key
demo_key.pub
$ cut -d' ' -f1,3 demo_key.pub
ssh-ed25519 rohan@laptop
$ stat -c '%a %n' demo_key
600 demo_key
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

ssh-keygen

What it does: Creates an SSH key pair (a private key and a public key).

When to use it: Setting up passwordless, safer login to servers.

-t ed25519 key type-f FILE file name-N "" no passphrase (lab use only)
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
stat

What it does: Shows detailed information about a file: size, permissions, owner, times, inode.

When to use it: Checking exact permissions in octal, or the last modification time.

-c '%a %U %n' custom format (octal permissions, owner, name)

Open the full command reference

The private key is 600 (SSH refuses a key others can read). The public key is added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server (ssh-copy-id does it for you). To avoid typing the options every time, use ~/.ssh/config:

~/.ssh/config
Host ev01
    HostName ev01.example.com
    User evadmin
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/ev_key

Now ssh ev01 is enough. Never share or commit a private key; if it leaks, remove the public key from servers and generate a new pair.

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers and common mistakes

The crontab line for 02:30 every Sunday (fields: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week; Sunday is 0 or 7):

Example output (not run here)
# 
30 2 * * 0  /opt/ev/backup.sh >> /var/log/ev-backup.log 2>&1

Check how it will be read with the cron explainer from this lesson, or test the idea locally:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "30 2 * * 0" | awk '{printf "minute=%s hour=%s day-of-month=%s month=%s day-of-week=%s (0 = Sunday)\n", $1,$2,$3,$4,$5}'
minute=30 hour=2 day-of-month=* month=* day-of-week=0 (0 = Sunday)
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100

Open the full command reference

>> file 2>&1 appends normal output and error output to one log. Without it cron tries to email the output (or drops it), and you will not know a job failed.

Common mistakes
  • Relative paths and commands that work in your terminal but not in cron's minimal environment. Use absolute paths, and set PATH at the top of the crontab if needed.
  • % characters in a crontab command: cron treats an unescaped % as a newline. Escape as \%.
  • Day-of-month and day-of-week both set is an OR, not an AND (0 2 1 * 1 runs on the 1st and every Monday).
  • No log, no alert. A silent backup that fails for weeks is worse than no backup.
  • Overlapping runs. If a job can take longer than its interval, guard it with flock.
  • Passwords in cron lines (visible in ps and backups). Use key files with 600 permissions.
  • SSH key permissions. Private keys must be 600 and ~/.ssh 700, or SSH refuses them.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Environment variables are inherited by child processes only when exported; PATH decides where commands are found.
  • cron: five time fields plus a command. Use full paths and log output.
  • SSH uses keys. Private stays secret (600), public goes in authorized_keys.
  • ~/.ssh/config shortens connection details.

Write the crontab line that runs /opt/ev/backup.sh at 02:30 every Sunday and appends output to a log file.

Linux · Lesson 11

Troubleshooting and performance

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • follow a simple troubleshooting method
  • check CPU, memory, disk and load
  • read logs quickly and find which process holds a file or port
  • trace a failing command with strace

A method, not a guess

When something is wrong, work in layers and change one thing at a time:

  1. What exactly is the symptom? Error text, since when, who is affected.
  2. What changed? Deploy, update, config edit, new disk usage.
  3. Look at the four resources: CPU, memory, disk, network.
  4. Read the logs around the time it started.
  5. Form a hypothesis, test it, write down what you did.

CPU, load and memory

Real output
$ nproc
4
$ awk '{print "/proc/loadavg has", NF, "fields; the first three are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load"}' /proc/loadavg
/proc/loadavg has 5 fields; the first three are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load
$ free -m | head -1
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
nproc

What it does: Prints the number of CPU cores.

When to use it: Comparing system load to the number of cores.

awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
free

What it does: Shows memory and swap usage.

When to use it: Checking memory pressure. Look at the "available" column, not "free".

-m megabytes-h human-readable
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

  • Load average counts processes running or waiting. Compare with the number of CPU cores (nproc): load 4 on a 4-core machine is "full", load 20 means things are waiting.
  • free -m shows memory in MB. The available column (not "free") is what matters: Linux uses spare memory as a disk cache.
  • top / htop: press P to sort by CPU, M by memory.
  • vmstat 1 5 and iostat -x 1 (package sysstat) show whether the bottleneck is CPU, memory swapping or disk.

Find the biggest consumers:

Real output
$ ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%mem | head -1
  PID COMMAND         %CPU %MEM
$ ps -eo comm --sort=-%mem | head -3 | wc -l
3
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ps

What it does: Shows a snapshot of running processes.

When to use it: Checking whether a program is running, or finding its process ID (PID).

aux every process with CPU/memory-ef full listing with parent PID-o pid,comm choose columns-p PID just that process
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

Disk space and speed

You met df -h, du and df -i in the storage lesson. High iowait in top (the wa value) says processes are waiting on the disk.

Who is using this file or port?

Real output
$ sleep 300 > ~/lab/held.txt &
$ pid=$!
$ sleep 0.3
$ lsof ~/lab/held.txt 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1{print $1, "has it open"}'
sleep has it open
$ kill $pid
$ python3 -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ spid=$!
$ sleep 1
$ ss -ltnp 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR>1 && /8765/{print "port 8765 listening"}'
port 8765 listening
$ kill $spid
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

lsof

What it does: Lists open files, including network connections, and which process owns them.

When to use it: Which process has this file or port open? Why is the disk still full after deleting a file (lsof +L1)?

-i :80 who uses port 80+L1 deleted files still open
kill

What it does: Sends a signal to a process (by default asks it to stop politely, SIGTERM).

When to use it: Stopping a process or job: kill PID. Use kill -9 PID only if it ignores the polite request.

-15 (default) please terminate-9 force kill, no cleanup-0 only check the process exists-l list signals
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON
ss

What it does: Shows network sockets: listening ports and connections.

When to use it: Which program is listening on port 8080? Is the service up?

-l listening-t TCP-u UDP-n numbers not names-p show the process

Open the full command reference

ss -ltnp lists listening TCP ports and the process using each. lsof -i :80 shows who uses port 80. This answers "address already in use" errors.

Logs, fast

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ grep -c ERROR ev/logs/indexing.log
5
$ grep -B1 -A1 "aborted" ev/logs/indexing.log | head -6
2026-09-30 09:12:34 ERROR SQL connection timeout (SQL01)
2026-09-30 09:12:35 ERROR Indexing task aborted
2026-09-30 09:13:01 INFO  Indexing service stopped
--
2026-09-30 12:15:41 ERROR Name resolution failed for SQL01
2026-09-30 12:15:42 ERROR Indexing task aborted
$ awk '/ERROR/{print $2}' ev/logs/indexing.log | cut -c1-2 | sort | uniq -c
      3 09
      2 12
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
uniq

What it does: Collapses repeated adjacent lines; with -c it counts them.

When to use it: Counting how often something occurs: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn.

-c prefix lines with counts-d show only duplicated lines

Open the full command reference

The last line is a quick histogram: errors per hour. Patterns like "always at 12:15" often point to a scheduled job.

strace: what is this program actually doing?

When a program fails with a vague error, strace shows every request it makes to the kernel. Searching for ENOENT (no such file) or EACCES (permission denied) often reveals the cause.

Real output
$ strace -f -e trace=openat cat /etc/does-not-exist 2>&1 | grep -E 'does-not-exist'
openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/does-not-exist", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory)
cat: /etc/does-not-exist: No such file or directory
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
strace

What it does: Shows the system calls a program makes (file opens, network calls, errors).

When to use it: A program fails with a vague error and you want to see which file or permission it trips on.

-f follow child processes-e trace=openat only file-open calls

Open the full command reference

The line says openat(...) = -1 ENOENT (No such file or directory): the program tried to open a file that is not there.

DNS and reachability (a preview)

Many "server down" reports are a name problem. This lab's EV logs show Name resolution failed for SQL01. The networking track covers it in detail; the quick triage is:

Example output (not run here)
$ ping -c1 SQL01             # does the name resolve and reply?
$ getent hosts SQL01         # what does this machine think the name is?
$ nc -zv SQL01 1433          # is the SQL port reachable?
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
ping

What it does: Sends small test packets to see if a host answers and how long it takes.

When to use it: First reachability check for a server.

-c N send N packets-W N wait N seconds
getent

What it does: Looks up entries the way the system does (users, groups, host names).

When to use it: getent hosts NAME shows how a name resolves, including /etc/hosts.

nc

What it does: Netcat: opens raw TCP/UDP connections, can test whether a port is open or act as a simple server.

When to use it: Is port 1433 reachable? nc -zv HOST PORT.

-z just test, send no data-v verbose-w N timeout seconds-u UDP-l listen

Open the full command reference

<!-- deeper -->

Worked answers

A sensible first five commands for "the server is slow", and what each tells you:

#CommandWhat it tells you
1uptimeload averages; compare with nproc (cores)
2top (then P/M) or `ps aux --sort=-%cpu \head`which process is using CPU or memory
3free -mis memory available, or is the system swapping?
4df -h and df -iany full file system or exhausted inodes?
5journalctl -p err -b or tail /var/log/syslogrecent errors and clues about what changed

Then, by what you found: iostat -x 1 (disk waits), ss -tn (connections), lsof -p PID (what a process has open), strace -p PID (what it is doing).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ echo "cores: $(nproc)"; awk '{print "load averages 1/5/15 min: " $1 " " $2 " " $3}' /proc/loadavg | sed -E 's/[0-9.]+/<n>/g'
cores: 4
load averages <n>/<n>/<n> min: <n> <n> <n>
$ free -m | head -1
               total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
$ df -h / | tail -1 | awk '{print "root file system use:", $5}' | sed -E 's/[0-9]+%/<n>%/'
root file system use: <n>%
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

df

What it does: Shows free and used space for each mounted file system.

When to use it: First check when a disk is full; df -i shows inodes (number of files) instead.

-h human-readable sizes-i inode usage
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

Open the full command reference

(Numbers are masked here because they differ on every machine; on your server read the real values.)

Common mistakes
  • Changing things before looking. Observe first; one change at a time; write down what you did.
  • Judging memory by the "free" column. Check "available".
  • Reading load without core count. A load of 8 is fine on 16 cores, terrible on 2.
  • Fixing the symptom (restarting) and never finding the cause; capture logs and metrics before restarting.
  • Assuming it is the application when it is DNS, disk or a full queue downstream.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Method: symptom, what changed, resources, logs, hypothesis. One change at a time.
  • Load vs cores, available memory, iowait, disk space and inodes.
  • lsof and ss -ltnp find who holds a file or port.
  • strace reveals missing files and permission errors.

Linux · Lesson 12

How containers work (namespaces and cgroups)

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain namespaces and cgroups in plain words
  • create an isolated process by hand with unshare
  • see why a container is "just a process"

The big idea

A container is not a small virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been told to isolate (it sees only its own view of the system) and limit (it may use only so much CPU and memory). Two kernel features do that:

FeatureWhat it doesExample
Namespacesgive a process its own view of somethingits own process list (PID), hostname (UTS), network, mounts, users
cgroups (control groups)limit and account for resourcesat most 256 MB memory, half a CPU

Docker adds a friendly tool, image packaging and a registry on top. Everything else is these two features.

Namespaces by hand

unshare runs a command in new namespaces. Give the process its own hostname:

Real output
$ hostname
vm
$ sudo unshare --uts bash -c 'hostname container-demo; hostname'
container-demo
$ hostname
vm
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
hostname

What it does: Shows (or sets) the computer's name.

When to use it: Confirming which server you are on, especially when you have several terminals open.

unshare

What it does: Runs a program in new Linux namespaces (its own hostname, process list, network...).

When to use it: Experimenting with how containers isolate processes.

Open the full command reference

The host's name did not change. Now its own process list:

Real output
$ sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'echo "PID inside: $$"; ps -e -o pid,comm | head -3'
PID inside: 1
    PID COMMAND
      1 bash
      2 ps
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ps

What it does: Shows a snapshot of running processes.

When to use it: Checking whether a program is running, or finding its process ID (PID).

aux every process with CPU/memory-ef full listing with parent PID-o pid,comm choose columns-p PID just that process
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Inside, the shell believes it is PID 1 and sees almost nothing else. From the host the same process has an ordinary large PID. That is the "container" illusion.

Its own network:

Real output
$ sudo unshare --net bash -c 'ip -brief link'
lo               DOWN           00:00:00:00:00:00 <LOOPBACK> 
$ echo "--- host:"
--- host:
$ ip -brief link | awk '{print $1}' | grep -c '^lo$'
1
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

ip link

What it does: Shows and changes the link layer of interfaces: up/down, creating virtual links and bridges.

When to use it: Bringing an interface up (ip link set X up), creating a veth pair or a bridge.

add NAME type veth peer name OTHER make a virtual cableset X master BR plug into a bridge
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Inside there is only a loopback device, no connection to anything. Docker later plugs a virtual cable (veth) between this namespace and a bridge.

cgroups: limits

cgroups are exposed as files. Resource limits are written into them. (Which cgroup version a host uses varies; this lab shows what is there.)

Real output
$ cat /proc/self/cgroup | head -2
9:name=systemd:/
8:pids:/
$ ls /sys/fs/cgroup | head -5
blkio
cpu
cpuacct
cpuset
devices
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

Docker uses this when you run docker run --memory 256m --cpus 0.5 .... Try a real one in the Docker track. In a cgroup, if a process uses more memory than allowed, the kernel kills it (an "OOM kill"), which is the origin of the Kubernetes status OOMKilled.

Files: images and layers

A container needs a root filesystem: the files of a small Linux userland. An image is that filesystem stored as stacked read-only layers, and a container adds a thin writable layer on top. Combining layers uses a union filesystem (overlayfs).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab && rm -rf ov && mkdir -p ov/lower ov/upper ov/work ov/merged
$ echo "from the image" > ov/lower/base.txt
$ sudo mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=ov/lower,upperdir=ov/upper,workdir=ov/work ov/merged
$ echo "added by the container" > ov/merged/new.txt
$ rm ov/merged/base.txt
$ echo "merged view:"; ls ov/merged
merged view:
new.txt
$ echo "lower (image) untouched:"; ls ov/lower
lower (image) untouched:
base.txt
$ echo "upper (container changes):"; sudo ls -a ov/upper | grep -v '^\.\.\?$'
upper (container changes):
base.txt
new.txt
$ sudo umount ov/merged
$ sudo rm -rf ov
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
mount

What it does: Attaches a disk or file system to a folder (or lists what is mounted).

When to use it: Using a new disk, a network share or a disk image.

umount

What it does: Detaches a mounted file system.

When to use it: Before removing a disk, or to clean up a test image. It fails if something is still using it.

Open the full command reference

The image layer (lower) is never modified. Deleting base.txt created a "whiteout" marker in upper. When the container is removed, the upper layer is thrown away, which is why data in a container disappears unless you use a volume.

What this means for you
  • "It is just a process" explains why ps on the host shows container processes.
  • A container shares the host kernel (unlike a VM), so it starts in a moment and a Linux container cannot run a different kernel.
  • Isolation is good but not a security boundary as strong as a VM. Run containers as non-root users where possible.

<!-- deeper -->

Practice with worked answers

  1. Which kernel feature gives a process its own process list? A PID namespace. Prove it:
Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'echo "inside the namespace my PID is $$ (a fresh numbering starts at 1)"'
inside the namespace my PID is 1 (a fresh numbering starts at 1)
$ echo "outside, the same kind of command has a normal large PID: $$ is typically > 1"
outside, the same kind of command has a normal large PID: 7047 is typically > 1
  1. How would you limit a container's memory? With a cgroup memory limit (docker run --memory 256m), which the kernel enforces by killing the process (OOM kill) if it exceeds it. You saw the exit code 137 in the Docker track.
  1. Why does deleting a file inside a container not change the image? The image layers are read-only; the change lives in the container's writable layer (the "upper" directory in the overlay demo), which is discarded with the container.
Common mistakes
  • Thinking a container is a small VM. It shares the host kernel; a kernel bug or privileged container can affect the host.
  • Running containers as root and with --privileged, which removes most of the isolation.
  • Expecting data to survive. The writable layer is deleted with the container; use volumes.
  • Forgetting cgroup limits, so one container can use all the host's memory.

<!-- /deeper -->

In plain words

  • Container = process + namespaces (isolation) + cgroups (limits) + a layered root filesystem.
  • unshare creates namespaces; /sys/fs/cgroup holds the limits; overlayfs stacks image layers.
  • These ideas return in the Docker and Kubernetes tracks.

Linux networking · Lesson 1

How networks work

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • describe the layers of networking using a postal analogy
  • tell apart MAC address, IP address and port
  • read ip addr, ip link and ip route on a Linux machine

The postal analogy

Sending a message between two computers is like posting a parcel. You need to know which building, which flat and which letterbox rule to follow. Networking splits that into layers, each doing one job and trusting the layer below.

Layer (simplified)JobPostal analogyExamples
Applicationthe actual conversationthe letter's contentHTTP, DNS, SSH, SQL
Transportwhich program, reliable or notthe flat number and "signed for"TCP, UDP, ports
Internet / Networkwhich machine, across networksthe postal addressIP address, routing
Linkhop to the next device on the same networkthe local delivery vanEthernet, Wi-Fi, MAC address

Each layer wraps the one above it, like envelopes inside envelopes. This is called encapsulation. When troubleshooting, you walk the layers from the bottom up: is the cable/link up, does the machine have an address, can it reach other networks, does the port answer, does the application behave.

Three kinds of address

AddressLooks likeIdentifiesScope
MAC52:54:00:12:34:56a network cardone local network
IP10.0.0.5 or 2001:db8::1a machine's connectionacross networks
Port443a program on that machineone machine

A full destination is usually written IP:port, for example 10.0.0.5:1433 for SQL Server. Well-known ports to memorise:

PortProtocolPortProtocol
22SSH80HTTP
443HTTPS53DNS
25SMTP (email)3389RDP
1433SQL Server5432PostgreSQL
3306MySQL389/636LDAP / LDAPS

TCP and UDP

  • TCP sets up a connection first (a three-step "handshake"), numbers the data and retransmits what is lost. Reliable. Used for web, SSH, databases.
  • UDP just sends. No connection, no guarantee. Fast. Used for DNS queries, video calls, games.

Looking at your own machine

The modern tool is ip (it replaced ifconfig). Your machine always has a loopback interface lo with address 127.0.0.1, meaning "myself".

Real output
$ ip -brief link show lo
lo               UNKNOWN        00:00:00:00:00:00 <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> 
$ ip -brief addr show lo
lo               UNKNOWN        127.0.0.1/8 
$ ip route show | wc -l
3
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
ip link

What it does: Shows and changes the link layer of interfaces: up/down, creating virtual links and bridges.

When to use it: Bringing an interface up (ip link set X up), creating a veth pair or a bridge.

add NAME type veth peer name OTHER make a virtual cableset X master BR plug into a bridge
ip addr

What it does: Shows (or sets) IP addresses on network interfaces.

When to use it: What IP address does this machine have? ip -br addr gives a short table.

add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth0 assign an addressflush dev eth0 remove addresses
ip route

What it does: Shows or edits the routing table: where traffic for each network is sent.

When to use it: Why can I not reach that network? Adding a static route or default gateway.

add default via GW set the default gatewayadd NET via GW static route
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

Output columns of ip -brief addr: interface name, state (UP, DOWN, or UNKNOWN for loopback), then addresses with their prefix length (/8). The prefix length says which part of the address is the "network" and which is the "host"; the next lesson explains it.

CommandShows
ip addr (or ip a)interfaces and their IP addresses
ip linkthe link layer: up/down, MAC
ip routewhere traffic is sent (the routing table)
ip neighthe ARP table: IP to MAC for neighbours
ss -tulpnlistening TCP/UDP ports and their programs

On the Windows side the equivalents are ipconfig /all, route print, arp -a, netstat -ano (covered in the PowerShell track).

Your machine talking to itself

Start a tiny web server on loopback and fetch from it. The whole stack (IP, TCP, HTTP) runs inside your machine:

Real output
$ python3 -m http.server 8099 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ pid=$!
$ sleep 1
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "HTTP status: %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8099/
HTTP status: 200
$ ss -ltn | awk '$4 ~ /:8099$/ {print "listening on", $4}'
listening on 127.0.0.1:8099
$ kill $pid
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method
ss

What it does: Shows network sockets: listening ports and connections.

When to use it: Which program is listening on port 8080? Is the service up?

-l listening-t TCP-u UDP-n numbers not names-p show the process
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
kill

What it does: Sends a signal to a process (by default asks it to stop politely, SIGTERM).

When to use it: Stopping a process or job: kill PID. Use kill -9 PID only if it ignores the polite request.

-15 (default) please terminate-9 force kill, no cleanup-0 only check the process exists-l list signals

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Layers: application, transport (TCP/UDP + ports), internet (IP), link (MAC).
  • MAC = card, IP = machine, port = program.
  • TCP is reliable and connection based; UDP is fast and connectionless.
  • ip addr, ip link, ip route, ip neigh, ss are the core inspection tools.
Your turn

A user says "I cannot open the EV search page". Order these checks from the lowest layer up: web page loads, name resolves, port 443 reachable, cable connected, machine has an IP address, gateway reachable.

Linux networking · Lesson 2

IP addressing and subnets

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read an IPv4 address in binary and decimal
  • explain subnet masks and CIDR (/24)
  • work out network, broadcast and usable range
  • recognise private address ranges

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number

192.168.1.10 is four numbers (0 to 255) called octets, each 8 bits: 11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010. Humans use the dotted form.

Real output
$ python3 - <<'EOF'
> import ipaddress
> ip = ipaddress.ip_address("192.168.1.10")
> print("as a number:", int(ip))
> print("as binary  :", ".".join(f"{o:08b}" for o in ip.packed))
> EOF
as a number: 3232235786
as binary  : 11000000.10101000.00000001.00001010
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON

Open the full command reference

Network part and host part

An address has two parts: which network it is on and which host within it. The subnet mask (or prefix length) marks the split. Written with a slash it is CIDR notation:

CIDRMaskNetwork bitsHost bitsAddresses
/8255.0.0.082416,777,216
/16255.255.0.0161665,536
/24255.255.255.0248256
/25255.255.255.128257128
/26255.255.255.19226664
/30255.255.255.2523024

192.168.1.10/24 means: the first 24 bits (192.168.1) are the network, the last 8 bits are the host. Two machines can talk directly only if they are on the same network; otherwise traffic goes through a router (gateway).

Of the addresses in a subnet, the first (all host bits 0) is the network address and the last (all host bits 1) is the broadcast address. Neither can be given to a host, so usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2.

Real output
$ python3 - <<'EOF'
> import ipaddress
> for cidr in ["192.168.1.10/24", "10.0.5.77/26", "172.16.0.9/30"]:
>     n = ipaddress.ip_interface(cidr).network
>     hosts = list(n.hosts())
>     print(f"{cidr:16} network={n.network_address}  broadcast={n.broadcast_address}  usable={len(hosts)}  range={hosts[0]} - {hosts[-1]}")
> EOF
192.168.1.10/24  network=192.168.1.0  broadcast=192.168.1.255  usable=254  range=192.168.1.1 - 192.168.1.254
10.0.5.77/26     network=10.0.5.64  broadcast=10.0.5.127  usable=62  range=10.0.5.65 - 10.0.5.126
172.16.0.9/30    network=172.16.0.8  broadcast=172.16.0.11  usable=2  range=172.16.0.9 - 172.16.0.10

Try the calculator

Same network or not?

Real output
$ python3 - <<'EOF'
> import ipaddress
> def same(a, b, prefix):
>     net = ipaddress.ip_network(f"{a}/{prefix}", strict=False)
>     return ipaddress.ip_address(b) in net
> print("10.0.0.5 and 10.0.0.200 on /24 :", same("10.0.0.5", "10.0.0.200", 24))
> print("10.0.0.5 and 10.0.1.5   on /24 :", same("10.0.0.5", "10.0.1.5", 24))
> print("10.0.0.5 and 10.0.1.5   on /23 :", same("10.0.0.5", "10.0.1.5", 23))
> EOF
10.0.0.5 and 10.0.0.200 on /24 : True
10.0.0.5 and 10.0.1.5   on /24 : False
10.0.0.5 and 10.0.1.5   on /23 : True

A very common real fault: two machines have the right addresses but different masks and cannot reach each other.

Private ranges and special addresses

RangeCIDRUse
10.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.25510.0.0.0/8private networks
172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255172.16.0.0/12private (Docker uses 172.17.x)
192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255192.168.0.0/16home and small office
127.0.0.0/8loopback
169.254.0.0/16link-local: assigned when DHCP fails (a "169.254" address means DHCP did not answer)
0.0.0.0"any address" or "unknown"

Private addresses are not routed on the internet. A NAT device (your router, a cloud gateway) rewrites them to a public address; a later lesson builds one.

Real output
$ python3 - <<'EOF'
> import ipaddress
> for a in ["10.1.2.3", "172.20.0.5", "192.168.0.9", "169.254.10.1", "8.8.8.8"]:
>     ip = ipaddress.ip_address(a)
>     print(f"{a:14} private={ip.is_private} link_local={ip.is_link_local}")
> EOF
10.1.2.3       private=True link_local=False
172.20.0.5     private=True link_local=False
192.168.0.9    private=True link_local=False
169.254.10.1   private=True link_local=True
8.8.8.8        private=False link_local=False

How addresses are assigned

  • Static: you type it in. Used for servers.
  • DHCP: a server hands out an address, mask, gateway and DNS server automatically (lease). Used for most clients.
  • IPv6: 128-bit addresses like 2001:db8::1, written in hex. The ideas (prefix, host part, routing) are the same; it removes the shortage of IPv4 addresses.

In plain words

  • IPv4 = 32 bits shown as four octets. The prefix (/24) says how many bits are the network.
  • Network address and broadcast address are not usable. Usable = 2^host bits - 2.
  • Same network means direct delivery; otherwise via a gateway.
  • Private ranges: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16. 169.254 means DHCP failed.
Your turn

How many usable hosts in a /27? Is 10.0.0.130 in 10.0.0.0/25? Check your answers with the calculator.

Linux networking · Lesson 3

Build a network on one machine

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • create network namespaces and virtual cables (veth)
  • assign addresses and bring links up
  • see ARP resolve an IP address into a MAC address
  • use a bridge as a virtual switch for more than two machines

A lab with no hardware

Linux can create network namespaces: each has its own interfaces, addresses and routing table, so it behaves like a separate computer. A veth pair is a virtual network cable with a plug at each end. With these two features we can build real networks and use real tools on them. (This is also exactly how containers get their networking.)

Create two "computers", red and blue:

Real output
$ sudo ip netns add red
$ sudo ip netns add blue
$ ip netns list | sort
blue
red
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ip netns

What it does: Manages network namespaces: separate virtual machines' worth of network stack inside one Linux machine.

When to use it: Building practice networks, and understanding how containers get their network.

add NAME createexec NAME CMD run a command insidedel NAME deletelist show namespaces
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G

Open the full command reference

Inside a namespace the machine is empty: not even loopback is up. Run commands in it with ip netns exec NAME command.

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec red ip -brief link
lo               DOWN           00:00:00:00:00:00 <LOOPBACK>

Cable, addresses, power on

Real output
$ sudo ip link add vr type veth peer name vb
$ sudo ip link set vr netns red
$ sudo ip link set vb netns blue
$ sudo ip -n red  addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev vr
$ sudo ip -n blue addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev vb
$ sudo ip -n red  link set vr up
$ sudo ip -n blue link set vb up
$ sudo ip -n red  -brief addr show vr
vr@if27          UP             10.0.0.1/24 
$ sudo ip -n blue -brief addr show vb
vb@if28          UP             10.0.0.2/24
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ip link

What it does: Shows and changes the link layer of interfaces: up/down, creating virtual links and bridges.

When to use it: Bringing an interface up (ip link set X up), creating a veth pair or a bridge.

add NAME type veth peer name OTHER make a virtual cableset X master BR plug into a bridge
ip

What it does: The modern tool to show and configure network interfaces, addresses and routes.

When to use it: Check your IP address (ip addr), the routing table (ip route), links (ip link).

-br brief one-line-per-interface output

Open the full command reference

The same recipe on any machine: 1. interface exists, 2. it has an address and mask, 3. it is up.

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 2 -W 1 10.0.0.2
PING 10.0.0.2 (10.0.0.2) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.0.0.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.455 ms
64 bytes from 10.0.0.2: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.043 ms

--- 10.0.0.2 ping statistics ---
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1014ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 0.043/0.249/0.455/0.206 ms

Success. Before the first packet could be sent, red had to ask "who has 10.0.0.2?" That question is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol), broadcast to everyone on the link; blue answers with its MAC address. Red remembers the answer in its neighbour table:

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec red ip neigh show | awk '{print $1, $4=="lladdr" ? "has a MAC" : $4, $NF}'
10.0.0.2 has a MAC REACHABLE
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100

Open the full command reference

What if we forget a step?

Break things on purpose. This is how you learn to diagnose.

Real output
$ sudo ip -n blue link set vb down
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.0.2 2>&1 | tail -2
1 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 0ms
$ sudo ip -n blue link set vb up
$ sudo ip -n blue addr flush dev vb
$ sudo ip -n blue addr add 10.0.1.2/24 dev vb
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.0.2 2>&1 | tail -2
1 packets transmitted, 0 received, 100% packet loss, time 0ms
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.1.2 2>&1 | tail -2
ping: connect: Network is unreachable
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

Open the full command reference

Two different failures. With the link down, nothing arrives. After the address change, nobody owns 10.0.0.2 any more, so the ARP question goes unanswered and the ping gets no reply either. With blue on a different subnet (10.0.1.0/24), red does not even try to reach it directly: it has no route to 10.0.1.2, so it reports Network is unreachable. That message always means "I have no route for that address", not "the other machine is off".

More than two machines: a bridge

A bridge is a virtual switch. Plug several cables into it and all machines on it share one network. Add green and put all three on a bridge:

Real output
$ sudo ip -n blue addr flush dev vb
$ sudo ip -n blue link set vb down
$ sudo ip netns del red
$ sudo ip netns del blue
$ sudo ip link add br0 type bridge
$ sudo ip link set br0 up
$ for h in red blue green; do
>   sudo ip netns add $h
>   sudo ip link add v-$h type veth peer name p-$h
>   sudo ip link set v-$h netns $h
>   sudo ip link set p-$h master br0
>   sudo ip link set p-$h up
>   sudo ip -n $h link set v-$h up
> done
$ sudo ip -n red   addr add 10.0.0.1/24 dev v-red
$ sudo ip -n blue  addr add 10.0.0.2/24 dev v-blue
$ sudo ip -n green addr add 10.0.0.3/24 dev v-green
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.0.2 | grep -c "1 received"
1
$ sudo ip netns exec red ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.0.3 | grep -c "1 received"
1
$ sudo ip netns exec green ping -c 1 -W 1 10.0.0.2 | grep -c "1 received"
1
$ bridge link | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's/@.*//' | sort
p-blue
p-green
p-red
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
for

What it does: A loop that repeats commands once for each item in a list.

When to use it: Doing the same thing to several files, servers or numbers: for h in ev01 sql01; do ...; done.

grep

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

When to use it: Seeing which interfaces are plugged into a bridge such as docker0.

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

In plain words

  • A namespace is a virtual computer; a veth pair is a cable; a bridge is a switch.
  • Connectivity checklist: interface exists, has address and mask, is up.
  • ARP maps an IP to a MAC on the local network.
  • "Network is unreachable" means no route; no reply means something else.

Linux networking · Lesson 4

Routing and gateways

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • read a routing table
  • explain the default gateway
  • build a router between two networks and enable forwarding
  • use traceroute to see the path

The routing table

Every machine decides where to send each packet by looking at its routing table. The rule is simple: find the most specific matching route (longest prefix) and send the packet there. Anything that matches nothing else goes to the default route (default via ...), the default gateway, which is the router that knows the way out.

A router between two networks

Topology: host a is in 10.1.0.0/24, host b is in 10.2.0.0/24, and r sits between them with a leg in each.

a (10.1.0.2) --- (10.1.0.1) r (10.2.0.1) --- (10.2.0.2) b
Real output
$ for n in a r b; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
$ sudo ip link add a-r type veth peer name r-a
$ sudo ip link add b-r type veth peer name r-b
$ sudo ip link set a-r netns a; sudo ip link set r-a netns r
$ sudo ip link set b-r netns b; sudo ip link set r-b netns r
$ sudo ip -n a addr add 10.1.0.2/24 dev a-r
$ sudo ip -n r addr add 10.1.0.1/24 dev r-a
$ sudo ip -n r addr add 10.2.0.1/24 dev r-b
$ sudo ip -n b addr add 10.2.0.2/24 dev b-r
$ for p in "a a-r" "r r-a" "r r-b" "b b-r"; do set -- $p; sudo ip -n $1 link set $2 up; done
$ sudo ip netns exec a ip route
10.1.0.0/24 dev a-r proto kernel scope link src 10.1.0.2

default via 10.1.0.1 dev a-r

Still no reply. The packet reaches r, but by default Linux does not forward packets between interfaces. A router is just a computer with forwarding switched on:

Real output

net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
$ sudo ip netns exec a ping -c 2 -W 1 10.2.0.2 | grep -E "received"
2 packets transmitted, 2 received, 0% packet loss, time 1003ms
$ sudo ip netns exec a traceroute -n -m 3 10.2.0.2 | awk '{print $1, $2}'
traceroute to
1 10.1.0.1
2 10.2.0.2

The traceroute shows two hops: first the router 10.1.0.1, then the destination 10.2.0.2. Each hop is a router decrementing the packet's TTL (time to live); when it reaches 0 the router reports back, which is how traceroute discovers the path.

Reading the table, line by line

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec r ip route
10.1.0.0/24 dev r-a proto kernel scope link src 10.1.0.1 
10.2.0.0/24 dev r-b proto kernel scope link src 10.2.0.1

Each line is destination via gateway dev interface. A line without via means "directly connected": deliver on that interface. Everything the router needs is there because both its networks are directly attached.

Static versus dynamic routing

KindHow routes appearWhere
Directly connectedautomatically from interface addresseseverywhere
Staticyou add them (ip route add)small networks, cloud route tables
Dynamic (OSPF, BGP)routers exchange themlarge networks, the internet

In AWS or Azure, "route tables" are exactly this idea: a list of destination -> target lines, with 0.0.0.0/0 as the default route pointing to an internet gateway or NAT.

On Windows

route print shows the table, route add 10.2.0.0 mask 255.255.255.0 10.1.0.1 adds a static route, and tracert is traceroute.

Real output
$ for n in a r b; do sudo ip netns del $n; done
$ sudo ip netns list | wc -l
0

wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • A route is "to reach this network, send to this next hop".
  • The default gateway (default via) catches everything not matched by a more specific route.
  • Forwarding (ip_forward) turns a Linux machine into a router.
  • traceroute reveals hops using TTL.
