Linux networking · Lesson 5

Ports, TCP and sockets

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain listening ports and connections
  • use ss, nc and curl to test a service
  • read a TCP three-way handshake in tcpdump
  • tell "connection refused" from "timed out"

Servers listen, clients connect

A server program asks the operating system to listen on a port. A client then connects to IP:port. Each connection is identified by four values: client IP, client port, server IP, server port. The client's port is a random "ephemeral" high port.

Build the same two-computer lab as before, with a web server on srv:

Real output
$ for n in srv cli; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
$ sudo ip link add s0 type veth peer name c0
$ sudo ip link set s0 netns srv; sudo ip link set c0 netns cli
$ sudo ip -n srv addr add 10.9.0.1/24 dev s0; sudo ip -n cli addr add 10.9.0.2/24 dev c0
$ sudo ip -n srv link set s0 up; sudo ip -n cli link set c0 up
$ sudo ip netns exec srv python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.9.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sleep 1
$ sudo ip netns exec srv ss -ltn | awk 'NR==1 || /8080/ {print $1, $4}'
State Local
LISTEN 10.9.0.1:8080

Testing a port, three ways

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec cli curl -s -o /dev/null -w "curl: HTTP %{http_code}\n" http://10.9.0.1:8080/
curl: HTTP 200
$ sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv 10.9.0.1 8080 2>&1 | tail -1
Connection to 10.9.0.1 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!
$ sudo ip netns exec cli bash -c 'timeout 2 bash -c "</dev/tcp/10.9.0.1/8080" && echo "bash /dev/tcp: open"'

What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Open the full command reference

nc -zv host port is the quick "is this port open?" tool. The bash /dev/tcp trick works even when nc is not installed.

Refused versus timed out

The two failure messages mean different things. This is the most useful diagnosis rule in networking.

Real output
$ echo "-- nothing listening on port 9999:"
-- nothing listening on port 9999:
$ sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.1 9999 2>&1 | tail -1
nc: connect to 10.9.0.1 port 9999 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
$ echo "-- host that does not exist on the network:"
-- host that does not exist on the network:
$ sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.77 8080 2>&1 | tail -1
nc: connect to 10.9.0.77 port 8080 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
SymptomMeaning
Connection refusedthe machine is reachable, but nothing listens on that port (or it actively rejects). The service is down or the port is wrong
Timed out (no answer)packets are being dropped or never arrive: firewall, wrong route, host down
No route to host / unreachableyour machine has no path to it

The three-way handshake

TCP starts every connection with three packets: SYN (client: "let us talk"), SYN-ACK (server: "okay"), ACK (client: "okay"). tcpdump lets us see them. [S] is SYN, [S.] is SYN-ACK, [.] is ACK, [F.] is FIN (close).

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec srv timeout 5 tcpdump -n -l -i s0 'tcp port 8080' 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $3, ">", $5, $7}' | sed 's/:$//' | head -4 &
$ sleep 1
$ sudo ip netns exec cli curl -s -o /dev/null http://10.9.0.1:8080/
$ wait %2 2>/dev/null
10.9.0.2.37282 > 10.9.0.1.8080: [S],
10.9.0.1.8080 > 10.9.0.2.37282: [S.],
10.9.0.2.37282 > 10.9.0.1.8080: [.],
10.9.0.2.37282 > 10.9.0.1.8080: [P.],
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
wait

What it does: Waits for background jobs to finish.

When to use it: In scripts, after starting several jobs with &.

Open the full command reference

(The first four lines show: client SYN [S], server SYN-ACK [S.], client ACK [.], then the HTTP request [P.]. Port numbers on the client side are random.)

UDP is different

UDP has no handshake: a datagram is sent and may simply vanish. DNS queries use it. A UDP "port open" test cannot get a refusal in the same way, so it is harder to test.

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec srv bash -c 'timeout 3 nc -u -l 10.9.0.1 5353 > /tmp/udp.out &'
$ sleep 0.5
$ echo "hello over UDP" | sudo ip netns exec cli nc -u -w 1 10.9.0.1 5353
$ sleep 0.5
$ cat /tmp/udp.out; sudo rm -f /tmp/udp.out
hello over UDP
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

$ sudo ip netns del srv; sudo ip netns del cli

Open the full command reference

A reusable triage

Cannot reach a service? Run in this order: ping IP (route and link), nc -zv IP PORT (port), curl -v URL (application). The first one that fails tells you the layer.

In plain words

  • Servers listen on ports; clients connect from random high ports.
  • ss -ltn lists listeners, nc -zv and curl test them.
  • Refused = reachable but nothing listening. Timeout = dropped or unreachable.
  • TCP handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. tcpdump shows it.

Linux networking · Lesson 6

DNS: names to addresses

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what DNS does and the main record types
  • trace how a machine resolves a name (/etc/hosts, resolver, DNS server)
  • run a small DNS server and query it with dig
  • diagnose resolution failures like the EV "Name resolution failed for SQL01"

Why DNS exists

People remember names (sql01.corp.local); networks use addresses (10.0.5.20). DNS (Domain Name System) is the global phone book that translates one into the other. It is also a hierarchy: read a name right to left. sql01.corp.local is host sql01 in domain corp in the top-level local. Each level of the hierarchy is run by different name servers.

Main record types

RecordMeaningExample
Aname to IPv4 addresssql01.lab -> 10.0.0.20
AAAAname to IPv6 address
CNAMEalias to another namewww -> web01
MXmail server for a domain
TXTfree text (SPF, verification)
PTRreverse: address to name
NSwhich servers are authoritative for the zone
SRVservice location (used by Active Directory)

How your machine resolves a name

  1. Check local overrides: the hosts file (/etc/hosts; on Windows C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts).
  2. Check the local cache.
  3. Ask the DNS server listed in /etc/resolv.conf (given by DHCP or typed in). That server may ask others on your behalf (recursion) and caches the answer for the record's TTL (time to live).

The order is controlled by /etc/nsswitch.conf:

Real output
$ grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf
hosts:          files dns
$ cat /etc/hosts | head -3
127.0.0.1 localhost
160.79.104.10 api.anthropic.com
127.0.0.1 runsc
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Tools: getent hosts NAME resolves the way programs do (hosts file, then DNS). dig and nslookup query DNS directly, skipping the hosts file.

Real output
$ echo "10.0.0.20 sql01.lab" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts > /dev/null
$ getent hosts sql01.lab
10.0.0.20       sql01.lab
$ sudo sed -i '/sql01.lab/d' /etc/hosts
$ getent hosts sql01.lab || echo "no answer: name does not resolve"
no answer: name does not resolve

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

What it does: Copies its input to both the screen and a file.

A DNS server of our own

dnsmasq is a tiny DNS (and DHCP) server. We run one in a network namespace, with two records, and ask it with dig.

Real output
$ for n in dns cli; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
$ sudo ip link add d0 type veth peer name c0
$ sudo ip link set d0 netns dns; sudo ip link set c0 netns cli
$ sudo ip -n dns addr add 10.7.0.1/24 dev d0; sudo ip -n cli addr add 10.7.0.2/24 dev c0
$ sudo ip -n dns link set d0 up; sudo ip -n cli link set c0 up
$ sudo ip netns exec dns dnsmasq --no-daemon --no-resolv --no-hosts --listen-address=10.7.0.1 --bind-interfaces \
>   --local=/lab/ --address=/sql01.lab/10.0.0.20 --address=/ev01.lab/10.0.0.10 --cname=www.lab,ev01.lab \
>   --pid-file=/tmp/dnsmasq-lab.pid > /tmp/dnsmasq-lab.log 2>&1 &
$ sleep 1
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.1 sql01.lab A +short
10.0.0.20
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.1 ev01.lab A +short
10.0.0.10
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.1 www.lab +short
ev01.lab.

+short prints just the answer. Without it, dig shows the full response. The useful parts:

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.1 sql01.lab A +noall +answer +comments | grep -v "^;; OPT\|^;; flags\|^$" | sed 's/id: [0-9]*/id: NNNN/'
;; Got answer:
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: NNNN
; EDNS: version: 0, flags:; udp: 1232
;; ANSWER SECTION:
sql01.lab.		0	IN	A	10.0.0.20

The answer line reads: name, TTL, class IN, type A, value. status: NOERROR means the server answered. Now see failures, because that is what you will actually meet:

Real output
$ echo "-- a name the server does not know:"
-- a name the server does not know:
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.1 nosuch.lab A +noall +comments | grep -o "status: [A-Z]*"
status: NXDOMAIN
$ echo "-- a DNS server that is not there:"
-- a DNS server that is not there:
$ sudo ip netns exec cli dig @10.7.0.99 sql01.lab +time=1 +tries=1 2>&1 | grep -E "timed out|no servers" | head -1
;; communications error to 10.7.0.99#53: timed out
ResultMeaning
NOERROR with an answerall good
NXDOMAINthe name does not exist (typo, missing record)
SERVFAILthe server tried and failed (upstream problem)
timeout / "no servers could be reached"cannot reach the DNS server at all (network, firewall, wrong server)

This maps directly to the EV log line Name resolution failed for SQL01: it is either NXDOMAIN (record missing, wrong domain suffix), or a timeout (DNS server unreachable), and the quickest way to know which is dig/nslookup against the server your machine actually uses.

Real output
$ sudo pkill -f "[d]nsmasq.*sql01.lab" ; sleep 0.3
$ sudo ip netns del dns; sudo ip netns del cli
$ sudo rm -f /tmp/dnsmasq-lab.log /tmp/dnsmasq-lab.pid
$ sudo ip netns list | wc -l
0
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
pkill

What it does: Sends a signal to processes selected by name.

When to use it: Stopping all processes of a program.

-f match full command line-9 force kill

Careful: A loose pattern can kill things you did not intend. Check first with pgrep -a.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

Windows side

nslookup sql01, Resolve-DnsName sql01, ipconfig /flushdns (clear cache), ipconfig /displaydns. In an EV/Active Directory world, DNS also stores where the domain controllers are (SRV records), so broken DNS breaks logins, not just names.

In plain words

  • DNS translates names to addresses; records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, PTR, NS, SRV.
  • Resolution order: hosts file, cache, the configured DNS server (which recurses and caches by TTL).
  • dig NAME / dig @server NAME, getent hosts, nslookup.
  • NXDOMAIN = name missing; timeout = server unreachable; SERVFAIL = upstream error.

ping sql01 says "unknown host" but ping 10.0.0.20 works. Name three things you would check, in order, and which commands you would use.

Linux networking · Lesson 7

Firewalls and NAT

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a firewall rule is (match, action) and why order matters
  • write nftables rules to allow and block ports
  • explain NAT and port forwarding and build them

A firewall is a list of rules

A firewall inspects packets and decides: accept, drop (silently discard, the client times out) or reject (refuse loudly, the client sees "refused"). Rules are checked in order and the first match wins. The usual design is: default deny, then allow only what is needed (SSH, HTTPS...).

Linux's firewall is netfilter, configured with nftables (command nft) or the older iptables. Tools like ufw (Ubuntu) and firewalld (Red Hat) are friendlier front ends. In cloud platforms the same idea is called a security group or network security group. On Windows it is Windows Defender Firewall.

Block a port, see the difference

Rebuild the server and client from the ports lesson. The server runs two web services, on ports 8080 and 9090.

Real output
$ for n in srv cli; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
$ sudo ip link add s0 type veth peer name c0
$ sudo ip link set s0 netns srv; sudo ip link set c0 netns cli
$ sudo ip -n srv addr add 10.9.0.1/24 dev s0; sudo ip -n cli addr add 10.9.0.2/24 dev c0
$ sudo ip -n srv link set s0 up; sudo ip -n cli link set c0 up
$ sudo ip netns exec srv python3 -m http.server 8080 --bind 10.9.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sudo ip netns exec srv python3 -m http.server 9090 --bind 10.9.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sleep 1
$ for p in 8080 9090; do sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.1 $p 2>&1 | tail -1; done
Connection to 10.9.0.1 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!
Connection to 10.9.0.1 9090 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
for

What it does: A loop that repeats commands once for each item in a list.

When to use it: Doing the same thing to several files, servers or numbers: for h in ev01 sql01; do ...; done.

ip netns

What it does: Manages network namespaces: separate virtual machines' worth of network stack inside one Linux machine.

When to use it: Building practice networks, and understanding how containers get their network.

add NAME createexec NAME CMD run a command insidedel NAME deletelist show namespaces
ip

What it does: The modern tool to show and configure network interfaces, addresses and routes.

When to use it: Check your IP address (ip addr), the routing table (ip route), links (ip link).

-br brief one-line-per-interface output
ip link

What it does: Shows and changes the link layer of interfaces: up/down, creating virtual links and bridges.

When to use it: Bringing an interface up (ip link set X up), creating a veth pair or a bridge.

add NAME type veth peer name OTHER make a virtual cableset X master BR plug into a bridge
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

Open the full command reference

Now give the server a firewall with default deny, allowing only 8080:

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec srv nft -f - <<'EOF'
> table inet filter {
>   chain input {
>     type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
>     iif lo accept
>     ct state established,related accept
>     icmp type echo-request accept
>     tcp dport 8080 accept
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ sudo ip netns exec srv nft list chain inet filter input
table inet filter {
	chain input {
		type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop;
		iif "lo" accept
		ct state established,related accept
		icmp type echo-request accept
		tcp dport 8080 accept
	}
}

Read the rules in order: allow loopback, allow replies to connections we started (established,related), allow ping, allow TCP port 8080, and everything else is dropped by the policy drop.

Real output
$ for p in 8080 9090; do sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.1 $p 2>&1 | tail -1; done
Connection to 10.9.0.1 8080 port [tcp/http-alt] succeeded!
nc: connect to 10.9.0.1 port 9090 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress

8080 works; 9090 times out (silent drop), as predicted in the last lesson. Switch to an active reject and the symptom changes to "refused":

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec srv nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 9090 reject with tcp reset
$ sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.1 9090 2>&1 | tail -1
nc: connect to 10.9.0.1 port 9090 (tcp) failed: Connection refused
$ sudo ip netns exec srv nft flush ruleset
$ sudo ip netns exec cli nc -zv -w 2 10.9.0.1 9090 2>&1 | tail -1
Connection to 10.9.0.1 9090 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
Two classic mistakes
  1. Setting default deny on a remote server before allowing SSH, and locking yourself out. Always add the allow rule first (and have a console or a timed rollback).
  2. Rules that are correct but in the wrong order: an early accept or drop hides later rules.

NAT: many private addresses behind one public one

Private addresses (10.x, 192.168.x) cannot travel on the internet. NAT (network address translation) fixes that: a gateway rewrites the source address of outgoing packets to its own public address, remembers the mapping, and translates replies back. This is why your home router lets all your devices share one connection.

TypeRewritesUsed for
SNAT / masqueradesource address of outgoing packetsprivate network to the internet
DNAT / port forwarddestination of incoming packetspublish an internal service: "public:80 -> 10.0.0.10:8080"

Build it: inside (10.1.0.2) -> gw (10.1.0.1 inside, 192.0.2.1 outside) -> outside (192.0.2.2), where the outside server records who connected to it.

Real output
$ sudo pkill -f "[h]ttp.server" ; for n in srv cli; do sudo ip netns del $n; done
$ for n in inside gw outside; do sudo ip netns add $n; sudo ip -n $n link set lo up; done
$ sudo ip link add i0 type veth peer name g0; sudo ip link set i0 netns inside; sudo ip link set g0 netns gw
$ sudo ip link add g1 type veth peer name o0; sudo ip link set g1 netns gw; sudo ip link set o0 netns outside
$ sudo ip -n inside addr add 10.1.0.2/24 dev i0;  sudo ip -n gw addr add 10.1.0.1/24 dev g0
$ sudo ip -n gw addr add 192.0.2.1/24 dev g1;     sudo ip -n outside addr add 192.0.2.2/24 dev o0
$ for p in "inside i0" "gw g0" "gw g1" "outside o0"; do set -- $p; sudo ip -n $1 link set $2 up; done
$ sudo ip -n inside route add default via 10.1.0.1
$ sudo ip netns exec gw sysctl -qw net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
$ sudo ip netns exec outside python3 -c "
> import http.server
> class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
>     def do_GET(self):
>         self.send_response(200); self.end_headers()
>         self.wfile.write(('you connected from ' + self.client_address[0] + '\n').encode())
>     def log_message(self, *a): pass
> http.server.HTTPServer(('192.0.2.2', 8000), H).serve_forever()" &
$ sleep 1
$ echo "-- without NAT:"
-- without NAT:
$ sudo ip netns exec inside curl -s -m 2 http://192.0.2.2:8000/ || echo "no reply (the outside host has no route back to 10.1.0.0/24)"
no reply (the outside host has no route back to 10.1.0.0/24)
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
pkill

What it does: Sends a signal to processes selected by name.

When to use it: Stopping all processes of a program.

-f match full command line-9 force kill

Careful: A loose pattern can kill things you did not intend. Check first with pgrep -a.

set

What it does: Shows shell settings and variables, or changes shell options (set -e, set -x).

When to use it: In scripts, set -euo pipefail makes the script stop at the first error.

-e exit on error-u error on unset variables-x print each command as it runs-o pipefail a pipeline fails if any part fails
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

The request leaves, but the reply cannot find its way back to a private address. Turn on masquerade on the gateway:

Real output
$ sudo ip netns exec gw nft -f - <<'EOF'
> table ip nat {
>   chain postrouting {
>     type nat hook postrouting priority 100;
>     oif "g1" masquerade
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ echo "-- with NAT:"
-- with NAT:
$ sudo ip netns exec inside curl -s -m 2 http://192.0.2.2:8000/
you connected from 192.0.2.1

The outside server sees 192.0.2.1 (the gateway), not 10.1.0.2. That is NAT. DNAT is the mirror image for inbound traffic: nft add rule ip nat prerouting tcp dport 80 dnat to 10.1.0.2:8080 publishes an internal server. Docker's -p 8080:80 does exactly this behind the scenes.

Real output
$ sudo pkill -f "[H]TTPServer" ; sudo ip netns pids outside | xargs -r sudo kill
$ for n in inside gw outside; do sudo ip netns del $n; done
$ sudo ip netns list | wc -l
0
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Firewall rules: match, then accept/drop/reject; first match wins; default deny.
  • drop causes timeouts; reject causes "refused".
  • nftables: tables, chains, rules. nft list ruleset to inspect.
  • SNAT/masquerade shares one public address; DNAT/port forwarding publishes an internal service.
  • Cloud security groups and Docker port mapping are the same ideas.

Write nft rules for a web server that allows SSH only from 10.0.0.0/24 and HTTPS from anywhere, dropping the rest. Which rule must come before the default drop takes effect?

Linux networking · Lesson 8

Troubleshooting, HTTP and TLS

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • follow a bottom-up network troubleshooting checklist
  • read an HTTP request and response with curl -v
  • create a certificate and understand what TLS verifies

The checklist

When "it is not working", walk up the layers, stop at the first failure:

StepQuestionCommand
1Is my link up and do I have an address?ip -br addr, ip -br link
2Can I reach my gateway?ip route, ping GATEWAY
3Can I reach the target by IP?ping IP, traceroute IP
4Does the name resolve?getent hosts NAME, dig NAME
5Is the port open?nc -zv IP PORT, ss -ltn on the server
6Does the application answer correctly?curl -v URL, logs
7Is a firewall in the way?nft list ruleset, cloud security groups, traceroute stopping

Also remember that ping can be blocked while the service is fine (ICMP filtered), so a failed ping is a hint, not proof.

HTTP, line by line

HTTP is plain text on top of TCP. A client sends a request line and headers; the server answers with a status code, headers and a body.

Real output
$ python3 -m http.server 8077 --bind 127.0.0.1 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sleep 1
$ curl -s -v -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8077/ 2>&1 | grep -E '^(> |< )' | grep -vE '(Date|Server|Last-Modified|Content-Length):' | tr -d '\r'
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:8077
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
> 
< HTTP/1.0 200 OK
< Content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
< 
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "missing page -> HTTP %{http_code}\n" http://127.0.0.1:8077/nope
missing page -> HTTP 404
$ pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8077"
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

tr

What it does: Translates or deletes single characters.

When to use it: Converting case (tr a-z A-Z), squeezing spaces, or turning separators into newlines.

-d delete the characters-s squeeze repeats into one
pkill

What it does: Sends a signal to processes selected by name.

When to use it: Stopping all processes of a program.

-f match full command line-9 force kill

Careful: A loose pattern can kill things you did not intend. Check first with pgrep -a.

Open the full command reference

> lines are what the client sent, < lines what came back. Status codes you must know:

CodeMeaningThink
200OKworks
301 / 302redirectfollow the Location: header
401 / 403not authenticated / not allowedcredentials or permissions
404not foundwrong URL
500 / 502 / 503 / 504server error / bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeoutthe problem is behind the web server

TLS: what the padlock means

HTTPS is HTTP inside TLS, which gives encryption (nobody on the path can read it) and authentication (you are really talking to that server). Authentication uses a certificate: a signed statement "this public key belongs to ev01.corp.local". The signer is a certificate authority (CA) that your machine already trusts. A client checks that the name matches, the dates are valid and the signature chains up to a trusted CA.

Create a certificate yourself (self-signed: signed by itself, so nobody trusts it, but the structure is identical):

Real output
$ cd ~/lab && rm -f ev.key ev.crt
$ openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout ev.key -out ev.crt -days 365 \
>   -subj "/CN=ev01.corp.local" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:ev01.corp.local" 2>/dev/null
$ openssl x509 -in ev.crt -noout -subject -issuer -ext subjectAltName | sed 's/^ *//'
subject=CN = ev01.corp.local
issuer=CN = ev01.corp.local
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: 
DNS:ev01.corp.local
$ openssl x509 -in ev.crt -noout -dates | sed 's/=.*20/=...20/' | cut -c1-12
notBefore=..
notAfter=...
$ stat -c '%a %n' ev.key ev.crt
600 ev.key
644 ev.crt
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

openssl

What it does: Toolkit for certificates, keys and encryption.

When to use it: Creating a test certificate, inspecting a certificate's names and dates, testing TLS connections.

req -x509 make a self-signed certificatex509 -noout -dates show validity datess_client connect and show a server's certificate
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
stat

What it does: Shows detailed information about a file: size, permissions, owner, times, inode.

When to use it: Checking exact permissions in octal, or the last modification time.

-c '%a %U %n' custom format (octal permissions, owner, name)

Open the full command reference

subject is who the certificate is for, issuer who signed it (the same here, hence self-signed), subjectAltName the names it is valid for, and the expiry date is the thing that causes many outages. Serve it and see the client's reaction:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ openssl s_server -quiet -accept 8443 -cert ev.crt -key ev.key -www > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sleep 1
$ echo "-- strict client (does not trust the signer):"
-- strict client (does not trust the signer):
$ curl -s -m 3 https://127.0.0.1:8443/ -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" 2>&1 | head -1
000
$ curl -sS -m 3 https://127.0.0.1:8443/ -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -o "certificate[^,]*\|SSL certificate problem[^(]*" | head -1
SSL certificate problem: self-signed certificate
$ echo "-- client told to trust this certificate, but name mismatch (IP, not ev01.corp.local):"
-- client told to trust this certificate, but name mismatch (IP, not ev01.corp.local):
$ curl -sS -m 3 --cacert ev.crt https://127.0.0.1:8443/ -o /dev/null 2>&1 | head -1
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name '127.0.0.1'
$ echo "-- client trusting it and using the right name:"
-- client trusting it and using the right name:
$ curl -s -m 3 --cacert ev.crt --resolve ev01.corp.local:8443:127.0.0.1 https://ev01.corp.local:8443/ -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}\n"
HTTP 200
$ pkill -f "[o]penssl s_server"
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Three different results from one server: untrusted issuer, name mismatch, success. Real-world TLS errors are almost always one of: expired, wrong name, untrusted/incomplete chain, or a clock that is wrong. Check with openssl x509 -in cert.crt -noout -dates or, against a live server, openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host.

Keep your private key private

ev.key is 600 for a reason. Anyone with it can impersonate the server. Never commit keys to Git; use a secrets manager (the Terraform and Jenkins tracks return to this).

In plain words

  • Troubleshoot bottom-up: link, address, route, IP reachability, DNS, port, application, firewall.
  • HTTP status classes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client problem, 5xx server problem.
  • TLS = encryption + identity via certificates signed by a trusted CA.
  • Certificate failures: expired, wrong name, untrusted chain, wrong clock.

Users see "certificate expired" for the EV web app but the server has been fine for months. Which command checks the expiry date, and what two other TLS problems would you rule out?

Git · Lesson 1

Git first steps

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what version control is and why every automation project uses it
  • create a repository and make commits
  • understand the working folder, the staging area and the history
  • read git status, git diff and git log

The problem Git solves

Without version control you end up with script_final.sh, script_final2.sh, script_REALLY_final.sh. Git records every change to a set of files as a commit: a labelled snapshot with who made it, when, and why. You can compare snapshots, go back to any of them, and work on changes in parallel with other people. Everything in the rest of this course (Docker files, Terraform, Ansible, Jenkins pipelines) lives in Git, so this is the most reusable skill you will learn.

Three places a change can live

PlaceNameThink of it as
Your filesworking directorythe desk where you are editing
git add puts changes herestaging area (index)the box where you pack what goes in the next snapshot
git commit writes hererepository (history)the album of finished snapshots

Make a repository and a first commit

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ev-tools && cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /home/student/lab/ev-tools/.git/
$ echo "#!/bin/bash" > check.sh
$ echo 'echo "checking EV01"' >> check.sh
$ git status --short
?? check.sh
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

git init

What it does: Turns the current folder into a Git repository by creating the hidden .git folder.

When to use it: Starting version control for a new project.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

git status

What it does: Shows what changed since the last commit and what is staged.

When to use it: Before every commit, and whenever you are unsure what state the repository is in.

-s short format-sb short with branch information

Open the full command reference

?? means "untracked": Git sees the file but is not recording it yet.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ git add check.sh
$ git status --short
A  check.sh
$ git commit -m "Add EV check script"
[main (root-commit) c17d9b0] Add EV check script
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
 create mode 100644 check.sh
$ git log --format='%s (%an)'
Add EV check script (Rohan Student)
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
git add

What it does: Puts changes into the staging area, selecting what goes into the next commit.

When to use it: After editing files and reviewing the diff.

file stage one file. stage everything in this folder-p choose pieces of a file interactively
git commit

What it does: Records the staged changes as a new snapshot with a message.

When to use it: After finishing a logical piece of work. Write a message saying what and why.

-m "message" give the message on the command line-a also stage changes to tracked files--amend redo the last commit

Careful: Do not amend commits that you have already pushed.

git log

What it does: Shows the commit history.

When to use it: Finding who changed what and when; understanding the history of a file.

--oneline one line per commit--graph --all draw branches-p include the changes--format='%s' choose the output fields-S"text" commits that added or removed this text

Open the full command reference

A means "added to staging". After commit, the working directory, staging area and history all agree and git status is clean.

The edit, review, commit loop

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ echo 'echo "checking SQL01"' >> check.sh
$ git status --short
 M check.sh
$ git diff
diff --git a/check.sh b/check.sh
index 7610655..a979e49 100644
--- a/check.sh
+++ b/check.sh
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@

+echo "checking SQL01"
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
git diff

What it does: Shows line-by-line what changed.

When to use it: Reviewing your edits before staging or committing.

--staged changes already staged--stat summary per file

Open the full command reference

M is "modified". git diff shows what changed (lines starting with + were added, - removed). Always read your diff before committing.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ git add check.sh
$ git diff --staged --stat
 check.sh | 1 +
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git commit -m "Also check SQL01"
[main 5fe602a] Also check SQL01
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)
$ git log --format='%h %s' | sed 's/^[0-9a-f]*/<id>/'
<id> Also check SQL01
<id> Add EV check script
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

Every commit has a unique ID (a long hash like 3f2a9c1...; the short form is 7 characters). Hashes differ on every machine, so the output above hides them.

CommandWhat it does
git initstart a repository in this folder
git statuswhat changed, what is staged
git add file / git add .stage changes
git commit -m "msg"save the staged snapshot
git diffunstaged changes; --staged for staged ones
git loghistory; --oneline, --graph, -p (with patches)
git show IDone commit in detail

Good commit messages

A message is a note to your future self at 2am. Say what and why, in the imperative: "Fix SQL timeout retry", not "changes" or "stuff". One logical change per commit, so it can be reviewed or undone on its own.

Ignoring files

Some files must never be committed: logs, build output, local settings and above all secrets (passwords, keys, tokens). List patterns in .gitignore:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ printf '*.log\n.env\nbuild/\n' > .gitignore
$ echo "DB_PASSWORD=hunter2" > .env
$ echo "noise" > run.log
$ git status --short
?? .gitignore
$ git add .gitignore && git commit -q -m "Ignore logs and env files"
$ git status --short | wc -l
0
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

.env and run.log no longer appear. A password committed once stays in history forever, even if you delete the file later, so ignore it before the first commit.

Looking at the past

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-tools
$ git log -p --format='--- commit: %s' -- check.sh | head -12
--- commit: Also check SQL01

diff --git a/check.sh b/check.sh
index 7610655..a979e49 100644
--- a/check.sh
+++ b/check.sh
@@ -1,2 +1,3 @@
 #!/bin/bash
 echo "checking EV01"
+echo "checking SQL01"
--- commit: Add EV check script
$ git show HEAD~2:check.sh
#!/bin/bash
echo "checking EV01"
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
git show

What it does: Shows one commit (or a file as it was in a commit).

When to use it: Looking at exactly what a commit changed; git show HEAD~2:file prints an old version.

Open the full command reference

HEAD means "the commit I am on now"; HEAD~1 is its parent and HEAD~2 its grandparent. git show HEAD~2:check.sh prints the file as it was two commits ago.

In plain words

  • Git stores snapshots (commits). Working directory, staging area, repository.
  • Loop: edit, git diff, git add, git commit.
  • Write meaningful messages; one logical change per commit.
  • .gitignore keeps logs and secrets out. Secrets in history are forever.
Your turn

Create a repository for a tiny backup script, commit three times with sensible messages, then use git log -p to find the commit that introduced a particular line.

Git · Lesson 2

Branches, merging and conflicts

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain a branch as a movable label on a commit
  • create, switch and merge branches
  • resolve a merge conflict
  • tell a fast-forward from a merge commit

A branch is a label

A branch is just a movable name that points at a commit. Creating one is instant and free. The convention: main holds working, reviewable code; each piece of work happens on its own short-lived branch and is merged back when ready. That keeps half-finished work away from everyone else.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ev-branches && cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ git init -q
$ printf 'server=EV01\nretries=3\n' > evault.conf
$ git add . && git commit -q -m "Initial config"
$ git branch --show-current
main
$ git switch -c feature/more-retries
Switched to a new branch 'feature/more-retries'
$ git branch
* feature/more-retries
  main
What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

git init

What it does: Turns the current folder into a Git repository by creating the hidden .git folder.

When to use it: Starting version control for a new project.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
git add

What it does: Puts changes into the staging area, selecting what goes into the next commit.

When to use it: After editing files and reviewing the diff.

file stage one file. stage everything in this folder-p choose pieces of a file interactively
git commit

What it does: Records the staged changes as a new snapshot with a message.

When to use it: After finishing a logical piece of work. Write a message saying what and why.

-m "message" give the message on the command line-a also stage changes to tracked files--amend redo the last commit

Careful: Do not amend commits that you have already pushed.

git branch

What it does: Lists, creates or deletes branches.

When to use it: Seeing which branches exist; git branch -d NAME removes a merged branch.

-d delete a merged branch--show-current print the current branch name
git switch

What it does: Moves to another branch (and -c creates one).

When to use it: Starting a new piece of work on its own branch, or going back to main.

-c NAME create and switch

Open the full command reference

The * marks the branch you are on. git switch -c name creates and switches (older: git checkout -b name).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ sed -i 's/retries=3/retries=5/' evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Raise retries to 5"
$ git switch -q main
$ echo "on main:" ; cat evault.conf
on main:
server=EV01
retries=3
$ git switch -q feature/more-retries
$ echo "on feature:" ; cat evault.conf
on feature:
server=EV01
retries=5
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

Open the full command reference

Files in the folder change as you switch branches. Each branch has its own history.

Merging

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ git switch -q main
$ git merge feature/more-retries
Updating 369072e..eda731a
Fast-forward
 evault.conf | 2 +-
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
$ git log --graph --format='%s' --all
* Raise retries to 5
* Initial config
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
git merge

What it does: Brings the changes of another branch into the current branch.

When to use it: Finishing a feature branch. If both sides changed the same lines you must resolve a conflict.

--abort cancel a conflicted merge--no-ff always create a merge commit
git log

What it does: Shows the commit history.

When to use it: Finding who changed what and when; understanding the history of a file.

--oneline one line per commit--graph --all draw branches-p include the changes--format='%s' choose the output fields-S"text" commits that added or removed this text

Open the full command reference

Fast-forward means main had no new commits of its own, so Git just moved the label forward. Branch is done; delete it:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ git branch -d feature/more-retries
Deleted branch feature/more-retries (was eda731a).
$ git branch
* main

When both sides changed: merge commit and conflict

If main moved while you worked, Git creates a merge commit with two parents. If both branches changed the same lines, Git cannot choose and reports a conflict. Let us create one on purpose:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ git switch -q -c feature/timeout
$ echo "timeout=30" >> evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Add timeout 30"
$ git switch -q main
$ echo "timeout=60" >> evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Add timeout 60 on main"
$ git merge feature/timeout
Auto-merging evault.conf
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in evault.conf
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ echo "exit status: $?"
exit status: 0
$ git status --short
UU evault.conf
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
git status

What it does: Shows what changed since the last commit and what is staged.

When to use it: Before every commit, and whenever you are unsure what state the repository is in.

-s short format-sb short with branch information

Open the full command reference

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ cat evault.conf
server=EV01
retries=5
<<<<<<< HEAD
timeout=60
=======
timeout=30
>>>>>>> feature/timeout

Git writes both versions into the file between conflict markers: <<<<<<< HEAD (your current branch's version), =======, and >>>>>>> branch (the incoming version). Your job: edit the file to what it should be, remove the markers, git add, then git commit.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-branches
$ printf 'server=EV01\nretries=5\ntimeout=45\n' > evault.conf
$ git add evault.conf
$ git commit -q -m "Merge feature/timeout: settle on 45s"
$ git log --graph --format='%s'
*   Merge feature/timeout: settle on 45s
|\  
| * Add timeout 30
* | Add timeout 60 on main
|/  
* Raise retries to 5
* Initial config
$ cat evault.conf
server=EV01
retries=5
timeout=45

The graph shows both lines of work joining at the merge commit. Conflicts are normal, not a failure. Tips: merge small and often, communicate about who edits which file, and read both sides before choosing. git merge --abort cancels a conflicted merge and takes you back.

CommandPurpose
git branchlist branches (-d delete)
git switch name / -c namechange / create and change
git merge namebring name into the current branch
git merge --abortcancel a conflicted merge
git log --graph --oneline --allpicture of the history

In plain words

  • A branch is a label on a commit. Create one per piece of work.
  • Merge brings changes together: fast-forward when possible, otherwise a merge commit.
  • A conflict means two branches changed the same lines. Edit, add, commit.
Your turn

Create two branches that both edit the same line of a config file differently, merge both into main, and resolve the conflict. Use git merge --abort once to see how to back out.

Git · Lesson 3

Remotes and working with others

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain local versus remote repositories
  • clone, push, fetch and pull
  • handle a rejected push
  • describe the pull request workflow

Local and remote

Git is distributed: every clone is a full repository with the whole history. A remote is just another copy that your team agrees to treat as the shared one, usually hosted on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps. The conventional remote name is origin. Moving data between copies:

CommandDirectionEffect
git clone URLremote to new localcopy everything, set origin
git fetchremote to localdownload new commits, do not change your files
git pullremote to localfetch + merge into the current branch
git pushlocal to remoteupload your commits

A remote does not need a website. Any folder can be a remote. We make a bare repository (no working files, only history) to act as the shared server, then two people clone it:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab && mkdir git-remote && cd git-remote
$ git init -q --bare shared.git
$ cd ~/lab
$ git clone -q git-remote/shared.git alice 2>&1 | head -1
warning: You appear to have cloned an empty repository.
$ cd alice
$ git config user.name Alice; git config user.email alice@example.com
$ echo "# EV runbook" > README.md
$ git add . && git commit -q -m "Start runbook"
$ git push -q -u origin main
$ git status -sb | head -1
## main...origin/main
What do these 10 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
git init

What it does: Turns the current folder into a Git repository by creating the hidden .git folder.

When to use it: Starting version control for a new project.

git clone

What it does: Copies a repository, with its whole history, to your machine.

When to use it: Starting work on an existing project.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
git config

What it does: Reads or sets Git settings such as your name, email and default branch.

When to use it: First-time setup on a machine: git config --global user.name "Your Name".

--global for all your repositories--list show current settings
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

git add

What it does: Puts changes into the staging area, selecting what goes into the next commit.

When to use it: After editing files and reviewing the diff.

file stage one file. stage everything in this folder-p choose pieces of a file interactively
git commit

What it does: Records the staged changes as a new snapshot with a message.

When to use it: After finishing a logical piece of work. Write a message saying what and why.

-m "message" give the message on the command line-a also stage changes to tracked files--amend redo the last commit

Careful: Do not amend commits that you have already pushed.

git push

What it does: Uploads your commits to the remote repository.

Open the full command reference

-u origin main links the local branch to the remote one, so later a plain git push / git pull works. [origin/main] in the status shows you are in sync.

Second person joins

cat

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

git fetch

What it does: Downloads new commits from the remote without changing your files.

When to use it: Looking at what others have pushed before deciding how to combine it.

git status

What it does: Shows what changed since the last commit and what is staged.

When to use it: Before every commit, and whenever you are unsure what state the repository is in.

-s short format-sb short with branch information
git log

What it does: Shows the commit history.

--oneline one line per commit--graph --all draw branches-p include the changes--format='%s' choose the output fields-S"text" commits that added or removed this text

Open the full command reference

Alice ran fetch and learned she is behind by one commit, without her files changing. git pull would now merge it in:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/alice
$ git pull -q
$ cat README.md
# EV runbook
Restart order: SQL, then EV
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
git pull

What it does: Downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into your branch (fetch plus merge).

When to use it: Updating your local branch before you start work or before pushing.

--rebase replay your commits on top instead of making a merge commit

Open the full command reference

A rejected push

If you push while someone else pushed first, Git refuses, because your history and the remote's have diverged. This message is not an error in your work; it just means "integrate their changes first".

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/alice
$ echo "Contact: ops@example.com" >> README.md
$ git commit -q -am "Add contact"
$ cd ~/lab/bob
$ echo "Backup: nightly" >> README.md
$ git commit -q -am "Add backup note"
$ git push -q
$ cd ~/lab/alice
$ git push 2>&1 | grep -E "rejected|hint" | head -2
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Fix: pull (merge or rebase), resolve conflicts if any, push again.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/alice
$ git pull --no-rebase -q --no-edit 2>&1 | head -3
Auto-merging README.md
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in README.md
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
$ git status --short
UU README.md
$ cat README.md
# EV runbook
Restart order: SQL, then EV
<<<<<<< HEAD
Contact: ops@example.com
=======
Backup: nightly
>>>>>>> 9965d0579f45090a2c288348b99c8b90a58f673a

Both edits touched the end of the file, so a conflict appears. This is routine teamwork: resolve it exactly like the last lesson. For the demonstration we keep both lines:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/alice
$ printf '# EV runbook\nRestart order: SQL, then EV\nContact: ops@example.com\nBackup: nightly\n' > README.md
$ git add README.md && git commit -q -m "Merge Bob's backup note"
$ git push -q
$ git log --format='%an: %s' | head -4
Alice: Merge Bob's backup note
Alice: Add contact
Bob: Add backup note
Bob: Document restart order
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line

Open the full command reference

Merge or rebase?

git pull --rebase replays your commits on top of the updated branch instead of creating a merge commit. The history stays a straight line, which many teams prefer. Golden rule: never rebase commits that others have already pulled (it rewrites history). Plain merging is always safe.

Pull requests

On GitHub and similar sites, teams do not push directly to main. The workflow:

  1. Create a branch and push it: git push -u origin feature/x
  2. Open a pull request (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request): a page showing the diff, discussion and automated checks
  3. A teammate reviews; CI (Jenkins/GitHub Actions) runs tests
  4. When approved and green, the PR is merged; the branch is deleted

This gives review, history and a safety net. Branch protection rules can require an approval and passing checks before anyone can merge.

Authentication

Real remotes need credentials. Use SSH keys (see the Linux track) or tokens. Never put a token in a URL you share or commit it. A credential helper stores it securely.

In plain words

  • Every clone is a full copy. origin is the usual shared remote.
  • fetch downloads, pull = fetch + merge, push uploads.
  • A rejected push means integrate first (pull, resolve, push).
  • Teams use branches and pull requests with review and CI.

Undoing things and rescuing work

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • undo an edit, a staged file and a commit
  • choose between revert and reset
  • use stash to park work
  • recover "lost" commits with reflog

Know where the mistake lives

MistakeStateFix
Bad edit not yet stagedworking directorygit restore file
Staged by accidentstaging areagit restore --staged file
Typo in the last commit message or a forgotten filelast local commitgit commit --amend
Bad commit already sharedhistorygit revert ID (adds a new undoing commit)
Bad commit only localhistorygit reset (moves the branch back)

Restore an edit

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-undo
$ echo "retries=999" > evault.conf
$ git diff --stat | tail -1

$ git restore evault.conf
$ cat evault.conf
retries=3
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

git diff

What it does: Shows line-by-line what changed.

When to use it: Reviewing your edits before staging or committing.

--staged changes already staged--stat summary per file

restore is permanent

git restore discards uncommitted changes with no recovery. Check git diff first.

Initial config
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
git add

What it does: Puts changes into the staging area, selecting what goes into the next commit.

When to use it: After editing files and reviewing the diff.

file stage one file. stage everything in this folder-p choose pieces of a file interactively
git status

What it does: Shows what changed since the last commit and what is staged.

When to use it: Before every commit, and whenever you are unsure what state the repository is in.

-s short format-sb short with branch information

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

What it does: Records the staged changes as a new snapshot with a message.

When to use it: After finishing a logical piece of work. Write a message saying what and why.

-m "message" give the message on the command line-a also stage changes to tracked files--amend redo the last commit

git log

What it does: Shows the commit history.

--oneline one line per commit--graph --all draw branches-p include the changes--format='%s' choose the output fields-S"text" commits that added or removed this text

--amend rewrites the last commit. Do it only before you push.

Revert: the safe undo for shared history

revert creates a new commit that applies the opposite of an old one. History is kept, so it is safe even after others pulled.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-undo
$ echo "debug=true" >> evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Enable debug"
$ git revert --no-edit HEAD > /dev/null
$ git log --format='%s'
Revert "Enable debug"
Enable debug
Add timeout
Initial config
$ cat evault.conf
retries=3
timeout=30
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
git revert

What it does: Creates a new commit that undoes an earlier commit.

When to use it: Safely undoing a change that is already shared.

Open the full command reference

Reset: moving the branch back (local only)

reset moves the branch label to an earlier commit. --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) keeps them unstaged, --hard throws them away.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-undo
$ echo "oops=1" >> evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Bad idea"
$ git reset --hard HEAD~1
HEAD is now at fe1e467 Revert "Enable debug"
$ git log --format='%s' | head -3
Revert "Enable debug"
Enable debug
Add timeout
$ cat evault.conf
retries=3
timeout=30
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
git reset

What it does: Moves the current branch back to an earlier commit.

When to use it: Undoing local commits you have not shared. --hard also throws away file changes.

--soft keep changes staged--mixed (default) keep changes unstaged--hard discard changes

Careful: Never reset commits that others already have; use git revert instead.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Never reset commits you have pushed

Others will have them; rewriting shared history causes pain. Use revert there.

Stash: park unfinished work

You are mid-edit and must switch tasks. stash shelves your changes.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-undo
$ echo "retries=10" > evault.conf
$ git stash -q
$ git status --short | wc -l
0
$ git stash list | sed 's/:.*WIP/: WIP/'
stash@{0}: WIP on main: fe1e467 Revert "Enable debug"
$ git stash pop -q
$ cat evault.conf
retries=10
$ git restore evault.conf
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
git stash

What it does: Sets your uncommitted work aside so you can switch tasks; git stash pop brings it back.

When to use it: You are mid-edit and need a clean working folder for a moment.

wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

reflog: the safety net

Even after reset --hard, Git remembers where HEAD has been for about 90 days. git reflog lists those moves, so a "lost" commit can be brought back.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-undo
$ echo "important=yes" >> evault.conf
$ git commit -q -am "Important work"
$ git reset -q --hard HEAD~1
$ git reflog --format='%gs' | head -3
reset: moving to HEAD~1
commit: Important work
reset: moving to HEAD
$ lost=$(git reflog --format='%h %gs' | grep "commit: Important work" | cut -d' ' -f1)
$ git reset -q --hard $lost
$ git log --format='%s' | head -2
Important work
Revert "Enable debug"
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
git reflog

What it does: Shows where HEAD has been, including commits no branch points to any more.

When to use it: Recovering "lost" work after a reset or a bad rebase.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

The commit was never deleted, only unreachable. This is why Git feels forgiving: committed work is very hard to lose. (Uncommitted work is another matter, so commit often.)

In plain words

  • restore for edits, restore --staged to unstage, amend for the last local commit.
  • revert for shared history, reset for local-only history.
  • stash parks work. reflog finds "lost" commits.
Your turn

Make three commits. Reset hard to the first, then recover the third using reflog. Then revert the middle commit instead and compare the log.

Git · Lesson 5

Tags, hooks and team practices

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • mark releases with tags
  • use blame, bisect and grep to investigate history
  • add a pre-commit hook that blocks secrets
  • describe common branching workflows and the "everything as code" idea

Tags: named releases

A tag is a permanent label on one commit, used for release versions (v1.4.0). Unlike branches, tags do not move. Pipelines often deploy "whatever is tagged".

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-team
$ git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First release"
$ echo "v2" > app.txt && git commit -q -am "Second release prep"
$ git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "Second release"
$ git tag
v1.0.0
v1.1.0
$ git show v1.0.0:app.txt
v1
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

git tag

What it does: Puts a permanent name on a commit, normally a release such as v1.2.0.

When to use it: Marking releases that pipelines deploy.

-a NAME -m "msg" an annotated tag
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

git commit

What it does: Records the staged changes as a new snapshot with a message.

When to use it: After finishing a logical piece of work. Write a message saying what and why.

-m "message" give the message on the command line-a also stage changes to tracked files--amend redo the last commit

Careful: Do not amend commits that you have already pushed.

git show

What it does: Shows one commit (or a file as it was in a commit).

When to use it: Looking at exactly what a commit changed; git show HEAD~2:file prints an old version.

Open the full command reference

Tags are shared with git push --tags. Version numbers commonly follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (breaking change, new feature, bug fix).

Investigating history

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-team
$ printf 'line one\nline two\n' > notes.txt
$ git add . && git commit -q -m "Add notes"
$ echo "line three" >> notes.txt
$ git commit -q -am "Extend notes"
$ git blame -s notes.txt | sed -E 's/^[0-9a-f]+ +/<id> /'
<id> 1) line one
<id> 2) line two
<id> 3) line three
$ git log --format='%s' -S"line three"
Extend notes
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
git add

What it does: Puts changes into the staging area, selecting what goes into the next commit.

When to use it: After editing files and reviewing the diff.

file stage one file. stage everything in this folder-p choose pieces of a file interactively
git blame

What it does: Shows who last changed each line of a file and in which commit.

When to use it: Asking "why is this line like this?"

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

git log

What it does: Shows the commit history.

When to use it: Finding who changed what and when; understanding the history of a file.

--oneline one line per commit--graph --all draw branches-p include the changes--format='%s' choose the output fields-S"text" commits that added or removed this text

Open the full command reference

  • git blame file shows who last changed each line and in which commit.
  • git log -S"text" finds commits that added or removed that text.
  • git bisect binary-searches history for the commit that broke something: mark one commit good, one bad, and Git checks out midpoints for you to test (it can run a test script automatically).

Hooks: guard rails on your machine

A hook is a script Git runs at certain moments. The pre-commit hook runs before a commit is recorded; if it exits non-zero the commit is refused. Here is one that blocks obvious secrets:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-team
$ cat > .git/hooks/pre-commit <<'EOF'
> #!/bin/bash
> if git diff --cached | grep -E '^\+.*(PASSWORD|SECRET|API_KEY)=' > /dev/null; then
>   echo "pre-commit: possible secret in staged changes. Commit refused."
>   exit 1
> fi
> EOF
$ chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit
$ echo "DB_PASSWORD=hunter2" > config.env
$ git add config.env
$ git commit -m "Add config" ; echo "exit code: $?"
pre-commit: possible secret in staged changes. Commit refused.
exit code: 1
$ git restore --staged config.env; rm config.env
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

git restore

What it does: Discards uncommitted changes in a file, or unstages it.

When to use it: Undoing a bad edit (git restore file) or unstaging (git restore --staged file).

Careful: Discarded edits cannot be recovered.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

Local hooks can be skipped (--no-verify) and are not shared by git clone, so teams enforce the same checks again in CI and with server-side rules. Tools like pre-commit and secret scanners (gitleaks) package this properly.

Workflows

WorkflowIdeaFits
Trunk-basedtiny branches, merge to main many times a day, feature flagsteams with good tests and CI
GitHub flowbranch, PR, review, merge to main, deploymost web and ops teams
Git flowlong-lived develop, release/*, hotfix/* branchesscheduled releases, packaged software

Whatever you choose, agree on: branch naming, PR review rules, who may merge, and how releases are tagged.

Git is the spine of DevOps

Once configuration and infrastructure are text files in Git you gain review, history and rollback for everything. This is the idea of GitOps and infrastructure as code:

WhatLives in Git as
Server setupAnsible playbooks
Cloud resourcesTerraform files
Build/deploy processJenkinsfile
Container imagesDockerfile
Cluster stateKubernetes YAML

A change to production becomes: edit a file, open a PR, get a review, merge, and let automation apply it. The Capstone track connects all of them.

Cheat sheet

Real output
$ cat <<'EOF'
> git status -sb              where am I, what changed
> git add -p                  stage selected pieces of a file
> git commit -m "msg"         record
> git switch -c name          new branch
> git pull --rebase           update my branch, keep history linear
> git push -u origin name     publish a branch
> git log --graph --oneline --all
> git restore file            drop uncommitted edit
> git revert ID               undo shared commit
> git stash / stash pop       park / resume
> git reflog                  find lost commits
> EOF
git status -sb              where am I, what changed
git add -p                  stage selected pieces of a file
git commit -m "msg"         record
git switch -c name          new branch
git pull --rebase           update my branch, keep history linear
git push -u origin name     publish a branch
git log --graph --oneline --all
git restore file            drop uncommitted edit
git revert ID               undo shared commit
git stash / stash pop       park / resume
git reflog                  find lost commits

In plain words

  • Tags mark releases; semantic versioning is common.
  • blame, log -S and bisect find who/when/why.
  • Hooks stop mistakes locally; CI repeats the check for everyone.
  • Pick a workflow (GitHub flow is a good default); everything-as-code lives in Git.
Your turn

Add a pre-commit hook that refuses to commit files larger than 1 MB. Test it with a generated file.
