Docker · Lesson 1

Containers: first steps

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a container is and why teams use them
  • distinguish an image from a container
  • run, list, inspect, stop and remove containers
  • read container logs and run commands inside a container

The "works on my machine" problem

An application needs more than its own code: a language runtime, libraries, config files, the right versions. Installing all that by hand on every server leads to drift and surprises. A container packages the application with everything it needs and runs it in isolation on any Linux host with a container engine. You met the mechanics in the Linux track (namespaces, cgroups, layered filesystems). Docker is the most popular tool that makes this easy.

TermMeaningAnalogy
Imageread-only template: files plus default commanda class, a recipe, an installer
Containera running (or stopped) instance of an imagean object, a cooked meal, an installed app
Registrya server that stores images (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, ACR)an app store
Dockerfilethe recipe text file for building an imagethe recipe
Docker Enginethe background service (dockerd) that does the workthe kitchen

You type docker ... (the client); it talks to the daemon, which pulls images and creates containers.

Real output
$ docker version --format 'client {{.Client.Version}} / server {{.Server.Version}}'
client 29.6.2 / server 29.6.2
$ docker images --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' | sort
alpine:3.20
busybox:latest
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker version

What it does: Shows the client and server versions.

When to use it: Checking Docker is running and which version.

docker images

What it does: Lists images stored locally.

When to use it: What is on this machine, and how big is it?

sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G

Open the full command reference

Run your first container

Real output
$ docker run --rm busybox echo "hello from inside a container"
hello from inside a container
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits

Open the full command reference

What happened: Docker found the image busybox (using it from the local cache; otherwise it would download from Docker Hub), created a container, ran echo ... as its only process, printed the output, and --rm removed the container when it exited. A container lives exactly as long as its main process.

Real output
$ docker run --rm busybox sh -c 'echo "I am: $(hostname)"; echo "my pid: $$"; ps | head -3; cat /etc/os-release | head -1'
I am: 4bd319f2edb8
my pid: 1
PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
    1 root      0:00 sh -c echo "I am: $(hostname)"; echo "my pid: $$"; ps | head -3; cat /etc/os-release | head -1
    8 root      0:00 ps
cat: can't open '/etc/os-release': No such file or directory
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
hostname

What it does: Shows (or sets) the computer's name.

When to use it: Confirming which server you are on, especially when you have several terminals open.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

ps

What it does: Shows a snapshot of running processes.

When to use it: Checking whether a program is running, or finding its process ID (PID).

aux every process with CPU/memory-ef full listing with parent PID-o pid,comm choose columns-p PID just that process
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

Open the full command reference

Inside, the shell is PID 1 and sees almost nothing else; the hostname is the container ID. The host's processes are invisible. That is namespace isolation.

Long-running containers

Servers do not exit. Run one in the background with -d (detached) and give it a name:

Real output
$ docker run -d --name web busybox sh -c 'echo started; i=0; while true; do i=$((i+1)); echo "tick $i"; sleep 1; done'
481f2b51a9ed72f4e29f51392948dfbd686018547ca0462f3ad7ed363b251b74
$ docker ps --format 'table {{.Names}}\t{{.Image}}\t{{.Status}}' | sed 's/Up [0-9]* [a-z]*/Up .../'
NAMES     IMAGE     STATUS
web       busybox   Up Less than a second
$ sleep 3
$ docker logs web | head -4
started
tick 1
tick 2
tick 3
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

docker ps

What it does: Lists containers (only running ones unless -a).

When to use it: Which containers are up? Why did that one stop (ps -a)?

-a include stopped-q only IDs--format choose columns
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

docker logs

What it does: Shows what a container printed to its output.

When to use it: A container misbehaves or exits: read its logs first.

-f follow--tail N last N lines

Open the full command reference

CommandPurpose
docker psrunning containers (-a includes stopped)
docker logs NAMEwhat the container printed (-f follow, --tail 20)
docker exec -it NAME shopen a shell inside a running container
docker stop NAMEask it to stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 10 s)
docker start NAMEstart a stopped container again
docker rm NAMEdelete a stopped container (-f force)
docker inspect NAMEall details as JSON
Real output
$ docker exec web sh -c 'echo "running inside web: $(hostname)"; ls /'
running inside web: 481f2b51a9ed
bin
dev
etc
home
lib
lib64
proc
root
sys
tmp
usr
var
$ docker inspect -f 'state={{.State.Status}} image={{.Config.Image}}' web
state=running image=busybox
$ docker stop web
web
$ docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}: {{.Status}}' | sed 's/Exited ([0-9]*) .*/Exited/'
web: Exited
$ docker rm web
web
$ docker ps -a | wc -l
1
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker exec

What it does: Runs a command inside a running container.

When to use it: Looking around inside it: docker exec -it NAME sh.

-it interactive terminal
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
docker inspect

What it does: Prints detailed JSON about a container, image, network or volume.

When to use it: Finding IPs, mounts, exit codes, health status. Use -f '{{...}}' to pick one field.

-f TEMPLATE pick fields
docker stop

What it does: Asks a container to stop (SIGTERM, then kill after 10 seconds).

When to use it: Shutting down a container cleanly.

docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

docker stop sends SIGTERM (you saw signals in the Linux track), then SIGKILL if the process ignores it for 10 seconds. A well-written container handles SIGTERM and exits cleanly.

Containers are disposable

The container's writable layer vanishes when the container is removed. Files written inside are not kept:

Real output
$ docker run --name tmp busybox sh -c 'echo "important data" > /data.txt'
$ docker start -a tmp > /dev/null
$ docker cp tmp:/data.txt - | tar -xO 2>/dev/null
important data
$ docker rm tmp > /dev/null
$ docker run --rm busybox ls /data.txt 2>&1 | tail -1
ls: /data.txt: No such file or directory
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker start

What it does: Starts a stopped container again.

When to use it: Restarting a container you kept.

docker cp

What it does: Copies files between a container and the host.

When to use it: Getting a log or config out of a container, or putting a file in.

tar

What it does: Bundles many files into one archive, optionally compressed.

When to use it: Backups and moving a folder as one file.

-c create-x extract-t list contents-z gzip compression-f FILE archive file name-C DIR change folder first
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

Open the full command reference

A fresh container from the same image does not have the file. Data that must survive belongs in volumes (lesson 5). Treat containers as cattle, not pets: easy to replace, never hand-fixed.

Exit codes and failures

Real output
$ docker run --name bad busybox sh -c 'echo "failing"; exit 3'
failing
$ docker inspect -f 'exit code: {{.State.ExitCode}}' bad
exit code: 3
$ docker rm bad > /dev/null
$ docker run --rm busybox no-such-command 2>&1 | tail -1
Run 'docker run --help' for more information
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
exit

What it does: Ends the shell or script and returns a status code (0 means success, anything else means failure).

When to use it: In scripts, to tell the caller that something failed: exit 1.

Open the full command reference

Exit code 0 means success; 125 means Docker itself failed; 126/127 mean the command could not be run or was not found; 137 means killed by SIGKILL (often out of memory); 143 means SIGTERM.

On Windows

Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM and gives you the same docker command in PowerShell. Windows containers also exist but Linux containers are by far the norm.

In plain words

  • Image = template, container = running instance. A container lives as long as its main process.
  • run, ps, logs, exec, stop, rm, inspect.
  • Detached containers (-d) run servers; give them names.
  • Container filesystems are disposable. Use volumes for data.
Your turn

Start a named background container that prints the date every 2 seconds. Read its last 3 log lines, run date inside it with docker exec, then stop and remove it. What exit code does it report after docker stop?

Docker · Lesson 2

Images, layers and registries

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain image layers and why they save space and time
  • read image names, tags and digests
  • inspect an image with history and inspect
  • explain registries and pull/push

An image is a stack of layers

An image is not one big file. It is a stack of read-only layers, each recording the file changes from one build step. A container adds a thin writable layer on top. Layers are shared: ten images that start from the same base store that base once, and pulling a new version downloads only the layers you do not have.

Real output
$ docker image ls busybox --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}  {{.Size}}'
busybox:latest  6.81MB
$ docker history busybox --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' | cut -c1-70
BusyBox 1.38.0 (glibc), Debian 13
$ docker image inspect busybox --format 'layers: {{len .RootFS.Layers}}  os/arch: {{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
layers: 1  os/arch: linux/amd64
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker image

What it does: Image management subcommands (ls, inspect, prune...).

When to use it: Inspecting an image's layers or removing unused ones: docker image prune.

docker history

What it does: Shows the layers of an image and the commands that created them.

When to use it: Seeing why an image is large, or what a build did.

cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

docker history lists the steps that built the image, newest first. The SIZE of each step matters when you optimise.

Names, tags and digests

A full image name: registry/namespace/name:tag. For example docker.io/library/nginx:1.27-alpine. Parts you leave out get defaults: registry docker.io, namespace library (official images), tag latest.

WrittenMeans
nginxdocker.io/library/nginx:latest
nginx:1.27-alpinea specific version, small Alpine-based variant
ghcr.io/acme/app:2.3.1GitHub's registry
nginx@sha256:...an exact, immutable digest
Avoid latest in real systems

A tag is a movable label. latest is whatever was pushed last, so a rebuild next month may pull something different. Pin versions (:1.27.2) in production, or even the digest, so deployments are repeatable.

Tagging gives an image another name; it does not copy data:

Real output
$ docker tag busybox ev-tools:1.0
$ docker tag busybox ev-tools:latest
$ docker image ls ev-tools --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}' | sort
ev-tools:1.0
ev-tools:latest
$ docker image inspect ev-tools:1.0 busybox --format '{{.Id}}' | uniq | wc -l
1
$ docker rmi ev-tools:1.0 ev-tools:latest | sed 's/sha256:.*/.../'
Untagged: ev-tools:1.0
Untagged: ev-tools:latest
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
uniq

What it does: Collapses repeated adjacent lines; with -c it counts them.

When to use it: Counting how often something occurs: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn.

-c prefix lines with counts-d show only duplicated lines
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes
docker rmi

What it does: Deletes images.

When to use it: Freeing disk space or removing an old tag.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

The two ev-tools tags and busybox all point to one image ID (the uniq count is 1).

Registries

A registry stores and serves images. Docker Hub is the public default. Companies run private ones: Amazon ECR, Azure ACR, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Container Registry, Harbor, or a simple self-hosted registry container. Typical flow:

Example output (not run here)
$ docker login registry.example.com
$ docker tag ev-tools:1.0 registry.example.com/ops/ev-tools:1.0
$ docker push registry.example.com/ops/ev-tools:1.0
$ docker pull registry.example.com/ops/ev-tools:1.0
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker

What it does: The Docker command-line client. Subcommands such as run, ps and build do the work.

When to use it: Everything you do with containers.

docker tag

What it does: Gives an image another name (such as a registry path and version).

When to use it: Before pushing: docker tag app registry.example.com/team/app:1.2.

docker push

What it does: Uploads an image to a registry.

When to use it: Publishing a built image so servers and pipelines can pull it.

docker pull

What it does: Downloads an image from a registry.

When to use it: Getting an image ahead of time, or updating it.

Open the full command reference

A registry is just an HTTP server speaking a standard API (the OCI distribution spec). You can run your own with docker run -d -p 5000:5000 registry:2 and push to localhost:5000/name:tag.

Saving images as files

When there is no registry (air-gapped networks), images can move as tar files:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ docker save busybox -o busybox.tar
$ tar -tf busybox.tar | head -4 | sed 's/[0-9a-f]\{64\}/<id>/'
blobs/
blobs/sha256/
blobs/sha256/<id>
blobs/sha256/<id>
$ ls -lh busybox.tar | awk '{print "tar size:", $5}'
tar size: 2.2M
$ rm busybox.tar
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

docker save

What it does: Writes an image to a tar file.

When to use it: Moving images to a machine with no registry access.

tar

What it does: Bundles many files into one archive, optionally compressed.

When to use it: Backups and moving a folder as one file.

-c create-x extract-t list contents-z gzip compression-f FILE archive file name-C DIR change folder first
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

Inside the tar you see the layers and a manifest. docker load -i file.tar brings it back.

Housekeeping

Images and stopped containers pile up and fill disks (a classic incident, see the Linux storage lesson).

Real output
$ docker system df --format 'table {{.Type}}\t{{.Active}}\t{{.Reclaimable}}' | sed 's/([0-9]*%)//'
TYPE            ACTIVE    RECLAIMABLE
Images          0         18.99MB 
Containers      0         0B
Local Volumes   0         0B
Build Cache     0         0B
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
docker system

What it does: System-wide information and clean-up: disk use (df) and prune.

When to use it: The Docker host is running out of disk.

Careful: docker system prune -a --volumes removes unused images and volumes, including data.

Open the full command reference

CommandEffect
docker image pruneremove unused (dangling) images
docker container pruneremove stopped containers
docker system prune -aremove everything unused (careful)
docker system dfwhat is using space

Choosing a base image

BaseSizeNotes
ubuntu, debian30-80 MBfamiliar, full package manager
alpine~5-10 MBtiny, uses musl libc and apk
-slim variants~30-50 MBtrimmed Debian
distroless~2-20 MBno shell or package manager, hard to attack
scratch0empty; for static binaries

Smaller images pull faster and have fewer things to patch (a smaller attack surface).

In plain words

  • An image = stacked read-only layers shared between images; a container adds a writable layer.
  • Name = registry/namespace/name:tag. Pin versions; avoid latest in production.
  • Registries store images: login, tag, push, pull.
  • Clean up with prune; prefer small bases.

Run docker history on another image you have and find its biggest layer. Tag an image with a registry-style name and list it.

Docker · Lesson 3

Running containers properly

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • publish ports with -p
  • pass configuration with environment variables
  • set memory and CPU limits and see what happens when exceeded
  • use restart policies and healthchecks

Publishing ports

A container has its own network namespace. A server listening on port 80 inside is not reachable from outside until you publish the port: -p HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT. Docker adds a NAT rule (you built exactly this with nftables in the networking track).

Real output
$ docker run -d --name web -p 8081:80 busybox sh -c 'mkdir -p /www; echo "hello from EV web" > /www/index.html; httpd -f -p 80 -h /www'
5e17f85e9434c70dedd73726131f7642378016eac019522ff0d2159b7bc483bb
$ sleep 1
$ curl -s http://localhost:8081/
hello from EV web
$ docker port web
80/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:8081
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

httpd

What it does: BusyBox's tiny web server (in other systems httpd is Apache).

When to use it: Serving files from a folder inside small containers.

sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method
docker port

What it does: Shows which host ports map to a container's ports.

When to use it: Checking that a published port is what you expect.

Open the full command reference

8081:80 means "traffic to port 8081 on this host goes to port 80 in the container". The container could not see the host's port number; it still listens on 80. Two containers can both use 80 inside if their host ports differ.

Real output
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "wrong port 8082: curl exit %{exitcode}\n" http://localhost:8082/ ; true
wrong port 8082: curl exit 7
$ docker rm -f web > /dev/null
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force

Open the full command reference

To bind only to the local machine use -p 127.0.0.1:8081:80. -P publishes all EXPOSEd ports to random host ports.

Configuration through environment variables

Never bake settings or secrets into an image; pass them at run time.

Real output
$ docker run --rm -e EV_SERVER=EV01 -e RETRIES=5 busybox sh -c 'echo "server=$EV_SERVER retries=$RETRIES"'
server=EV01 retries=5
$ printf 'EV_SERVER=EV02\nRETRIES=9\n' > ~/lab/app.env
$ docker run --rm --env-file ~/lab/app.env busybox sh -c 'echo "server=$EV_SERVER retries=$RETRIES"'
server=EV02 retries=9
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line

Open the full command reference

--env-file loads many at once. Keep secrets files out of Git (.gitignore) and prefer your platform's secret store (Kubernetes Secrets, Docker secrets, a vault) for real passwords.

Resource limits (cgroups at work)

Without limits, one container can eat the whole host. Limits use cgroups (Linux track, lesson 12).

Real output
$ docker run --rm --memory 64m --cpus 0.5 busybox sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes 2>/dev/null || cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max'
67108864
$ docker run --name hog --memory 16m --memory-swap 16m busybox sh -c 'x=$(head -c 40000000 /dev/zero | tr "\0" "a"); echo "should not get here"' ; echo "exit code: $?"
exit code: 137
$ docker inspect -f 'OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}}' hog
OOMKilled=true
$ docker rm hog > /dev/null
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
tr

What it does: Translates or deletes single characters.

When to use it: Converting case (tr a-z A-Z), squeezing spaces, or turning separators into newlines.

-d delete the characters-s squeeze repeats into one
docker inspect

What it does: Prints detailed JSON about a container, image, network or volume.

When to use it: Finding IPs, mounts, exit codes, health status. Use -f '{{...}}' to pick one field.

-f TEMPLATE pick fields

Open the full command reference

The container tried to use more memory than its 16 MB limit and the kernel killed it: exit code 137, OOMKilled=true. You will see the same status in Kubernetes. The fix is either raising the limit or fixing the memory use.

Restart policies

Containers can come back automatically. This is how simple single-host setups stay up.

PolicyBehaviour
no (default)never restart
on-failure[:N]restart if exit code is non-zero (up to N times)
alwaysalways restart, including after Docker restarts
unless-stoppedlike always, but not if you stopped it manually
Real output
$ docker run -d --name flaky --restart on-failure:3 busybox sh -c 'echo "crashing"; exit 1' > /dev/null
$ sleep 6
$ docker inspect -f 'restarts so far: {{.RestartCount}}  status: {{.State.Status}}' flaky
restarts so far: 3  status: exited
$ docker rm -f flaky > /dev/null
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
exit

What it does: Ends the shell or script and returns a status code (0 means success, anything else means failure).

When to use it: In scripts, to tell the caller that something failed: exit 1.

Open the full command reference

Healthchecks

"Running" does not mean "working". A healthcheck runs a command periodically; Docker reports healthy or unhealthy. Orchestrators use this to replace broken containers.

Real output
$ docker run -d --name hc --health-cmd 'test -f /ready' --health-interval 1s --health-retries 2 busybox sh -c 'sleep 3; touch /ready; sleep 60' > /dev/null
$ sleep 2
$ docker inspect -f 'after 2s: {{.State.Health.Status}}' hc
after 2s: starting
$ sleep 4
$ docker inspect -f 'after 6s: {{.State.Health.Status}}' hc
after 6s: healthy
$ docker rm -f hc > /dev/null
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

Open the full command reference

It starts as starting or unhealthy until /ready appears, then becomes healthy.

Running as a non-root user

By default processes in a container are root (of the container). Run as an unprivileged user wherever possible, so a break-in has less power:

Real output
$ docker run --rm busybox id
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root),10(wheel)
$ docker run --rm --user 1000:1000 busybox id
uid=1000 gid=1000 groups=1000
$ docker run --rm --read-only --user 1000:1000 busybox sh -c 'touch /x 2>&1 | head -1'
touch: /x: Read-only file system

In plain words

  • -p host:container publishes ports. -e / --env-file pass configuration.
  • --memory and --cpus set limits; exceeding memory means OOM kill, exit 137.
  • Restart policies self-heal; healthchecks tell "running" from "working".
  • Prefer non-root and read-only containers.

Start a container that listens on port 80 inside, publish it on host port 9000, fetch it with curl, then restart it with -p 127.0.0.1:9000:80 instead. What is the difference?

Docker · Lesson 4

Writing Dockerfiles

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write a Dockerfile with FROM, COPY, RUN, ENV, CMD and ENTRYPOINT
  • build and run your image
  • explain the build cache and order instructions for speed
  • use multi-stage builds and .dockerignore

A Dockerfile is a recipe

Each instruction adds a layer. Common ones:

InstructionPurpose
FROM imagethe base to start from (always first)
WORKDIR /appset the working directory
COPY src destcopy files from your folder into the image
RUN cmdrun a command at build time (install, compile)
ENV KEY=valueset an environment variable
ARG name=defaultbuild-time variable
EXPOSE 80document the port (does not publish it)
USER namerun as this user
CMD [...]default command at run time (easy to override)
ENTRYPOINT [...]the fixed program; CMD becomes its default arguments

Build a small web image

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-web
$ mkdir site
$ echo "<h1>EV status page</h1>" > site/index.html
$ cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
> FROM busybox:latest
> WORKDIR /www
> COPY site/ /www/
> ENV GREETING="hello"
> EXPOSE 80
> CMD ["httpd", "-f", "-p", "80", "-h", "/www"]
> EOF
$ docker build -q -t ev-web:1 . | sed 's/sha256:.*/<image id>/'
<image id>
$ docker images ev-web --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}'
ev-web:1
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

docker build

What it does: Builds an image from a Dockerfile.

When to use it: Packaging your application.

-t NAME:TAG name the image-f FILE use a different Dockerfile-q print only the image ID--progress=plain show full build output
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

docker images

What it does: Lists images stored locally.

When to use it: What is on this machine, and how big is it?

Open the full command reference

docker build -t name:tag . builds from the Dockerfile in . (the build context: all files sent to the daemon). Run it:

Real output
$ docker run -d --name ev-web -p 8090:80 ev-web:1 > /dev/null
$ sleep 1
$ curl -s http://localhost:8090/
<h1>EV status page</h1>
$ docker rm -f ev-web > /dev/null
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method
docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force

Open the full command reference

CMD versus ENTRYPOINT

CMD is a default the user can replace; ENTRYPOINT is the program itself and anything after the image name becomes its arguments.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-web
$ cat > Dockerfile.echo <<'EOF'
> FROM busybox:latest
> ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "EV says:"]
> CMD ["nothing"]
> EOF
$ docker build -q -t ev-echo -f Dockerfile.echo . > /dev/null
$ docker run --rm ev-echo
EV says: nothing
$ docker run --rm ev-echo "restart indexing"
EV says: restart indexing
$ docker rmi ev-echo > /dev/null
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
docker rmi

What it does: Deletes images.

When to use it: Freeing disk space or removing an old tag.

Open the full command reference

Use the exec form (JSON array ["x","y"]) so the program is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM properly. The shell form (CMD x y) wraps it in sh -c, which often swallows signals.

The build cache: order matters

Docker reuses a layer if the instruction and everything before it are unchanged. The moment one step changes, it and all later steps rebuild. So put things that change rarely (installing dependencies) before things that change often (your source code).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-web
$ cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
> FROM busybox:latest
> WORKDIR /app
> COPY requirements.txt .
> RUN echo "installing dependencies (slow)..." && sleep 1 && cat requirements.txt | wc -l > /deps.count
> COPY app.sh .
> CMD ["sh", "app.sh"]
> EOF
$ echo "flask" > requirements.txt
$ echo 'echo "app v1"' > app.sh
$ echo "=== first build"
=== first build
$ bstat() {
>   docker build --progress=plain "$@" . 2>&1 | awk '
>     /^#[0-9]+ \[[0-9]+\/[0-9]+\]/ && !/ FROM / { id=$1; $1=""; name[id]=$0; order[++n]=id }
>     /^#[0-9]+ CACHED/ { cached[$1]=1 }
>     END { for (i=1;i<=n;i++) { id=order[i]; printf "%-7s%s\n", (cached[id] ? "CACHED" : "RAN"), substr(name[id],1,58) } }'
> }
$ bstat -t ev-web:2
RAN     [2/5] WORKDIR /app
RAN     [3/5] COPY requirements.txt .
RAN     [4/5] RUN echo "installing dependencies (slow)..." && sle
RAN     [5/5] COPY app.sh .
$ echo "=== change only the app code"
=== change only the app code
$ echo 'echo "app v2"' > app.sh
$ bstat -t ev-web:3
CACHED  [2/5] WORKDIR /app
CACHED  [3/5] COPY requirements.txt .
CACHED  [4/5] RUN echo "installing dependencies (slow)..." && sle
RAN     [5/5] COPY app.sh .
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
bstat

What it does: Lab helper defined in the Docker lesson: runs docker build and prints one line per build step saying whether it was CACHED or RAN.

When to use it: Seeing the effect of the build cache after you change a file.

Open the full command reference

(bstat is a small helper that prints one line per build step: CACHED or RAN.) On the second build the RUN (dependency install) layer says CACHED; only the COPY app.sh step and later ones run again. If you had written COPY . . before RUN, every code edit would reinstall all dependencies. Try it yourself in the simulator:

Keep builds small and safe

  • .dockerignore: lists files not to send in the build context (.git, node_modules, *.log, .env). Faster builds and no leaked secrets.
  • Combine related RUN steps and clean up in the same step, because deleting a file in a later layer does not shrink the earlier one.
  • Multi-stage builds: build in one stage, copy only the result into a tiny final image. Compilers and caches never reach production.
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-web
$ printf '.git\n*.log\n.env\n' > .dockerignore
$ cat > Dockerfile.multi <<'EOF'
> # Stage 1: "build" (pretend this has compilers, test tools, large caches)
> FROM busybox:latest AS build
> RUN echo "compiled artefact" > /artefact.txt && head -c 3000000 /dev/zero > /big-build-cache
> 
> # Stage 2: final image: only what we need
> FROM busybox:latest
> COPY --from=build /artefact.txt /artefact.txt
> CMD ["cat", "/artefact.txt"]
> EOF
$ docker build -q -t ev-multi -f Dockerfile.multi . > /dev/null
$ docker run --rm ev-multi
compiled artefact
$ docker run --rm ev-multi ls /big-build-cache 2>&1 | tail -1
ls: /big-build-cache: No such file or directory
$ docker rmi ev-multi > /dev/null
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines

Open the full command reference

The 3 MB junk file stayed in the build stage and never reached the final image.

Secrets: never in an image

Anything you COPY or RUN into an image is in its layers forever, and docker history shows commands. Do not put passwords, keys or tokens in a Dockerfile. Pass them at run time, or use BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret,...).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ev-web
$ printf 'FROM busybox\nENV DB_PASSWORD=hunter2\n' > Dockerfile.leaky
$ docker build -q -t ev-leaky -f Dockerfile.leaky . > /dev/null
$ docker history ev-leaky --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' | grep -o 'DB_PASSWORD=[a-z0-9]*'
DB_PASSWORD=hunter2
$ docker rmi ev-leaky > /dev/null
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker history

What it does: Shows the layers of an image and the commands that created them.

When to use it: Seeing why an image is large, or what a build did.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Anyone who can pull the image can read that. This is a real, common vulnerability.

In plain words

  • Dockerfile instructions: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, ENV, EXPOSE, USER, CMD, ENTRYPOINT.
  • docker build -t name:tag .. Build cache: rarely-changing steps first.
  • .dockerignore, multi-stage builds, small bases keep images lean.
  • Never bake secrets into images.

Write a Dockerfile for a script that prints the contents of an environment variable passed at run time. Build it and run it with two different values.

Docker · Lesson 5

Volumes and persistent data

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain why container data disappears and how volumes fix it
  • use named volumes and bind mounts
  • back up and restore a volume
  • choose the right storage for logs, databases and config

The problem

A container's writable layer is deleted with the container. A database, uploaded files or an EV index stored there would be lost on every redeploy. Docker offers two main ways to keep data outside the container:

TypeSyntaxWhere data livesBest for
Named volume-v mydata:/datamanaged by Docker (/var/lib/docker/volumes)databases, app state
Bind mount-v /host/path:/dataa folder you choose on the hostconfig files, source code in development
tmpfs--tmpfs /tmpmemory onlyscratch data, secrets that must not touch disk

Named volumes

Real output
$ docker volume create evdata
evdata
$ docker run --rm -v evdata:/data busybox sh -c 'echo "index entry 1" > /data/index.db; ls /data'
index.db
$ docker run --rm -v evdata:/data busybox cat /data/index.db
index entry 1
$ docker volume ls --format '{{.Name}}' | grep evdata
evdata
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker volume

What it does: Creates and manages named volumes (persistent storage).

When to use it: Keeping data after a container is removed.

create NAME ls rm NAME
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

The first container wrote a file and was removed; the second, a completely different container, found the file. The volume has its own lifetime. Volumes are only deleted by docker volume rm (or prune), never by removing a container.

Real output
$ docker volume inspect evdata --format 'driver={{.Driver}} mountpoint={{.Mountpoint}}'
driver=local mountpoint=/var/lib/docker/volumes/evdata/_data

If the volume does not exist when you use -v name:/path, Docker creates it automatically. A new empty volume mounted over a directory that contained files in the image is first populated with the image's files, a handy feature for first-run defaults.

Bind mounts

A bind mount maps a host folder into the container. Changes appear on both sides instantly, so it suits configuration and development.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/conf
$ echo "retries=3" > ~/lab/conf/evault.conf
$ docker run --rm -v ~/lab/conf:/etc/ev:ro busybox sh -c 'cat /etc/ev/evault.conf; echo "x" > /etc/ev/new.conf' 2>&1
retries=3
sh: line 0: can't create /etc/ev/new.conf: Read-only file system
$ echo "--- edit on host, container sees it:"
--- edit on host, container sees it:
$ echo "retries=7" > ~/lab/conf/evault.conf
$ docker run --rm -v ~/lab/conf:/etc/ev:ro busybox cat /etc/ev/evault.conf
retries=7
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

:ro makes the mount read-only inside the container; the write attempt failed as intended. A good habit for config.

Permissions on bind mounts

Files created by a container as root become root-owned on the host. If the container runs as a non-root user, that user must be allowed to write to the host folder. "Permission denied on a mounted folder" is nearly always a UID/GID mismatch (see the Linux permissions lesson).

Back up and restore a volume

A volume is just files. Back it up by mounting it in a throwaway container together with a host folder:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab
$ docker run --rm -v evdata:/data -v ~/lab:/backup busybox tar -czf /backup/evdata-backup.tar.gz -C /data .
$ ls -lh evdata-backup.tar.gz | awk '{print "backup file exists:", $9}'
backup file exists: evdata-backup.tar.gz
$ docker volume create evbackup > /dev/null
$ docker run --rm -v evbackup:/data -v ~/lab:/backup busybox sh -c 'tar -xzf /backup/evdata-backup.tar.gz -C /data && cat /data/index.db'
index entry 1
$ rm -f evdata-backup.tar.gz
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

This restore into a different volume shows the pattern for migrating data between hosts (scp the tarball). Databases have their own consistent-backup tools (for SQL Server, BACKUP DATABASE; for PostgreSQL pg_dump); copying a live database's files can capture a half-written state.

tmpfs and shared volumes

Real output
$ docker run --rm --tmpfs /scratch:size=1m busybox sh -c 'echo secret > /scratch/t; df -h /scratch | tail -1 | awk "{print \"tmpfs size:\", \$2}"'
tmpfs size: 1.0M
$ docker run -d --name writer -v evdata:/data busybox sh -c 'while true; do date +%s > /data/heartbeat; sleep 1; done' > /dev/null
$ sleep 2
$ docker run --rm -v evdata:/data:ro busybox sh -c 'test -s /data/heartbeat && echo "reader sees the writer heartbeat"'
reader sees the writer heartbeat
$ docker rm -f writer > /dev/null
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
df

What it does: Shows free and used space for each mounted file system.

When to use it: First check when a disk is full; df -i shows inodes (number of files) instead.

-h human-readable sizes-i inode usage
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
date

What it does: Prints (or formats) the current date and time.

When to use it: Timestamps in scripts and logs, for example date +%Y-%m-%d for a file name.

+%Y-%m-%d custom format-u UTC time+%s seconds since 1970
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force

Open the full command reference

Several containers can share one volume (careful with simultaneous writes). In Kubernetes the same idea appears as PersistentVolumes and PersistentVolumeClaims.

Clean up

Real output
$ docker volume rm evdata evbackup
evdata
evbackup
$ docker volume ls -q | wc -l
0
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Container storage is disposable; use volumes for data that must live on.
  • Named volume = Docker-managed; bind mount = a host folder; tmpfs = memory.
  • :ro protects config. Mind UID/GID for permissions.
  • Back up a volume by tarring it from a helper container.
Your turn

Run a container that appends the current time to /data/log.txt in a named volume, run it three times, and show all three lines from a fourth container.

Docker · Lesson 6

Docker networking

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • describe Docker's default bridge network
  • create user-defined networks and reach containers by name
  • explain what -p does using iptables/nftables
  • isolate services on separate networks

Networks Docker creates for you

On install Docker creates a bridge network (docker0, a Linux bridge like the one you built by hand) and gives each container a virtual cable (veth) plus an IP in a private range such as 172.17.0.0/16. A container reaches the outside world through NAT/masquerade on the host; the outside reaches it only through published ports.

DriverMeaning
bridgedefault, containers on one host talk through a virtual switch
hostcontainer shares the host's network stack (no isolation, no port mapping)
noneno networking at all
overlaymulti-host networks (Swarm, Kubernetes uses its own CNI plugins)
Real output
$ docker network ls --format '{{.Name}} ({{.Driver}})' | sort
bridge (bridge)
host (host)
none (null)
$ docker network inspect bridge --format 'subnet {{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Subnet}}'
subnet 172.17.0.0/16
$ ip -brief addr show docker0 | awk '{print $1, $2}'
docker0 DOWN
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
ip addr

What it does: Shows (or sets) IP addresses on network interfaces.

When to use it: What IP address does this machine have? ip -br addr gives a short table.

add 10.0.0.1/24 dev eth0 assign an addressflush dev eth0 remove addresses
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100

Open the full command reference

Default bridge versus user-defined bridge

On the default bridge, containers can reach each other only by IP. On a user-defined bridge, Docker runs an embedded DNS server: containers find each other by name. Always use your own network for multi-container apps.

Real output
$ docker network create evnet > /dev/null
$ docker run -d --name db --network evnet busybox sh -c 'mkdir -p /www; echo "pretend SQL answer" > /www/index.html; httpd -f -p 80 -h /www' > /dev/null
$ docker run -d --name web --network evnet busybox sleep 300 > /dev/null
$ sleep 1
$ docker exec web wget -q -O - http://db/
pretend SQL answer
$ docker exec web nslookup db 2>/dev/null | grep -E "^Name|^Address" | head -2 | sed 's/[0-9]*\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*/<ip>/'
Address:	<ip>:53
Name:	db
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

httpd

What it does: BusyBox's tiny web server (in other systems httpd is Apache).

When to use it: Serving files from a folder inside small containers.

sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

web reached db by the name db. The embedded DNS resolves container names to their current IPs, which change each time a container is recreated. Never hard-code container IPs.

Compare with the default bridge:

Real output
$ docker run -d --name old --network bridge busybox sleep 300 > /dev/null
$ docker exec old wget -q -T 2 -O - http://db/ 2>&1 | head -1
wget: bad address 'db'
$ docker rm -f old > /dev/null
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force

Open the full command reference

What does -p really do?

Publishing creates a DNAT rule on the host: traffic arriving at the host port is rewritten to the container's IP and port. You can see it:

Real output
$ docker run -d --name pub -p 8085:80 busybox sh -c 'mkdir -p /www; echo ok > /www/index.html; httpd -f -p 80 -h /www' > /dev/null
$ sleep 1
$ sudo iptables -t nat -S DOCKER | grep "dport 8085" | sed 's/172\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*/<container-ip>/'
-A DOCKER ! -i docker0 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 8085 -j DNAT --to-destination <container-ip>:80
$ curl -s http://localhost:8085/
ok
$ docker rm -f pub > /dev/null
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
iptables

What it does: The older command for the Linux firewall (still used by Docker and kube-proxy).

When to use it: Viewing or editing firewall and NAT rules on older systems.

-t nat -S list NAT rules-L -n list rules with numbers
curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method

Open the full command reference

The DNAT --to-destination <container-ip>:80 line is what you wrote with nftables in the networking track. Docker simply automates it. This also explains a security gotcha: Docker edits firewall rules itself, so a port you publish may be reachable from outside even if your host firewall tool (ufw) seems to deny it. Publish only to 127.0.0.1 unless the service must be public.

Isolating tiers with separate networks

A typical app: web talks to app, app talks to db, but web must not reach db. Put the database on a private network and connect only app to both:

Real output
$ docker network create backnet > /dev/null
$ docker rm -f db web > /dev/null
$ docker run -d --name db --network backnet busybox sleep 300 > /dev/null
$ docker run -d --name app --network evnet busybox sleep 300 > /dev/null
$ docker network connect backnet app
$ docker run -d --name web --network evnet busybox sleep 300 > /dev/null
$ sleep 1
$ echo -n "app -> db:  "; docker exec app ping -c1 -W1 db > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo reachable || echo blocked
app -> db:  reachable
$ echo -n "web -> app: "; docker exec web ping -c1 -W1 app > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo reachable || echo blocked
web -> app: reachable
$ echo -n "web -> db:  "; docker exec web ping -c1 -W1 db > /dev/null 2>&1 && echo reachable || echo blocked
web -> db:  blocked

Network membership is your firewall between tiers. The same idea returns as security groups in cloud and NetworkPolicies in Kubernetes.

Troubleshooting container networking

Example output (not run here)
$ docker exec -it web sh                     # get inside
$ docker exec web nslookup db                # DNS working?
$ docker exec web wget -qO- http://db:80/    # port reachable?
$ docker network inspect evnet               # who is attached, which IPs
$ docker logs db                             # is the server even running
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker exec

What it does: Runs a command inside a running container.

When to use it: Looking around inside it: docker exec -it NAME sh.

-it interactive terminal
docker network

What it does: Creates and manages Docker networks.

When to use it: Letting containers find each other by name on a user-defined network.

create NAME ls connect NET CONTAINER inspect NAME
docker logs

What it does: Shows what a container printed to its output.

When to use it: A container misbehaves or exits: read its logs first.

-f follow--tail N last N lines

Open the full command reference

All the tools from the Networking track (ping, nc, curl, dig) work the same way inside a container if they are in the image. Minimal images often lack them, so debug from a helper container attached to the same network (for example docker run --rm -it --network evnet busybox sh).

Real output
$ docker rm -f web app db > /dev/null
$ docker network rm evnet backnet
evnet
backnet
$ docker network ls -q | wc -l
3
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Default bridge = NAT'd virtual switch. User-defined bridge adds DNS by container name.
  • -p creates DNAT rules in the host firewall; bind to 127.0.0.1 when not public.
  • Separate networks isolate tiers; network connect links a container to more than one.

Create a network, start two containers on it, and show that one can resolve the other's name. Then start a third on the default bridge and show it cannot.

Docker · Lesson 7

Docker Compose

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write a compose.yaml with services, networks, volumes and environment
  • start, inspect and stop an application with one command
  • use depends_on, healthchecks and profiles
  • read the Compose file as documentation

Why Compose

Real applications are several containers: web, API, database, cache. Typing a long docker run for each (with networks, volumes, env vars) is slow and error-prone. Docker Compose describes everything in one YAML file, which you commit to Git and start with one command. It is the best way to define a development environment, a lab, or a small single-host deployment.

YAML basics: indentation (spaces, never tabs) shows nesting, key: value pairs, - item for lists. You will see YAML again in Ansible and Kubernetes, so this is a good place to get comfortable.

A two-service application

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/evapp
$ echo "<h1>EV status via Compose</h1>" > site/index.html
$ cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
> name: evapp
> services:
>   web:
>     image: busybox
>     command: ["httpd", "-f", "-p", "80", "-h", "/www"]
>     ports:
>       - "8095:80"
>     volumes:
>       - ./site:/www:ro
>     environment:
>       - EV_ENV=lab
>     depends_on:
>       checker:
>         condition: service_started
>     networks: [front]
>   checker:
>     image: busybox
>     command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do wget -q -O /dev/null http://web/ && echo web-ok || echo web-down; sleep 2; done"]
>     networks: [front]
>     restart: unless-stopped
> networks:
>   front: {}
> EOF
$ docker compose config --quiet && echo "compose file is valid"
compose file is valid
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

docker compose

What it does: Starts, stops and manages a whole multi-container application described in a compose.yaml file.

When to use it: Local development and small deployments with several services.

up -d create and start in the backgrounddown stop and removeps logs -f config validate the file

Open the full command reference

docker compose config validates the file. Read it as a story: two services on one network called front; web publishes port 8095, mounts the site folder read-only, depends on checker; the checker polls http://web/ using the service name as the hostname (Compose creates the network and DNS for you).

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

Open the full command reference

CommandPurpose
docker compose up -dcreate and start everything (builds/pulls as needed)
docker compose psstatus of the app's containers
docker compose logs -f [svc]follow logs
docker compose exec svc shshell in a service
docker compose downstop and remove containers and networks (-v also volumes)
docker compose up -d --buildrebuild images that have a build: section
docker compose pullrefresh images

Compose names things after the project (evapp-web-1). Edit the file and run up -d again: Compose changes only what differs (a mini version of the declarative idea that Terraform and Kubernetes also use).

Building your own image in Compose

Instead of image:, a service can have build: pointing at a Dockerfile:

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: ./api
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    image: ev-api:dev
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PASSWORD_FILE: /run/secrets/db_password
    secrets:
      - db_password
secrets:
  db_password:
    file: ./secrets/db_password.txt

This excerpt also shows secrets: mounted as files, not environment variables (variables leak into logs, docker inspect and crash dumps).

Healthchecks and start order

depends_on alone only waits for the container to start, not to be ready. A database can take 30 seconds to accept connections. Combine a healthcheck with the service_healthy condition:

compose.yaml (excerpt)
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5
  api:
    build: ./api
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy

(This excerpt is illustrative; we avoid pulling large images in this lab.) A robust application should also retry its database connection rather than rely on start order.

Variables and profiles

  • .env file next to compose.yaml supplies ${VARIABLES} used inside it.
  • docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up merges override files (dev vs prod).
  • profiles: [debug] makes a service start only when asked (--profile debug).
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/evapp
$ docker compose down 2>&1 | grep -E "Removed|Stopped" | sed 's/ [0-9.]*s$//' | sort | uniq | wc -l
5
$ docker ps -a | wc -l
1
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
uniq

What it does: Collapses repeated adjacent lines; with -c it counts them.

When to use it: Counting how often something occurs: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn.

-c prefix lines with counts-d show only duplicated lines
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes
docker ps

What it does: Lists containers (only running ones unless -a).

When to use it: Which containers are up? Why did that one stop (ps -a)?

-a include stopped-q only IDs--format choose columns

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Compose = whole application in compose.yaml: services, networks, volumes, env, ports.
  • Services reach each other by service name. up -d, ps, logs, exec, down.
  • depends_on + healthcheck for readiness; secrets as files; override files for environments.

Docker · Lesson 8

Production practice and troubleshooting

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • apply a security checklist to images and containers
  • manage logs and disk use
  • debug a container that will not start or keeps restarting
  • know where Docker stops and orchestration (Kubernetes) begins

A security checklist

PracticeWhyHow
Run as non-roota breakout has fewer rightsUSER 10001 in the Dockerfile or --user
Read-only root filesystemmalware cannot persist or modify binaries--read-only (+ tmpfs / volumes where needed)
Drop capabilitiesroot-in-container has fewer kernel powers--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE
No new privilegesblocks setuid escalation--security-opt no-new-privileges
Minimal base, pinned versionsfewer vulnerabilities, repeatablealpine / distroless, image:1.2.3 or digest
Scan imagesfind known CVEstrivy image NAME, docker scout cves
No secrets in images or env dumpsimages are widely readablerun-time secrets, vaults
Limit resourcesone container cannot starve the host--memory, --cpus, --pids-limit
Never mount docker.sockwhoever has it controls the hostavoid, or use a hardened proxy

Apply several at once and see the effects:

Real output
$ docker run --rm --user 10001:10001 --read-only --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --memory 32m --pids-limit 20 busybox sh -c 'id; echo "write test:"; touch /x 2>&1 | head -1; echo "chown test:"; chown 0:0 /tmp 2>&1 | head -1'
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001
write test:
touch: /x: Read-only file system
chown test:
chown: /tmp: Read-only file system
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker run

What it does: Creates a new container from an image and starts it.

When to use it: Running any program or service in a container.

-d run in the background--name N give it a name-p HOST:CONTAINER publish a port-v SRC:DEST mount storage-e KEY=VAL set an environment variable--rm delete the container when it exits
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

touch

What it does: Creates an empty file, or updates a file's modified time.

When to use it: Making a placeholder file, or marking a file as freshly changed.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
chown

What it does: Changes the owner (and optionally the group) of files.

When to use it: A service cannot write to its folder because it belongs to another user.

user:group set both-R recursive

Open the full command reference

The process runs as an unprivileged user, cannot write to the root filesystem, and cannot change ownership. If an attacker exploits the application inside, they land in a locked room.

The Docker socket is root

Access to /var/run/docker.sock (or membership in the docker group) is equivalent to root on the host: you can start a container that mounts the host filesystem. Treat the docker group like sudo.

Logs

By default Docker captures whatever a container writes to stdout/stderr (the right way for containers to log) and stores it as JSON files on the host. Without a limit these grow forever and fill the disk.

Real output
$ docker run -d --name chatty --log-opt max-size=10k --log-opt max-file=2 busybox sh -c 'i=0; while true; do i=$((i+1)); echo "line $i padding padding padding padding padding"; done' > /dev/null
$ sleep 3
$ docker inspect chatty --format 'log driver: {{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Type}}  options: {{.HostConfig.LogConfig.Config}}'
log driver: json-file  options: map[max-file:2 max-size:10k]
$ docker logs chatty --tail 1 | grep -c '^line'
0
$ docker rm -f chatty > /dev/null
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

docker inspect

What it does: Prints detailed JSON about a container, image, network or volume.

When to use it: Finding IPs, mounts, exit codes, health status. Use -f '{{...}}' to pick one field.

-f TEMPLATE pick fields
docker logs

What it does: Shows what a container printed to its output.

When to use it: A container misbehaves or exits: read its logs first.

-f follow--tail N last N lines
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

docker rm

What it does: Deletes containers.

When to use it: Cleaning up. -f stops and deletes a running container in one go.

-f force

Open the full command reference

Set max-size and max-file per container or in /etc/docker/daemon.json. In production, send logs to a central system (ELK, Loki, Splunk, CloudWatch) with a logging driver or agent; the Monitoring track covers it.

Debugging playbook

When a container misbehaves, ask in this order:

  1. Is it running? docker ps -a: status, exit code
  2. What did it say? docker logs --tail 50 NAME
  3. Why did it stop? docker inspect -f '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}} {{.State.Error}}' NAME
  4. What is it configured with? docker inspect NAME (env, mounts, command, network)
  5. Can I get inside? docker exec -it NAME sh; if it crashes immediately, start a shell instead: docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh IMAGE
  6. Is it the network or the data? DNS, ports, volume permissions

Walk through three typical failures:

Real output
$ echo "### 1. wrong command"
### 1. wrong command
$ docker run --name f1 busybox nosuchprogram 2>&1 | tail -1 | cut -c1-90
Run 'docker run --help' for more information
$ docker inspect -f 'exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' f1
exit=127
$ echo "### 2. crashes on start: read the logs and exit code"
### 2. crashes on start: read the logs and exit code
$ docker run --name f2 busybox sh -c 'echo "FATAL: cannot open /etc/ev/evault.conf" >&2; exit 2'
FATAL: cannot open /etc/ev/evault.conf
$ docker inspect -f 'exit={{.State.ExitCode}}' f2
exit=2
$ echo "### 3. fix by supplying the missing config"
### 3. fix by supplying the missing config
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/etc-ev && echo "ok=1" > ~/lab/etc-ev/evault.conf
$ docker run --rm -v ~/lab/etc-ev:/etc/ev:ro busybox sh -c 'test -r /etc/ev/evault.conf && echo "config found, service would start"'
config found, service would start
$ docker rm f1 f2 > /dev/null
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
exit

What it does: Ends the shell or script and returns a status code (0 means success, anything else means failure).

When to use it: In scripts, to tell the caller that something failed: exit 1.

mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists

Open the full command reference

Exit codes help: 125 Docker daemon error, 126 command not executable, 127 command not found, 137 SIGKILL (often OOM), 143 SIGTERM.

CrashLoop and "it works on my machine"

If a container restarts repeatedly (restart policy + crash), read the first crash's logs, not the latest. Common causes: missing environment variable or file, dependency not ready, wrong permissions on a mounted volume, out of memory, port already in use on the host. Reproduce locally with the same image tag (not latest) and the same environment.

Where Docker stops

A single host with Docker (or Compose) is fine for small systems. It does not by itself give you:

  • running containers across many machines
  • automatic replacement when a machine dies
  • rolling updates without downtime and automatic rollbacks
  • service discovery, load balancing and autoscaling across the cluster
  • central secrets and config, access control, quotas

That is the job of an orchestrator, almost always Kubernetes, which is the next big track. Everything you learned here (images, registries, ports, volumes, env, healthchecks, limits) carries over directly.

Clean-up and housekeeping

Real output
$ docker ps -aq | wc -l
0
$ docker system df --format '{{.Type}}: {{.Reclaimable}}' | sed 's/ ([0-9]*%)//'
Images: 12.24MB
Containers: 0B
Local Volumes: 0B
Build Cache: 36.99kB
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
docker ps

What it does: Lists containers (only running ones unless -a).

When to use it: Which containers are up? Why did that one stop (ps -a)?

-a include stopped-q only IDs--format choose columns
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes
docker system

What it does: System-wide information and clean-up: disk use (df) and prune.

When to use it: The Docker host is running out of disk.

Careful: docker system prune -a --volumes removes unused images and volumes, including data.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks and dangling images; add -a for all unused images and --volumes for unused volumes (data loss!).

In plain words

  • Harden: non-root, read-only, drop capabilities, scan images, no secrets in images, limits.
  • Log to stdout/stderr, cap log size, ship centrally.
  • Debug: status, logs, exit code, inspect, exec, network/data.
  • Single-host Docker has limits; Kubernetes solves multi-host scheduling and self-healing.
Your turn

Take the web image from the Dockerfile lesson and run it with non-root user, read-only filesystem, dropped capabilities and a memory limit. Does it still serve on port 8080 (non-privileged port)? Why is port 80 a problem for a non-root user?
