$ ansible-inventory --graph
@all:
  |--@ungrouped:
  |--@prod:
  |  |--@evservers:
  |  |  |--ev01
  |  |--@sqlservers:
  |  |  |--sql01
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

ansible-inventory

What it does: Shows the inventory (hosts and groups) as Ansible understands it.

When to use it: Checking that groups and variables are what you expect.

--graph tree of groups

Open the full command reference

An inventory has groups in [brackets], hosts under them, and [group:children] to nest groups. [all:vars] sets variables for everyone. Real inventories use real DNS names (ev01.corp.local) so ansible_host and the port are not needed; here they point at our local SSH servers. Every inventory also has the implicit groups all and ungrouped.

Ad-hoc commands

ansible PATTERN -m MODULE -a "ARGUMENTS" runs one module on matching hosts without writing a playbook.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible all -m ping
ev01 | SUCCESS => {
    "ansible_facts": {
        "discovered_interpreter_python": "/usr/bin/python3.13"
    },
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}
sql01 | SUCCESS => {
    "ansible_facts": {
        "discovered_interpreter_python": "/usr/bin/python3.13"
    },
    "changed": false,
    "ping": "pong"
}

ping is not ICMP: it checks that Ansible can log in and run Python on each node. SUCCESS with "ping": "pong" means the whole chain (SSH, keys, Python) works. This is the first thing to test on a new host.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible evservers -m command -a "uname -s"
ev01 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
Linux
$ ansible all -m shell -a "echo \$((6*7))"
sql01 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
42
ev01 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
42
$ ansible sqlservers -m setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*" | head -8
sql01 | SUCCESS => {
    "ansible_facts": {
        "ansible_distribution": "Ubuntu",
        "ansible_distribution_file_parsed": true,
        "ansible_distribution_file_path": "/etc/os-release",
        "ansible_distribution_file_variety": "Debian",
        "ansible_distribution_major_version": "24",
        "ansible_distribution_release": "noble",
  • command runs a program (no pipes or shell features), shell goes through a shell.
  • setup gathers facts about a node: OS, IP addresses, memory, and so on. Playbooks can use them in decisions.

Host patterns: all, evservers, ev01:sql01 (either), prod:!sqlservers (prod but not SQL), ev* (wildcards), --limit ev01 (restrict a run).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible 'prod:!sqlservers' --list-hosts
  hosts (1):
    ev01
$ ansible all --limit sql01 -m command -a "echo only-sql01" | grep -o "only-sql01"
only-sql01
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Idempotency: ad-hoc

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible ev01 -m file -a "path=/tmp/ev-demo-dir state=directory mode=0750" | grep -E '"changed"'
    "changed": true,
$ ansible ev01 -m file -a "path=/tmp/ev-demo-dir state=directory mode=0750" | grep -E '"changed"'
    "changed": false,
$ ansible ev01 -m file -a "path=/tmp/ev-demo-dir state=absent" | grep -E '"changed"'
    "changed": true,

The first call says changed: true (the directory was created); the second says changed: false (it already matches). That is idempotency: state, not action. Most modules take state= (present, absent, started, latest...).

In plain words

  • Ansible is agentless: SSH + Python on managed nodes. YAML describes the desired state.
  • Inventory = hosts and groups. ansible-inventory --graph shows it.
  • ansible PATTERN -m module -a args for one-off tasks; ping, command, shell, setup, file.
  • Modules are idempotent: changed: false on the second run.
Your turn

Add a third host ev02 to the evservers group (reuse port 2222), list the group, and run ping against only that host.

Check yourself

Ansible · Lesson 2

Playbooks

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write a playbook with tasks
  • read the run output and recap
  • use check mode and diff mode
  • explain become, task names and failure behaviour

Anatomy of a playbook

A playbook is a YAML list of plays. Each play says which hosts and then lists tasks in order. Every task calls one module.

site.yml
- name: Prepare EV servers          # a play
  hosts: evservers                  # which group from the inventory
  gather_facts: false               # skip the fact-collecting step (faster)
  tasks:
    - name: Create the config folder  # a task: name + module + arguments
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /tmp/ev01-conf
        state: directory

Rules to remember: indent with two spaces (never tabs), list items start with - , and each task should have a clear name: because that is what you read in the output. Module names are fully qualified (ansible.builtin.file); the short form file: also works.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ans && cd ~/lab/ans
$ cat > inventory.ini <<'EOF'
> [evservers]
> ev01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2222
> [sqlservers]
> sql01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2223
> [all:vars]
> ansible_user=student
> ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/sshlab/client_key
> ansible_ssh_common_args=-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o LogLevel=ERROR
> EOF
$ cat > ansible.cfg <<'EOF'
> [defaults]
> inventory = inventory.ini
> interpreter_python = auto_silent
> host_key_checking = False
> retry_files_enabled = False
> 
> [ssh_connection]
> usetty = False
> pipelining = True
> EOF
$ rm -rf /tmp/ev01-conf
$ cat > site.yml <<'EOF'
> - name: Prepare EV servers
>   hosts: evservers
>   gather_facts: false
>   tasks:
>     - name: Create the config folder
>       ansible.builtin.file:
>         path: /tmp/ev01-conf
>         state: directory
>         mode: "0750"
> 
>     - name: Write the EV config file
>       ansible.builtin.copy:
>         dest: /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf
>         content: |
>           server=EV01
>           retries=3
>         mode: "0640"
> 
>     - name: Make sure retries is set to 5
>       ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
>         path: /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf
>         regexp: '^retries='
>         line: retries=5
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook site.yml

PLAY [Prepare EV servers] ******************************************************

TASK [Create the config folder] ************************************************
changed: [ev01]

TASK [Write the EV config file] ************************************************
changed: [ev01]

TASK [Make sure retries is set to 5] *******************************************
changed: [ev01]

PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=3    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

ansible-playbook

What it does: Runs a playbook: an ordered list of tasks that bring hosts to the desired state.

When to use it: Configuring servers repeatably.

--check dry run, change nothing--diff show file differences--syntax-check validate only-e var=value set a variable--tags NAME / --skip-tags NAME run subsets--limit HOST

Open the full command reference

Read the output: each TASK lists hosts with a result. The colours (here not shown) mean: green ok = already correct, yellow changed = Ansible changed something, red failed. The PLAY RECAP at the end counts them per host. Notice the config file was first written with retries=3 and then fixed to 5 by the third task, so it shows as changed.

Run it again: idempotency

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | tail -3
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=3    changed=2    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ssh ev01 'cat /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf'
server=EV01
retries=5
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
ssh

What it does: Opens a secure shell on another machine, or runs one command there.

When to use it: Administering remote servers.

-p PORT port-i KEY private key filessh host 'command' run one command and return

Open the full command reference

changed=2 in the second run? The copy task rewrites the file to retries=3 each time and the lineinfile task changes it back to 5. That is a real bug in the playbook (two tasks fighting), and watching changed on a repeat run is how you spot it. Fix: write the final content once.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ sed -i '/Make sure retries/,$d' site.yml
$ sed -i 's/retries=3/retries=5/' site.yml
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | tail -2
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | tail -2
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

After one correcting run, the second run has changed=0. A well-written playbook reports no changes on a second run. That is your quality check.

Check mode and diff: look before you leap

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ sed -i 's/retries=5/retries=9/' site.yml
$ ansible-playbook site.yml --check --diff | grep -E '^(TASK|changed|ok|\+|-|PLAY RECAP|ev01)' | grep -v '^[-+]{3}'
TASK [Create the config folder] ************************************************
ok: [ev01]
TASK [Write the EV config file] ************************************************
--- before: /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf
+++ after: /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf
-retries=5
+retries=9
changed: [ev01]
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ssh ev01 'grep retries /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf'
retries=5
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

--check (a dry run) reports what would change without doing it, and --diff shows the file differences. The file still says retries=5. Use this before every production run. Apply for real:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | tail -2
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ssh ev01 'grep retries /tmp/ev01-conf/evault.conf'
retries=9

Privileges: become

Tasks that need root (install packages, edit /etc) use privilege escalation: become: true at play or task level, usually via sudo. Keep tasks unprivileged unless needed. The lab account has passwordless sudo:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ cat > who.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: ev01
>   gather_facts: false
>   tasks:
>     - name: Who am I?
>       ansible.builtin.command: whoami
>       register: me
>       changed_when: false
>     - name: Who am I with become?
>       ansible.builtin.command: whoami
>       become: true
>       register: me_root
>       changed_when: false
>     - name: Show both
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "normal={{ me.stdout }} escalated={{ me_root.stdout }}"
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook who.yml | grep -E 'msg|normal'
    "msg": "normal=student escalated=root"

register saves a task's result in a variable, debug prints it, and changed_when: false tells Ansible that a read-only command never counts as a change (otherwise command always reports changed).

When a task fails

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans
$ cat > fail.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: ev01
>   gather_facts: false
>   tasks:
>     - name: This works
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "first"
>     - name: This fails
>       ansible.builtin.command: ls /nonexistent-folder
>     - name: This is never reached
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "third"
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook fail.yml 2>&1 | grep -E "TASK|fatal|PLAY RECAP|ev01 " | sed 's/ => .*//' | cut -c1-100
TASK [This works] **************************************************************
TASK [This fails] **************************************************************
fatal: [ev01]: FAILED!
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=1    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=1    skipped=0    rescued=
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

By default a failure stops the play for that host. You can change that with ignore_errors: true (continue) or handle it with block: / rescue:. Exit code is non-zero, so CI systems notice.

In plain words

  • A playbook = plays (hosts + tasks). Each task = name + module + arguments.
  • Run twice: the second run should say changed=0. Anything else is a hint of a flawed task.
  • --check --diff previews changes. become: true escalates privileges.
  • register, debug, changed_when handle results; failures stop the host by default.
Your turn

Write a playbook that ensures /tmp/ev01-conf/motd.txt contains "Authorised use only", run it, confirm a second run reports changed=0, then edit the text and use --check --diff before applying.

Check yourself

Ansible · Lesson 3

Variables, templates, loops and handlers

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • define and use variables (play, host, group, command line)
  • render a config file from a Jinja2 template
  • use when, loop and facts
  • use handlers so services restart only when needed

Variables

Variables avoid copy-pasting. Use them in {{ double braces }} (quote the whole value if it starts with them).

example
vars:
  app_name: evault
  max_retries: 5
tasks:
  - debug:
      msg: "{{ app_name }} will retry {{ max_retries }} times"

Where variables come from, from weakest to strongest: role defaults, inventory and group_vars/, host_vars/, play vars:, command line -e name=value (always wins). Putting variables per group and host in files is the standard way to keep one playbook for many environments.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ans2/group_vars ~/lab/ans2/host_vars && cd ~/lab/ans2
$ cat > inventory.ini <<'EOF'
> [evservers]
> ev01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2222
> [sqlservers]
> sql01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2223
> [all:vars]
> ansible_user=student
> ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/sshlab/client_key
> ansible_ssh_common_args=-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o LogLevel=ERROR
> EOF
$ printf '[defaults]\ninventory = inventory.ini\ninterpreter_python = auto_silent\nretry_files_enabled = False\n[ssh_connection]\nusetty = False\npipelining = True\n' > ansible.cfg
$ printf 'app_name: evault\nmax_retries: 3\nbase_dir: /tmp/lab-hosts/{{ inventory_hostname }}\n' > group_vars/all.yml
$ printf 'max_retries: 7\nrole_note: indexing server\n' > host_vars/ev01.yml
$ printf 'role_note: database server\n' > host_vars/sql01.yml
$ cat > vars.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: all
>   gather_facts: false
>   tasks:
>     - name: Show variables for each host
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "{{ inventory_hostname }}: {{ role_note }}, max_retries={{ max_retries }}, dir={{ base_dir }}"
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook vars.yml | grep msg
    "msg": "ev01: indexing server, max_retries=7, dir=/tmp/lab-hosts/ev01"
    "msg": "sql01: database server, max_retries=3, dir=/tmp/lab-hosts/sql01"
$ ansible-playbook vars.yml -e max_retries=1 | grep msg | cut -d, -f2
 max_retries=1
 max_retries=1
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
ansible-playbook

What it does: Runs a playbook: an ordered list of tasks that bring hosts to the desired state.

When to use it: Configuring servers repeatably.

--check dry run, change nothing--diff show file differences--syntax-check validate only-e var=value set a variable--tags NAME / --skip-tags NAME run subsets--limit HOST
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

ev01 got max_retries=7 from its host_vars file (more specific than group), sql01 the group value 3. The -e max_retries=1 on the command line overrode both. inventory_hostname is a built-in "magic" variable.

Facts and conditionals

Facts are gathered by default at the start of a play (unless gather_facts: false). They describe the node: ansible_distribution, ansible_memtotal_mb, ansible_default_ipv4, and so on. when: runs a task only if a condition is true.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans2
$ cat > facts.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: ev01
>   tasks:
>     - name: Show some facts
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "{{ ansible_distribution }} {{ ansible_distribution_major_version }}, family={{ ansible_os_family }}"
>     - name: Only on Debian-family systems
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "this is a Debian-family host: use apt"
>       when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"
>     - name: Only on Red Hat family systems
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "this is a Red Hat family host: use dnf"
>       when: ansible_os_family == "RedHat"
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook facts.yml | grep -E "msg|skipping"
    "msg": "Ubuntu 24, family=Debian"
    "msg": "this is a Debian-family host: use apt"
skipping: [ev01]

The second task ran; the third was skipped. Playbooks that must support both Ubuntu and RHEL use exactly this pattern.

Loops

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans2
$ cat > loop.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: ev01
>   gather_facts: false
>   vars:
>     folders: [logs, config, archive]
>   tasks:
>     - name: Create several folders
>       ansible.builtin.file:
>         path: "{{ base_dir }}/{{ item }}"
>         state: directory
>       loop: "{{ folders }}"
> EOF
$ rm -rf /tmp/lab-hosts
$ ansible-playbook loop.yml | grep -E "ok|changed" | head -5
changed: [ev01] => (item=logs)
changed: [ev01] => (item=config)
changed: [ev01] => (item=archive)
ev01                       : ok=1    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ls /tmp/lab-hosts/ev01
archive
config
logs
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents

Open the full command reference

loop: repeats a task for each item, referenced as {{ item }}. Loops over lists of dictionaries are common for users and packages.

Templates: config files with holes

A template is a file with placeholders, written in Jinja2 ({{ variable }}, {% if %}, {% for %}). The template module fills it in per host. One template, many servers, each with the right values.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans2
$ mkdir -p templates
$ cat > templates/evault.conf.j2 <<'EOF'
> # Managed by Ansible. Do not edit by hand.
> server={{ inventory_hostname }}
> role={{ role_note }}
> retries={{ max_retries }}
> {% if max_retries > 5 %}
> # high retry count: network is unreliable
> {% endif %}
> EOF
$ cat > tmpl.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: all
>   gather_facts: false
>   tasks:
>     - name: Ensure the folder exists
>       ansible.builtin.file:
>         path: "{{ base_dir }}"
>         state: directory
>     - name: Render config
>       ansible.builtin.template:
>         src: evault.conf.j2
>         dest: "{{ base_dir }}/evault.conf"
>         mode: "0640"
>       notify: Report change
>   handlers:
>     - name: Report change
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "config changed on {{ inventory_hostname }}"
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook tmpl.yml | grep -E "RUNNING HANDLER|msg|PLAY RECAP|ok="
RUNNING HANDLER [Report change] ************************************************
    "msg": "config changed on ev01"
    "msg": "config changed on sql01"
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=3    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
sql01                      : ok=3    changed=2    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ echo "--- rendered for ev01:"; cat /tmp/lab-hosts/ev01/evault.conf
--- rendered for ev01:
# Managed by Ansible. Do not edit by hand.
server=ev01
role=indexing server
retries=7
# high retry count: network is unreliable
$ echo "--- rendered for sql01:"; cat /tmp/lab-hosts/sql01/evault.conf
--- rendered for sql01:
# Managed by Ansible. Do not edit by hand.
server=sql01
role=database server
retries=3
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

Same template, different output. The "managed by Ansible" comment warns humans not to edit files that will be overwritten.

Handlers: act only on change

A handler is a task that runs only when another task notifies it, and only once at the end of the play, even if notified many times. This is exactly right for "restart the service if its config changed":

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans2
$ echo "--- second run: no change, so the handler does not run"
--- second run: no change, so the handler does not run
$ ansible-playbook tmpl.yml | grep -E "RUNNING HANDLER|PLAY RECAP|ok="
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
sql01                      : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ sed -i 's/max_retries: 7/max_retries: 8/' host_vars/ev01.yml
$ echo "--- after changing a variable: the handler runs for ev01 only"
--- after changing a variable: the handler runs for ev01 only
$ ansible-playbook tmpl.yml | grep -E "RUNNING HANDLER|msg"
RUNNING HANDLER [Report change] ************************************************
    "msg": "config changed on ev01"
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

In a real playbook the handler would be ansible.builtin.service: name=evault state=restarted. You have just seen how Ansible restarts services only when needed, with no downtime on repeat runs.

In plain words

  • Variables from group_vars, host_vars, vars: and -e (strongest). inventory_hostname and facts are built in.
  • when: conditions, loop: repetition.
  • template renders Jinja2 files per host.
  • Handlers run once, only if notified by a task that changed something.

Ansible · Lesson 4

Roles and project structure

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain why roles exist and what is inside one
  • create a role skeleton and use it from a playbook
  • use defaults versus vars, tags, and import/include
  • lay out a real Ansible project

Why roles

A single playbook grows into hundreds of lines. A role packages related work (everything needed to set up "the EV indexing service") into a folder with a fixed layout, so it can be reused in many playbooks and shared. Playbooks then read like a summary:

site.yml
- hosts: evservers
  roles:
    - common
    - ev_indexing
- hosts: sqlservers
  roles:
    - common
    - sql_client

The role layout

roles/ev_indexing/
├── tasks/main.yml        what to do (the entry point)
├── handlers/main.yml     restart/reload actions
├── defaults/main.yml     default variables (lowest precedence: easy to override)
├── vars/main.yml         fixed variables (high precedence)
├── templates/            Jinja2 files (*.j2)
├── files/                static files to copy
└── meta/main.yml         dependencies, metadata

ansible-galaxy init NAME creates the skeleton. Build a small role:

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ans3/roles && cd ~/lab/ans3
$ cat > inventory.ini <<'EOF'
> [evservers]
> ev01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2222
> [all:vars]
> ansible_user=student
> ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/sshlab/client_key
> ansible_ssh_common_args=-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o LogLevel=ERROR
> EOF
$ printf '[defaults]\ninventory = inventory.ini\ninterpreter_python = auto_silent\nroles_path = roles\nretry_files_enabled = False\n[ssh_connection]\nusetty = False\npipelining = True\n' > ansible.cfg
$ cd roles && ansible-galaxy role init ev_indexing 2>&1 | sed 's/ was created.*/ created/'
- Role ev_indexing created
$ find ev_indexing -type f | sort
ev_indexing/README.md
ev_indexing/defaults/main.yml
ev_indexing/handlers/main.yml
ev_indexing/meta/main.yml
ev_indexing/tasks/main.yml
ev_indexing/tests/inventory
ev_indexing/tests/test.yml
ev_indexing/vars/main.yml
What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
ansible-galaxy

What it does: Creates role skeletons and installs community roles and collections.

When to use it: ansible-galaxy role init NAME for a new role.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

find

What it does: Searches a folder tree for files by name, type, size, age and more, and can run a command on each match.

When to use it: Locating a file, finding large or old files, cleaning up logs older than N days.

-name "*.log" match by name-type f/d files or directories-mtime +7 modified more than 7 days ago-size +100M bigger than 100 MB-exec CMD {} \ run a command on every match
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G

$ cd ~/lab/ans3/roles/ev_indexing
$ cat > defaults/main.yml <<'EOF'

> ev_index_threads: 4

> EOF
$ cat > templates/indexing.conf.j2 <<'EOF'

> host={{ inventory_hostname }}
> EOF
$ cat > tasks/main.yml <<'EOF'

>     path: "{{ ev_base_dir }}/{{ item }}"

> - name: Render indexing config

>     src: indexing.conf.j2
>     dest: "{{ ev_base_dir }}/conf/indexing.conf"
>     mode: "0640"
>   notify: Restart indexing
>   tags: [config]
> EOF
$ cat > handlers/main.yml <<'EOF'
> - name: Restart indexing
>   ansible.builtin.debug:
>     msg: "pretend: systemctl restart ev-indexing"
> EOF
$ rm -rf tests
$ cd ~/lab/ans3
$ cat > site.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: evservers
>   gather_facts: false
>   roles:
>     - ev_indexing
> EOF
$ rm -rf /tmp/ev-role-demo
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | grep -E "TASK|changed:|RUNNING|msg|ok="  | sed 's/ \*\*\*.*//'

changed: [ev01] => (item=conf)
changed: [ev01] => (item=logs)

changed: [ev01]
RUNNING HANDLER [ev_indexing : Restart indexing]

What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

ansible-playbook

What it does: Runs a playbook: an ordered list of tasks that bring hosts to the desired state.

When to use it: Configuring servers repeatably.

--check dry run, change nothing--diff show file differences--syntax-check validate only-e var=value set a variable--tags NAME / --skip-tags NAME run subsets--limit HOST
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Notice the task names are prefixed with the role name in real output (ev_indexing : Create...). Run it again to confirm idempotency, then override a default without editing the role:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans3
$ ansible-playbook site.yml | grep -E "ok="
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=0    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ansible-playbook site.yml -e ev_index_threads=8 | grep -E "RUNNING|ok="
RUNNING HANDLER [ev_indexing : Restart indexing] *******************************
ev01                       : ok=3    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ssh ev01 'cat /tmp/ev-role-demo/conf/indexing.conf'
# Managed by Ansible role ev_indexing
threads=8
log_level=info
host=ev01
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
ssh

What it does: Opens a secure shell on another machine, or runs one command there.

When to use it: Administering remote servers.

-p PORT port-i KEY private key filessh host 'command' run one command and return

Open the full command reference

defaults versus vars

Put anything a user might want to change in defaults/main.yml (weakest, so any inventory or play variable overrides it). Put internal constants in vars/main.yml (strong). Prefix variable names with the role name (ev_...) so roles do not collide.

Tags

Tags label tasks so you can run or skip subsets:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans3
$ ansible-playbook site.yml --list-tags | grep -E "TASK TAGS"
      TASK TAGS: [config, folders]
$ ansible-playbook site.yml --tags config -e ev_log_level=debug | grep -E "TASK|changed:|ok=" | sed 's/ \*\*\*.*//'
TASK [ev_indexing : Render indexing config]
changed: [ev01]
ev01                       : ok=2    changed=1    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0   
$ ansible-playbook site.yml --skip-tags folders | grep -E "TASK" | sed 's/ \*\*\*.*//'
TASK [ev_indexing : Render indexing config]

--tags config ran only the config task (and its handler). Tags are a precise tool for "just push the config".

Including other files

  • import_tasks / import_role: resolved when the playbook is parsed (static).
  • include_tasks / include_role: resolved while running (dynamic), so they can sit inside loops and conditions.
example
- name: Platform specific steps
  ansible.builtin.include_tasks: "{{ ansible_os_family | lower }}.yml"

A real project layout

ansible-project/
├── ansible.cfg
├── inventories/
│   ├── prod/hosts.ini          # and group_vars/, host_vars/ inside
│   └── test/hosts.ini
├── playbooks/
│   ├── site.yml
│   └── patch.yml
├── roles/
│   ├── common/
│   └── ev_indexing/
├── collections/requirements.yml
└── README.md

Separate inventories for test and production mean the same roles are run against both (-i inventories/test), which is how you test changes safely first. Collections (ansible-galaxy collection install community.general) are bundles of modules and roles from the community or vendors (for example ansible.windows, amazon.aws).

In plain words

  • A role = tasks, handlers, defaults, templates, files in a standard folder layout.
  • ansible-galaxy role init. Use roles: in a play.
  • defaults are easily overridden; prefix variables with the role name.
  • Tags run subsets. Separate inventories for test and prod, same roles.

Add a task to the role that writes a README.txt into logs, tag it docs, and run only that tag. Then run the playbook with --check to see it report no further changes.

Ansible · Lesson 5

Secrets with Ansible Vault

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain why secrets must not sit in plain text in Git
  • encrypt and use values and files with ansible-vault
  • keep the vault password out of the repository
  • use no_log to keep secrets out of output

The rule

Playbooks live in Git and are read by many people. Database passwords, API tokens and private keys must not be stored there in plain text. Even in a private repository, plain-text secrets leak through forks, laptops, backups, logs and ex-employees. Ansible Vault encrypts files or single values using a password, so the encrypted result is safe to commit; Ansible decrypts at run time.

(In larger environments you might instead fetch secrets at run time from a dedicated secrets manager such as HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault, using lookup plugins. The principle is the same: the repository holds no secrets.)

Encrypt a file

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/ans4/group_vars && cd ~/lab/ans4
$ cat > inventory.ini <<'EOF'
> [evservers]
> ev01 ansible_host=127.0.0.1 ansible_port=2222
> [all:vars]
> ansible_user=student
> ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/sshlab/client_key
> ansible_ssh_common_args=-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o LogLevel=ERROR
> EOF
$ printf '[defaults]\ninventory = inventory.ini\ninterpreter_python = auto_silent\nvault_password_file = .vault_pass\nretry_files_enabled = False\n[ssh_connection]\nusetty = False\npipelining = True\n' > ansible.cfg
$ echo "lab-only-vault-password" > .vault_pass && chmod 600 .vault_pass
$ printf 'db_password: S3cr3t-for-the-demo\napi_token: abc123\n' > group_vars/secrets.yml
$ echo "--- before:"; cat group_vars/secrets.yml
--- before:
db_password: S3cr3t-for-the-demo
api_token: abc123
$ ansible-vault encrypt group_vars/secrets.yml
$ echo "--- after:"; head -3 group_vars/secrets.yml | cut -c1-60
--- after:
$ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
616630323564643336653833616531653037333839646338646630303237
3631363532326537393065353131313336653233663064340a3065613230
What do these 9 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

chmod

What it does: Changes who may read, write or execute a file or folder.

When to use it: Making a script executable (chmod +x), or protecting a secret (chmod 600).

+x / -x add/remove executeu/g/o/a user, group, others, all644 rw-r--r--755 rwxr-xr-x600 rw--------R apply to everything inside a folder

Careful: Never use chmod 777: it lets everyone modify the file.

ansible-vault

What it does: Encrypts and decrypts secret files and values used by Ansible.

When to use it: Keeping passwords out of plain text in Git.

encrypt/decrypt/view/edit FILE encrypt_string 'value' encrypt a single value
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range

Open the full command reference

The file now begins with $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256 followed by encrypted text. This is safe to commit. Anyone with the vault password can view or edit it:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans4
$ ansible-vault view group_vars/secrets.yml
db_password: S3cr3t-for-the-demo
api_token: abc123
CommandPurpose
ansible-vault create filecreate a new encrypted file
ansible-vault edit filedecrypt, open in $EDITOR, re-encrypt on save
ansible-vault view fileread-only display
ansible-vault encrypt / decryptconvert in place
ansible-vault rekey filechange the password
ansible-vault encrypt_string 'value' --name varencrypt just one value inside a normal YAML file

Use it in a playbook

Vault-encrypted group_vars files load automatically like any other variable file. Use the secret, but do not print it:

Real output

$ mv group_vars/secrets.yml group_vars/all.yml
$ cat > use.yml <<'EOF'

>

> EOF
$ ansible-playbook use.yml | grep -E "TASK|changed:|msg|ok=" | sed 's/ \*\*\*.*//'
TASK [Write a connection file containing the secret]

TASK [Prove the secret reached the host without printing it here]

    "msg": "password line present: True"

$ ssh ev01 'stat -c "%a %n" /tmp/ev-conn.ini; rm -f /tmp/ev-conn.ini'

mv

-i ask before overwriting-n never overwrite
ansible-playbook

When to use it: Configuring servers repeatably.

--check dry run, change nothing--diff show file differences--syntax-check validate only-e var=value set a variable--tags NAME / --skip-tags NAME run subsets--limit HOST
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

When to use it: Administering remote servers.

-p PORT port-i KEY private key filessh host 'command' run one command and return
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Open the full command reference

no_log: true stops Ansible printing a task's arguments and results (on failure it would otherwise show the secret in the log). The remote file is 0600: secrets in files need strict permissions (Linux track). Never use debug to print a secret.

Handling the vault password

The password itself is a secret, so:

  • Never commit it. Add .vault_pass to .gitignore.
  • Locally use --ask-vault-pass, or a password file as above (vault_password_file in ansible.cfg).
  • In CI (Jenkins, GitHub Actions) store it as a credential/secret and write it to a temporary file at run time.
  • Use vault IDs (--vault-id prod@prompt) when production and test have different passwords.
  • A wrong password fails clearly:
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans4
$ echo "wrong-password" > /tmp/wrong_pass
$ (cd ~ && ansible-vault view ~/lab/ans4/group_vars/all.yml --vault-password-file /tmp/wrong_pass 2>&1 | head -2)
[ERROR]: Decryption failed (no vault secrets were found that could decrypt). for /home/student/lab/ans4/group_vars/all.yml
$ rm -f /tmp/wrong_pass

Other places secrets leak

LeakPrevention
Playbook output and logsno_log: true; avoid -vvv on secret tasks
ps and shell historydo not pass secrets on command lines; use files or stdin
Git history.gitignore, pre-commit secret scanning; rotate if committed
Templates rendered with wide permissionsset mode: "0600" and the right owner
Facts and registered variablesdon't register secret-bearing results without no_log

In plain words

  • Never store plain-text secrets in Git. ansible-vault encrypts files or single values.
  • The vault password stays out of the repo; CI stores it as a secret.
  • no_log: true hides sensitive tasks from output; give secret files strict permissions.

Ansible · Lesson 6

Real-world Ansible

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • write common admin tasks: packages, users, services, cron, firewall
  • run changes safely in batches (serial) with checks and error handling
  • describe how Ansible manages Windows and network devices
  • test automation and know where Ansible fits among the other tools

The everyday modules

JobModuleExample
install softwareansible.builtin.package (generic), apt, dnfname: nginx, state: present
manage servicesansible.builtin.service, systemdname: nginx, state: started, enabled: true
users and groupsuser, groupname: evsvc, groups: evteam
files and templatescopy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile, file
scheduled jobscronname: backup, minute: "30", hour: "2"
run commandscommand, shell, scriptuse only when no module fits, and make them idempotent
firewallansible.posix.firewalld, community.general.ufw
download/fetchget_url, uri, unarchive

Prefer a module over shell: a module knows the desired state and reports changed correctly; a raw command always "changes".

This lab host has no systemd and cannot reach package mirrors on all runs, so we apply the modules that work anywhere, and show service/package as illustrations.

What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line
ansible-playbook

What it does: Runs a playbook: an ordered list of tasks that bring hosts to the desired state.

When to use it: Configuring servers repeatably.

--check dry run, change nothing--diff show file differences--syntax-check validate only-e var=value set a variable--tags NAME / --skip-tags NAME run subsets--limit HOST
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

This is how you describe a machine: group, service account, shared folder, scheduled job, banner. Check the result with ordinary Linux commands and then clean up:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans5
$ ssh ev01 'id evsvc | cut -d" " -f1,3; stat -c "%a %G %n" /srv/evshare; sudo cat /etc/cron.d/ev-backup | tail -1; grep -c ANSIBLE /etc/motd'
uid=30034(evsvc) groups=30035(evsvc),30034(evteam)
2770 evteam /srv/evshare
30 2 * * * evsvc /opt/ev/backup.sh >> /var/log/ev-backup.log 2>&1
2
$ ansible ev01 -b -m user -a "name=evsvc state=absent" | grep -o '"changed": [a-z]*'
"changed": true
$ ansible ev01 -b -m group -a "name=evteam state=absent" | grep -o '"changed": [a-z]*'
"changed": true
$ ansible ev01 -b -m file -a "path=/srv/evshare state=absent" | grep -o '"changed": [a-z]*'
"changed": true

"changed": true
$ ansible ev01 -b -m copy -a "content='' dest=/etc/motd" | grep -o '"changed": [a-z]*'
"changed": true
What do these 5 commands do, and when would I use them?
ssh

What it does: Opens a secure shell on another machine, or runs one command there.

When to use it: Administering remote servers.

-p PORT port-i KEY private key filessh host 'command' run one command and return
cut

What it does: Extracts columns (fields or characters) from each line.

When to use it: Pulling one field out of structured text such as /etc/passwd or CSV.

-d ',' field separator-f 1,3 which fields-c 1-10 character range
stat

What it does: Shows detailed information about a file: size, permissions, owner, times, inode.

When to use it: Checking exact permissions in octal, or the last modification time.

-c '%a %U %n' custom format (octal permissions, owner, name)
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
ansible

What it does: Runs a single module on hosts from your inventory (an ad-hoc command).

When to use it: Quick checks and one-off actions: ansible all -m ping.

-m MODULE which module-a "ARGS" module arguments-i FILE inventory-b become root--limit HOST restrict the hosts

Open the full command reference

Installing and starting software (the standard pattern)

web.yml
- hosts: webservers
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: Install nginx
      ansible.builtin.package:
        name: nginx
        state: present

    - name: Deploy site config
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: nginx.conf.j2
        dest: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
        validate: nginx -t -c %s      # refuse to install a broken config
      notify: Reload nginx

    - name: Ensure nginx is running and starts at boot
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true

  handlers:
    - name: Reload nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: reloaded

This is Example (not run here). Note validate: (check config before replacing the live file) and the handler for reload: the same pattern covers almost any service.

Rolling updates and safety

Never change every server at once. serial limits the batch size; max_fail_percentage aborts if too many fail; any_errors_fatal stops everything on first failure.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans5
$ cat > rolling.yml <<'EOF'
> - hosts: evservers
>   gather_facts: false
>   serial: 1                  # one host at a time
>   tasks:
>     - name: Take host out of rotation (pretend)
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "draining {{ inventory_hostname }}"
>     - name: Upgrade (pretend)
>       ansible.builtin.debug:
>         msg: "upgrading {{ inventory_hostname }}"
>     - name: Health check before moving on
>       ansible.builtin.command: "true"
>       changed_when: false
> EOF
$ ansible-playbook rolling.yml | grep -E "^PLAY|msg" | sed 's/ \*\*\*.*//'
PLAY [evservers]
    "msg": "draining ev01"
    "msg": "upgrading ev01"
PLAY [evservers]
    "msg": "draining ev02"
    "msg": "upgrading ev02"
PLAY RECAP

The output shows ev01 fully processed (drain, upgrade, health check) before ev02 begins. For a database or EV cluster, that is the difference between a maintenance window with no outage and an outage.

Error handling: block / rescue / always works like try / catch / finally:

example
- block:
    - name: Upgrade the service
      ansible.builtin.command: /opt/ev/upgrade.sh
  rescue:
    - name: Roll back
      ansible.builtin.command: /opt/ev/rollback.sh
  always:
    - name: Record the result
      ansible.builtin.debug: msg="upgrade attempt finished"

Windows, network gear and the cloud

  • Windows servers (EV runs on Windows): Ansible connects with WinRM (or SSH) and uses ansible.windows.* modules, for example win_service, win_feature, win_package, win_copy, win_shell. The playbook structure is identical. Set ansible_connection=winrm in the inventory.
  • Network devices (Cisco, Juniper, Arista): modules like cisco.ios.ios_config.
  • Cloud: modules and dynamic inventories that discover hosts by tag from AWS, Azure or GCP, so the inventory never goes stale.

Testing and quality

ToolUse
ansible-playbook --syntax-checkcatches YAML and structure errors
ansible-lintstyle and best-practice checks (run in CI)
--check --diffpreview on real hosts
Moleculetest roles in throw-away containers or VMs, and verify idempotency
a staging inventoryprove changes on non-production first
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/ans5
$ ansible-playbook admin.yml --syntax-check

playbook: admin.yml
$ printf -- '- hosts: ev01\n  tasks:\n    - debug: msg=x\n   bad_indent: true\n' > broken.yml
$ ansible-playbook broken.yml --syntax-check 2>&1 | grep -iE "ERROR|syntax" | head -2
[ERROR]: YAML parsing failed: While parsing a block mapping did not find expected key.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

Where Ansible fits

ToolStrongest atStyle
Ansibleconfiguring servers and apps, orchestrating taskspush, procedural-declarative YAML
Terraformcreating infrastructure (networks, VMs, cloud services)declarative, tracks state
Docker/Kubernetespackaging and running applicationsimages and manifests
Jenkinsrunning pipelines on eventspipeline as code

A common flow: Terraform creates the servers, Ansible configures them, Jenkins runs both when you merge to Git. The Capstone track joins them.

In plain words

  • Use modules (package, service, user, file, cron, template) rather than raw commands.
  • serial for rolling changes, block/rescue for rollback, validate before replacing configs.
  • Windows uses WinRM and win_* modules; dynamic inventories track cloud hosts.
  • Test with --syntax-check, ansible-lint, --check --diff, Molecule and a staging inventory.

Terraform · Lesson 1

Infrastructure as code and your first Terraform run

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain infrastructure as code (IaC) and why click-ops does not scale
  • describe the Terraform workflow: write, init, plan, apply, destroy
  • read a plan
  • understand providers, resources and state at a first level

Click-ops versus code

Building servers, networks and databases by clicking in a cloud console is slow, undocumented, impossible to review and hard to repeat exactly. Infrastructure as code means you write files that describe the infrastructure you want, keep them in Git, review changes like code, and let a tool create it. The same files rebuild an identical environment for test, staging and production, or recreate everything after a disaster.

Terraform (by HashiCorp; OpenTofu is its open-source fork with the same language) is the most widely used IaC tool. You write HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language). Terraform compares what you want with what exists and works out the changes. This is declarative: you say what, not how.

TermMeaning
Providera plugin that talks to one platform's API (aws, azurerm, google, kubernetes, docker...)
Resourceone thing to manage (a VM, a network, a DNS record)
Data sourceread-only lookup of something that already exists
Variable / outputinputs and results of a configuration
StateTerraform's record of what it created (terraform.tfstate)
Planthe preview of changes Terraform would make
Modulea reusable bundle of resources

The lab note

Real providers (AWS, Azure...) need accounts, credentials and downloads from the Terraform registry, which this course lab does not have. Terraform ships with one built-in provider and a resource, terraform_data, that behaves like any other resource: it has inputs, an ID, a lifecycle, and it is tracked in state. With local-exec provisioners it can run commands, so we can watch a real Terraform plan/apply/destroy cycle with real output. Everything you learn about the workflow, state, variables, loops and modules transfers 1:1 to cloud resources; sections marked Example (not run here) show the cloud version.

A first configuration

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf1 && cd ~/lab/tf1
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> resource "terraform_data" "ev_server" {
>   input            = "EV01"
>   triggers_replace = "v1"
> 
>   provisioner "local-exec" {
>     command = "echo 'server ${self.input} created' > ev01.txt"
>   }
> }
> 
> output "server_name" {
>   value = terraform_data.ev_server.output
> }
> EOF
$ terraform version | head -1
Terraform v1.16.5
$ terraform init 2>&1 | grep -E "Terraform has been successfully initialized|Initializing"
Initializing the backend...
Initializing provider plugins...
Terraform has been successfully initialized!
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

terraform version

What it does: Shows the Terraform version.

When to use it: Checking which version is installed.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
terraform init

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

When to use it: The first command in a new folder, and again after adding a provider, module or backend.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

terraform init prepares the folder: it downloads the providers the configuration needs and sets up the backend (where state is kept). Run it once per new folder and again whenever you add a provider or module. It created a hidden .terraform directory and a lock file:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ ls -A | sort
main.tf
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G

Open the full command reference

Plan, apply, destroy

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ terraform plan

Terraform used the selected providers to generate the following execution
plan. Resource actions are indicated with the following symbols:
  + create

Terraform will perform the following actions:

  # terraform_data.ev_server will be created
  + resource "terraform_data" "ev_server" {
      + id               = (known after apply)
      + input            = "EV01"
      + output           = (known after apply)
      + triggers_replace = "v1"
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

Changes to Outputs:
  + server_name = (known after apply)
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform plan

What it does: Compares your code, the state and the real world, and shows what Terraform would change. It changes nothing.

When to use it: Before every apply, and in pull requests. Read it carefully, especially lines marked "replaced".

-out=FILE save the plan to apply later-var 'x=y' set a variable-replace=ADDR plan a rebuild of one resource

Open the full command reference

Read it like a diff: + create, ~ change in place, - destroy, -/+ destroy and recreate. At the bottom: Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. Nothing has been changed yet. Planning is read-only, which is why you can run it safely at any time.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Plan:|Apply complete|server_name"
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
  + server_name = (known after apply)
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
server_name = "EV01"
$ cat ev01.txt
server EV01 created
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform apply

What it does: Makes the changes shown in the plan, then updates the state.

When to use it: After reviewing the plan. Without -auto-approve it asks you to confirm.

-auto-approve skip the confirmation (for pipelines)PLANFILE apply a saved plan-var-file=F variable values from a file

Open the full command reference

Without -auto-approve, apply shows the plan and waits for you to type yes. Always read the plan before approving. Now look at the state, and run plan again:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ terraform state list
terraform_data.ev_server
$ terraform plan | grep -E "No changes|Plan:"
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform state

What it does: Inspects and edits the state: list, show, mv, rm.

When to use it: Seeing what Terraform manages, or renaming a resource without rebuilding it.

Careful: Do not edit the state file by hand.

Open the full command reference

No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration. This is Terraform's idempotency: the state, the real world and your code all agree, so there is nothing to do. Now change the code and see what Terraform decides:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ sed -i 's/input            = "EV01"/input            = "EV01-prod"/' main.tf
$ terraform plan | grep -E "^  # |Plan:"
  # terraform_data.ev_server will be updated in-place
Plan: 0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

Changing input is an in-place update (~): the resource keeps its identity. Now change an argument that forces replacement:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ sed -i 's/triggers_replace = "v1"/triggers_replace = "v2"/' main.tf
$ terraform plan | grep -E "^  # |Plan:"
  # terraform_data.ev_server must be replaced
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

-/+ and must be replaced mean destroy and create again (in real plans the attribute that caused it is tagged # forces replacement). Which attributes update in place and which force replacement depends on the resource type: for a cloud VM, changing a tag updates in place, but changing the image or the subnet destroys and recreates the machine. The plan always tells you which, and reading it carefully is the most important Terraform skill: a "replace" on a database means data loss.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Plan:|Apply complete"
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 1 destroyed.
$ cat ev01.txt
server EV01-prod created
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve | grep -E "Destroy complete|Plan:"
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.
$ terraform state list | wc -l
0
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
terraform destroy

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

Careful: In production this removes real infrastructure. Check the plan; use prevent_destroy for critical resources.

wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

The file shows the new name only because the replacement re-ran the provisioner. destroy removes everything the configuration manages, and the state is now empty.

The same thing for real cloud infrastructure

Example (not run here). With the AWS provider, the file would look like this; the workflow (init, plan, apply) is identical:

main.tf (Example, not run here)
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-2"        # credentials come from the environment, never from this file
}

resource "aws_instance" "ev_server" {
  ami           = "ami-0abcdef1234567890"
  instance_type = "t3.large"
  tags = {
    Name = "ev01"
    Env  = "prod"
  }
}

Providers are downloaded from the Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) the first time you run init. The ~> 5.0 version constraint means "any 5.x, not 6", so upgrades are deliberate.

The loop in one picture

  1. Write .tf files and commit them to Git.
  2. terraform init: get providers and set up the backend.
  3. terraform plan: preview. Review it (people do this in pull requests).
  4. terraform apply: make the changes. Updates state.
  5. terraform destroy: remove everything (use with great care).

In plain words

  • IaC replaces click-ops with reviewable, repeatable files in Git.
  • Terraform is declarative: it compares code, state and reality, and plans the difference.
  • init, plan, apply, destroy. Plans are read-only; read every plan before applying.
  • Plans show ~ in-place updates and -/+ replacements; look for forces replacement, because replacing stateful things destroys data.
Your turn

Create a configuration with two terraform_data resources where the second uses the first's output as its input. Plan, apply, change the first one's input and read what the plan says about both.

Terraform · Lesson 2

The HCL language: variables, locals, outputs and functions

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • declare variables with types, defaults and validation
  • use locals, outputs and terraform.tfvars
  • write expressions: conditionals, for, string templates
  • try built-in functions in terraform console

Blocks, arguments and expressions

HCL is built from blocks (resource "type" "name" { ... }), arguments (name = value) and expressions (anything that produces a value). Comments use # or // and /* */. Values have types: string, number, bool, list(...), map(...), set(...), object({...}).

Variables, locals, outputs

BlockRoleReferenced as
variable "x"an input to the configurationvar.x
locals { y = ... }named intermediate valueslocal.y
output "z"a result shown after apply and readable by other configsafter apply: terraform output z
Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf2 && cd ~/lab/tf2
$ cat > variables.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "environment" {
>   type        = string
>   description = "Which environment this is"
>   default     = "test"
> 
>   validation {
>     condition     = contains(["test", "prod"], var.environment)
>     error_message = "environment must be test or prod."
>   }
> }
> 
> variable "server_names" {
>   type    = list(string)
>   default = ["ev01", "sql01"]
> }
> 
> variable "db_password" {
>   type      = string
>   sensitive = true          # hidden in plan and output
>   default   = "demo-only-not-a-real-secret"
> }
> EOF
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> locals {
>   prefix = "${var.environment}-evault"
>   tags   = {
>     Env     = var.environment
>     Owner   = "ops-team"
>     Managed = "terraform"
>   }
>   instance_size = var.environment == "prod" ? "large" : "small"
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "config" {
>   input = {
>     name  = local.prefix
>     size  = local.instance_size
>     tags  = local.tags
>     count = length(var.server_names)
>   }
> }
> 
> output "summary" {
>   value = "${local.prefix}: ${length(var.server_names)} servers, size ${local.instance_size}"
> }
> 
> output "db_password" {
>   value     = var.db_password
>   sensitive = true
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Apply complete|summary|db_password"
  + db_password = (sensitive value)
  + summary     = "test-evault: 2 servers, size small"
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
db_password = <sensitive>
summary = "test-evault: 2 servers, size small"
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

terraform init

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

When to use it: The first command in a new folder, and again after adding a provider, module or backend.

terraform apply

What it does: Makes the changes shown in the plan, then updates the state.

When to use it: After reviewing the plan. Without -auto-approve it asks you to confirm.

-auto-approve skip the confirmation (for pipelines)PLANFILE apply a saved plan-var-file=F variable values from a file
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

Notice db_password = <sensitive>: Terraform hides sensitive values in its output. But they are still stored in plain text in the state file, which is why state must be protected (a later lesson).

Giving variables values

Several ways, from lowest to highest priority: the default, TF_VAR_name environment variables, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars, then -var-file=prod.tfvars and -var 'name=value' on the command line (later ones win).

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf2
$ terraform apply -auto-approve -var 'environment=prod' | grep -E "summary"
  ~ summary     = "test-evault: 2 servers, size small" -> "prod-evault: 2 servers, size large"
summary = "prod-evault: 2 servers, size large"
$ printf 'environment = "test"\nserver_names = ["ev01", "ev02", "sql01"]\n' > terraform.tfvars
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "summary"
  ~ summary     = "prod-evault: 2 servers, size large" -> "test-evault: 3 servers, size small"
summary = "test-evault: 3 servers, size small"
$ TF_VAR_environment=prod terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "summary"
summary = "test-evault: 3 servers, size small"
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
printf

What it does: Prints formatted text exactly as you describe it, including newlines (\n) and padded columns.

When to use it: When you need precise output or portable newlines in scripts; echo behaves differently between shells.

%s a string%d an integer\n new line

Open the full command reference

The command line (-var) beat the tfvars file, but the TF_VAR_ environment variable did not (the last line still says test), because the file has higher priority than the environment. A standard layout is one *.tfvars file per environment (test.tfvars, prod.tfvars), chosen with -var-file.

Validation catches mistakes early

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf2
$ terraform plan -var 'environment=staging' 2>&1 | grep -E "Error|environment must be"
Error: Invalid value for variable
environment must be test or prod.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform plan

What it does: Compares your code, the state and the real world, and shows what Terraform would change. It changes nothing.

When to use it: Before every apply, and in pull requests. Read it carefully, especially lines marked "replaced".

-out=FILE save the plan to apply later-var 'x=y' set a variable-replace=ADDR plan a rebuild of one resource
