Expressions

  • Conditional: condition ? a : b
  • String template: "web-${var.environment}-01"
  • for expression: build a new list or map from another
  • Splat: aws_instance.web[*].id gets an attribute from every instance
  • References: resource_type.name.attribute, var.x, local.x, module.m.output

Try functions in the console

terraform console is an interactive calculator for expressions, great for learning functions without changing anything. We feed it one line at a time:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf2
$ terraform console <<'EOF'
> upper("ev01")
> length(var.server_names)
> [for s in var.server_names : upper(s)]
> { for s in var.server_names : s => "${s}.corp.local" }
> join(",", var.server_names)
> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 3)
> format("%s-%03d", "ev", 7)
> lookup({ a = 1, b = 2 }, "c", 99)
> merge({ a = 1 }, { b = 2 })
> contains(var.server_names, "sql01")
> EOF
true
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform console

What it does: An interactive prompt to try expressions and functions.

When to use it: Learning functions or testing an expression without applying anything.

Open the full command reference

cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 3) is 10.0.3.0/24: carve the third /24 out of a /16. It uses what you learned in the Networking track, and it is how real VPC subnets are generated. Useful function families: string (upper, format, join, split, replace), collection (length, concat, merge, lookup, keys, values), numeric, encoding (jsonencode, yamlencode, base64encode), filesystem (file, templatefile), network (cidrsubnet, cidrhost).

Templates

templatefile() renders a text file with variables: perfect for configuration files and cloud-init scripts.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf2
$ cat > nginx.conf.tftpl <<'EOF'
> # generated for ${env}
> %{ for s in servers ~}
> upstream ${s} { server ${s}.corp.local:8080; }
> %{ endfor ~}
> EOF
$ terraform console <<'EOF'
> templatefile("nginx.conf.tftpl", { env = "test", servers = ["ev01", "ev02"] })
> EOF
<<EOT
# generated for test
upstream ev01 { server ev01.corp.local:8080; }
upstream ev02 { server ev02.corp.local:8080; }

EOT

Formatting and validation

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf2
$ printf 'locals {\n    messy   =  "spacing"\n}\n' > messy.tf
$ terraform fmt -check -diff messy.tf | grep -E '^[+-] '
-    messy   =  "spacing"
+  messy = "spacing"
$ terraform fmt messy.tf
messy.tf
$ terraform validate
Success! The configuration is valid.
$ rm messy.tf
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
terraform fmt

What it does: Rewrites .tf files into the standard style.

-check only report-diff show what would change-recursive
terraform validate

What it does: Checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and consistent, without contacting any cloud.

When to use it: A fast check in CI and before committing.

rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

What does this command do, and when would I use it?

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

In plain words

  • variable (input), locals (internal names), output (result). Types and validation catch errors early.
  • Value precedence: default < TF_VAR_ < tfvars < *.auto.tfvars < -var-file / -var.
  • sensitive hides values from output but not from state.
  • terraform console explores functions; fmt and validate keep code tidy and correct.

Resources, loops and dependencies

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • create multiple resources with count and for_each
  • explain implicit and explicit dependencies
  • use lifecycle rules

count and for_each

To create several similar resources use a meta-argument.

count = Nfor_each = set or map
Identityby position: res[0], res[1]by key: res["ev01"]
Remove from the middleshifts everything after it (dangerous)removes only that key
Best forN identical copies, on/off switch (count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0)named, distinct things

$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf3 && cd ~/lab/tf3
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'

> 
> resource "terraform_data" "server" {

> }
> 
> output "hosts" {

> }

$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1

What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

grep

Each instance is addressed by its key, for example terraform_data.server["ev02"]. Now remove the middle server from the list, which is the case where count goes wrong:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf3
$ terraform plan -var 'servers=["ev01","sql01"]' | grep -E "^  # |Plan:"

  # (because key ["ev02"] is not in for_each map)

What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform plan

What it does: Compares your code, the state and the real world, and shows what Terraform would change. It changes nothing.

When to use it: Before every apply, and in pull requests. Read it carefully, especially lines marked "replaced".

-out=FILE save the plan to apply later-var 'x=y' set a variable-replace=ADDR plan a rebuild of one resource

Open the full command reference

Only ev02 is destroyed; the others stay untouched, because their identity is the key. With count and a list, removing the second item would rename the third to index 1, and Terraform would destroy and recreate it. Prefer for_each for anything with an identity.

count as a switch

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf3
$ cat > flag.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "enable_monitoring" {
>   type    = bool
>   default = false
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "monitoring" {
>   count = var.enable_monitoring ? 1 : 0
>   input = "agent installed"
> }
> EOF
$ terraform plan | grep -E "Plan:|No changes"
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.
$ terraform plan -var enable_monitoring=true | grep -E "Plan:|# terraform_data.monitoring"
  # terraform_data.monitoring[0] will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

Dependencies

Terraform builds a graph of resources and creates them in the right order, in parallel where it can. Most dependencies are implicit: if resource B references resource A (A.attribute), B waits for A. That is how a VM references its subnet, and the subnet its network.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf3
$ cat > deps.tf <<'EOF'
> resource "terraform_data" "network" {
>   input = "10.0.0.0/16"
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "subnet" {
>   input = "subnet in ${terraform_data.network.output}"      # implicit dependency
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "firewall" {
>   input      = "rules"
>   depends_on = [terraform_data.subnet]                      # explicit dependency
> }
> EOF
$ terraform graph | grep -E '"terraform_data\.(subnet|firewall|network)' | grep -- '->' | sed 's/\[root\] //g; s/ (expand)//g'
  "terraform_data.firewall" -> "terraform_data.subnet";
  "terraform_data.subnet" -> "terraform_data.network";
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
terraform graph

What it does: Prints the dependency graph in DOT format.

When to use it: Understanding creation order.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

Edges point from a thing to what it depends on: subnet -> network, firewall -> subnet. Use depends_on only when the dependency is real but invisible in the code (for example, a policy that must exist before an application, without referencing any of its attributes).

Lifecycle rules

The lifecycle block tunes how Terraform treats a resource:

SettingEffect
prevent_destroy = trueany plan that would destroy it fails; guard for databases
create_before_destroy = trueon replacement, build the new one first (zero downtime)
ignore_changes = [attr]ignore drift on that attribute (for example tags set by another tool)
replace_triggered_by = [...]replace when another resource changes
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf3
$ cat > protect.tf <<'EOF'
> resource "terraform_data" "database" {
>   input = "prod-db"
>   lifecycle {
>     prevent_destroy = true
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 4 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve 2>&1 | grep -E "Error: Instance cannot be destroyed|prevent_destroy" | head -2
Error: Instance cannot be destroyed
Resource terraform_data.database has lifecycle.prevent_destroy set, but the

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Targeting and replacing

  • terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS: force a rebuild of one resource (the replacement for the old taint).
  • terraform apply -target=ADDRESS: limit the run to one resource and its dependencies. An emergency tool, not a normal workflow (it skips parts of the graph).
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf3
$ terraform apply -auto-approve > /dev/null
$ terraform plan -replace='terraform_data.server["ev01"]' | grep -E "# terraform_data.server\[\"ev01\"\] will be replaced|Plan:|replace"
-/+ destroy and then create replacement
  # terraform_data.server["ev01"] will be replaced, as requested
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve > /dev/null

In plain words

  • count for identical copies or a switch; for_each for named things (stable identity).
  • References create implicit dependencies; depends_on for hidden ones.
  • lifecycle: prevent_destroy, create_before_destroy, ignore_changes.
  • -replace rebuilds one resource; -target is for emergencies only.

Terraform · Lesson 4

State: what Terraform remembers

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what the state file stores and why it exists
  • inspect state with terraform state and terraform show
  • recognise drift and what a plan does about it
  • explain remote state, locking and state security

Why state exists

Terraform cannot guess which cloud resources belong to your configuration: it keeps a state file (terraform.tfstate) mapping each resource in your code to the real object (its ID, attributes). On each plan it refreshes (reads the real attributes), compares to your code, and shows the difference.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf4 && cd ~/lab/tf4
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> resource "terraform_data" "ev" {
>   input = "EV01"
>   provisioner "local-exec" {
>     command = "echo hello > ev.txt"
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ ls -A | grep -v '^\.terraform'
ev.txt
main.tf
terraform.tfstate
$ python3 - <<'PY'
> import json
> s = json.load(open("terraform.tfstate"))
> print("state format version:", s["version"])
> print("resources recorded  :", [(r["type"], r["name"]) for r in s["resources"]])
> print("keys at top level   :", sorted(s.keys()))
> PY
state format version: 4
resources recorded  : [('terraform_data', 'ev')]
keys at top level   : ['check_results', 'lineage', 'outputs', 'resources', 'serial', 'terraform_version', 'version']

Refactoring without rebuilding: moved blocks

If you rename a resource in code, Terraform thinks "old one deleted, new one added" and would destroy and recreate it. A moved block (or state mv) tells it they are the same thing:

Real output

$ sed -i 's/"ev"/"ev_server"/' main.tf
$ echo "--- after renaming without telling Terraform:"
--- after renaming without telling Terraform:
$ terraform plan | grep -E "Plan:|will be (destroyed|created)"
  # terraform_data.ev will be destroyed
  # terraform_data.ev_server will be created
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.
$ cat >> main.tf <<'EOF'
> 
> moved {
>   from = terraform_data.ev
>   to   = terraform_data.ev_server
> }
> EOF
$ echo "--- with a moved block:"
--- with a moved block:
$ terraform plan | grep -E "Plan:|has moved|No changes"
  # terraform_data.ev has moved to terraform_data.ev_server
Plan: 0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

terraform plan

Drift

Drift is when someone changes the real infrastructure outside Terraform (a manual console edit or a script). Terraform detects it at the next plan, because it compares real attributes to the config.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf4
$ cat > drift.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "msg" {
>   default = "expected"
> }
> resource "terraform_data" "note" {
>   input = var.msg
>   provisioner "local-exec" {
>     command = "echo ${var.msg} > note.txt"
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ echo "someone edited the real thing by hand" > note.txt
$ terraform plan | grep -E "No changes|Plan:"
No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.

Here the plan says no changes: Terraform can only see what the provider reports from the API, and a file changed behind a local-exec is invisible to it. For real cloud resources (a security group rule added in the console), the provider reads the live settings and a plan would show the drift and propose reverting it. Lesson: scheduled terraform plan runs in CI are a drift detector, and the ultimate fix is to make Terraform the only way changes are made.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf4
$ rm drift.tf note.txt
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 0 added, 0 changed, 1 destroyed.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
rm

What it does: Deletes files (there is no recycle bin).

When to use it: Removing files you no longer need. Add -r for folders.

-r remove folders and their contents-f do not ask and ignore missing files-i ask for each file

Careful: Deleting cannot be undone. Never run rm -rf with a variable that might be empty (rm -rf "$DIR/") and check the path with ls first.

Remote state and locking

The default local backend keeps terraform.tfstate on your disk. That breaks down in a team: two people with two state files will conflict and duplicate or destroy each other's work. Teams use a remote backend: shared storage with locking, so only one apply runs at a time.

backend.tf (Example, not run here)
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-terraform-state"
    key            = "ev/prod/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "eu-west-2"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"   # lock table
    encrypt        = true
  }
}

Other backends: Azure Storage, Google Cloud Storage, Terraform Cloud/HCP, GitLab, Consul. Run terraform init again after adding or changing a backend (-migrate-state copies existing state).

State security

State contains everything, including secrets such as generated passwords and keys, in plain text. Therefore:

  • keep state in an encrypted remote backend with strict access control and versioning
  • never commit terraform.tfstate to Git (put *.tfstate* and .terraform/ in .gitignore)
  • avoid putting secrets in Terraform at all where possible: reference a secrets manager
  • split large estates into several smaller states (per environment and per component) to limit blast radius and speed up plans
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf4
$ printf '.terraform/\n*.tfstate\n*.tfstate.*\n*.tfvars\ncrash.log\n' > .gitignore
$ cat .gitignore
.terraform/
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
*.tfvars
crash.log
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve | grep "Destroy complete"
Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

Careful: In production this removes real infrastructure. Check the plan; use prevent_destroy for critical resources.

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • State maps code to real objects. It is JSON; do not hand-edit it.
  • terraform state list/show/mv/rm; moved blocks refactor safely; import adopts existing resources.
  • Drift is detected by plan (for what providers can observe). Remote backends with locking are required for teams.
  • State holds secrets: encrypt it, restrict it, never commit it.

Terraform · Lesson 5

Modules

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a module is and when to write one
  • call a local module and pass inputs
  • return outputs from a module
  • describe registry modules, versioning and good module design

Why modules

Every Terraform folder is already a module (the root module). A child module is a folder of .tf files that you call from another configuration, like a function: inputs (variables) in, outputs out. Use modules to avoid copy-pasting the same pattern ("a server with a disk, a security group and a DNS record") in every environment, and to enforce company standards in one place.

A local module

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf5/modules/ev_server && cd ~/lab/tf5
$ cat > modules/ev_server/variables.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "name" {
>   type = string
> }
> 
> variable "environment" {
>   type = string
> }
> 
> variable "size" {
>   type    = string
>   default = "small"
> }
> EOF
$ cat > modules/ev_server/main.tf <<'EOF'
> locals {
>   fqdn = "${var.name}.${var.environment}.corp.local"
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "server" {
>   input = {
>     fqdn = local.fqdn
>     size = var.size
>   }
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "dns" {
>   input = "A record for ${local.fqdn}"
> }
> EOF
$ cat > modules/ev_server/outputs.tf <<'EOF'
> output "fqdn" {
>   description = "The server's full name"
>   value       = local.fqdn
> }
> 
> output "size" {
>   value = var.size
> }
> EOF
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> module "ev01" {
>   source      = "./modules/ev_server"
>   name        = "ev01"
>   environment = "test"
> }
> 
> module "sql01" {
>   source      = "./modules/ev_server"
>   name        = "sql01"
>   environment = "test"
>   size        = "large"
> }
> 
> output "servers" {
>   value = {
>     ev01  = module.ev01.fqdn
>     sql01 = "${module.sql01.fqdn} (${module.sql01.size})"
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init 2>&1 | grep -E "Initializing modules|successfully"
Initializing modules...
Terraform has been successfully initialized!
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Plan:|Apply complete"
Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 4 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ terraform output servers
{
  "ev01" = "ev01.test.corp.local"
  "sql01" = "sql01.test.corp.local (large)"
}
$ terraform state list
module.ev01.terraform_data.dns
module.ev01.terraform_data.server
module.sql01.terraform_data.dns
module.sql01.terraform_data.server
What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

terraform init

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

When to use it: The first command in a new folder, and again after adding a provider, module or backend.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

terraform apply

What it does: Makes the changes shown in the plan, then updates the state.

When to use it: After reviewing the plan. Without -auto-approve it asks you to confirm.

-auto-approve skip the confirmation (for pipelines)PLANFILE apply a saved plan-var-file=F variable values from a file
terraform output

What it does: Prints the output values from the last apply.

When to use it: Reading addresses or IDs created by Terraform for use in scripts.

terraform state

What it does: Inspects and edits the state: list, show, mv, rm.

When to use it: Seeing what Terraform manages, or renaming a resource without rebuilding it.

Open the full command reference

The module is called twice with different inputs, producing two independent sets of resources (module.ev01... and module.sql01...). To reach inside, only outputs are visible: module.sql01.fqdn. Everything else is private. That boundary lets you change a module's internals without breaking callers.

Module with for_each

Modules support for_each and count, so one block can build a whole fleet:

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf5
$ cat > fleet.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "fleet" {
>   type = map(object({ size = string }))
>   default = {
>     ev02 = { size = "small" }
>     ev03 = { size = "medium" }
>   }
> }
> 
> module "fleet" {
>   for_each    = var.fleet
>   source      = "./modules/ev_server"
>   name        = each.key
>   environment = "test"
>   size        = each.value.size
> }
> 
> output "fleet_names" {
>   value = [for k, m in module.fleet : m.fqdn]
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "Plan:|Apply complete"
Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
Apply complete! Resources: 4 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ terraform output fleet_names
[
  "ev02.test.corp.local",
  "ev03.test.corp.local",
]

Registry and versions

In real projects you often use modules published on the Terraform Registry or in your company's private registry:

vpc.tf (Example, not run here)
module "network" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "~> 5.0"            # pin the version!

  name = "ev-prod"
  cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs  = ["eu-west-2a", "eu-west-2b"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
  public_subnets  = ["10.0.101.0/24", "10.0.102.0/24"]
}

A module can also come from Git: source = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//ev_server?ref=v1.2.0" (always pin a tag). Pin versions so that a module update never changes your infrastructure unexpectedly.

Good module design

DoWhy
Keep modules small and focused ("a server", "a network")easier to understand and reuse
Give every variable a type and description; validate inputsself-documenting, fails early
Expose only the outputs callers needsmaller interface to maintain
Use sensible defaults; keep secrets as inputs, never hard-codedsafe and flexible
Version modules with tags; keep a changelogconsumers upgrade deliberately
Avoid provider configuration inside modulesthe caller decides credentials and region
Do not over-abstract: copy-paste twice before building a modulepremature modules are rigid

Environments

A typical layout puts reusable modules in one place and thin environment folders on top, each with its own state:

infra/
├── modules/
│   ├── network/
│   └── ev_server/
├── envs/
│   ├── test/    main.tf  test.tfvars  backend.tf
│   └── prod/    main.tf  prod.tfvars  backend.tf

Test and prod call the same modules with different inputs, which is the core benefit.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf5
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve | grep -E "Destroy complete"
Destroy complete! Resources: 8 destroyed.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform destroy

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

Careful: In production this removes real infrastructure. Check the plan; use prevent_destroy for critical resources.

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • A module is a folder of .tf files used like a function: variables in, outputs out.
  • module "x" { source = "./path" ... }; only outputs are visible from outside. for_each works on modules.
  • Pin versions of registry/Git modules. Keep modules small, typed and documented.
  • Environments reuse modules with different inputs and separate state.

Terraform · Lesson 6

Workflow, testing and teams

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • save and apply a reviewed plan file
  • use workspaces and understand when not to
  • write terraform test tests
  • design a safe team workflow with CI and approvals

Plan files: apply exactly what was reviewed

terraform plan followed by terraform apply re-plans internally, and the world may have changed in between. A saved plan removes that gap: you review a plan, then apply that very plan.

Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf6 && cd ~/lab/tf6
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> variable "replicas" {
>   type    = number
>   default = 2
> }
> 
> resource "terraform_data" "worker" {
>   count = var.replicas
>   input = "worker-${count.index}"
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform plan -out=tfplan | grep -E "Plan:"
Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
$ ls -l tfplan | awk '{print "plan file saved:", $9}'
plan file saved: tfplan
$ terraform show tfplan | grep -E "^  # "
  # terraform_data.worker[0] will be created
  # terraform_data.worker[1] will be created
$ terraform apply tfplan | grep -E "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 2 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
What do these 10 commands do, and when would I use them?
mkdir

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists
cd

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

terraform init

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

When to use it: The first command in a new folder, and again after adding a provider, module or backend.

terraform plan

What it does: Compares your code, the state and the real world, and shows what Terraform would change. It changes nothing.

When to use it: Before every apply, and in pull requests. Read it carefully, especially lines marked "replaced".

-out=FILE save the plan to apply later-var 'x=y' set a variable-replace=ADDR plan a rebuild of one resource
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
terraform show

What it does: Shows the state or a saved plan in readable form.

When to use it: Reviewing a plan file before applying it.

terraform apply

What it does: Makes the changes shown in the plan, then updates the state.

When to use it: After reviewing the plan. Without -auto-approve it asks you to confirm.

-auto-approve skip the confirmation (for pipelines)PLANFILE apply a saved plan-var-file=F variable values from a file

Open the full command reference

In CI the usual shape is: pipeline job 1 runs plan -out, stores the plan as an artifact and posts the summary to the pull request; after approval, job 2 runs apply on that same plan file. Plan files can contain secrets, so store them like state.

Workspaces

A workspace is a separate state within the same configuration and backend. The default is called default.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf6
$ terraform workspace new test | grep -E "Created"
Created and switched to workspace "test"!
$ terraform workspace list
  default
* test
$ terraform apply -auto-approve -var replicas=1 | grep -E "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ terraform workspace select default | grep Switched
Switched to workspace "default".
$ terraform state list
terraform_data.worker[0]
terraform_data.worker[1]
$ terraform workspace select test > /dev/null
$ terraform state list
terraform_data.worker[0]
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve | grep "Destroy complete"
Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.
$ terraform workspace select default > /dev/null
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
terraform workspace

What it does: Manages separate state files within one configuration.

When to use it: Short-lived copies of an environment.

terraform state

What it does: Inspects and edits the state: list, show, mv, rm.

When to use it: Seeing what Terraform manages, or renaming a resource without rebuilding it.

Careful: Do not edit the state file by hand.

terraform destroy

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

Careful: In production this removes real infrastructure. Check the plan; use prevent_destroy for critical resources.

Open the full command reference

Each workspace has its own resources: default has two workers, test has one. Workspaces suit quick, short-lived copies of the same thing (for example, a feature branch environment). For long-lived, differently configured environments such as test and prod, most teams prefer separate directories or separate state files with different variable files, because workspaces make it easy to apply to the wrong environment by accident and share one backend and credentials.

Testing with terraform test

Terraform has a built-in test framework. A *.tftest.hcl file runs real or mocked plans/applies and checks assertions.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf6
$ cat > tests.tftest.hcl <<'EOF'
> run "default_has_two_workers" {
>   command = plan
> 
>   assert {
>     condition     = length(terraform_data.worker) == 2
>     error_message = "expected 2 workers by default"
>   }
> }
> 
> run "scales_up" {
>   command = plan
>   variables {
>     replicas = 5
>   }
> 
>   assert {
>     condition     = length(terraform_data.worker) == 5
>     error_message = "expected 5 workers"
>   }
> }
> 
> run "rejects_nonsense_in_a_deliberately_failing_test" {
>   command = plan
>   variables {
>     replicas = 3
>   }
> 
>   assert {
>     condition     = length(terraform_data.worker) == 2
>     error_message = "this assertion is meant to fail, to show the output"
>   }
> }
> EOF
$ terraform test | sed -E 's/\.\.\. //; s/ \([0-9.]+s\)//' | grep -E "pass|fail|Success|Error|expected|meant"

Error: Test assertion failed

  on tests.tftest.hcl line 29, in run "rejects_nonsense_in_a_deliberately_failing_test":
  29:     condition     = length(terraform_data.worker) == 2
    ├────────────────
    │ Diff:
    │ --- actual
    │ +++ expected
    │ - 3
    │ + 2


this assertion is meant to fail, to show the output
  run "default_has_two_workers"pass
  run "scales_up"pass
  run "rejects_nonsense_in_a_deliberately_failing_test"fail
tests.tftest.hclfail
Failure! 2 passed, 1 failed.
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
terraform test

What it does: Runs the .tftest.hcl tests in the folder.

When to use it: Checking modules and variables in CI.

sed

What it does: A stream editor: applies edits such as search-and-replace to text as it flows through.

When to use it: Replacing a value in a config file or reformatting output in a pipeline.

s/old/new/g replace all occurrences on each line-i edit the file in place-n '5p' print only line 5/pattern/d delete matching lines

Careful: sed -i changes the file immediately. Test without -i first, or keep a backup (sed -i.bak).

Open the full command reference

Two tests pass and the third deliberately fails, so you see what failure output looks like (a non-zero exit code, which fails a CI job). Remove that run block in real life.

Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf6
$ python3 - <<'PY'
> import re
> s = open("tests.tftest.hcl").read()
> s = s[:s.index('run "rejects_nonsense')]
> open("tests.tftest.hcl", "w").write(s)
> PY
$ terraform test | grep -E "Success"
Success! 2 passed, 0 failed.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
python3

What it does: Runs the Python 3 interpreter: a script file, or a one-liner with -c.

When to use it: Quick calculations and data handling, running exporters and small tools.

-c 'code' run code-m http.server serve the current folder over HTTP-m json.tool pretty-print JSON

Open the full command reference

Other quality tools: terraform validate, terraform fmt -check, tflint (provider-aware linting), checkov / tfsec / trivy (security scanning: open ports, unencrypted disks, public buckets), terratest (Go-based integration tests), and Infracost (cost estimate in the PR).

A team workflow

  1. A change starts as a branch and pull request (see the Git track).
  2. CI runs: fmt -check, validate, tflint, security scan, terraform test, then plan.
  3. The plan output is posted on the PR. Reviewers read the plan, not only the code.
  4. After approval and merge to main, a pipeline runs apply (often with a manual approval for production).
  5. State is remote and locked; the pipeline uses short-lived credentials (OIDC role) rather than stored keys.

Rules that prevent disasters:

  • Nobody runs apply from their laptop against production.
  • Separate state per environment and per component; least-privilege credentials per environment.
  • prevent_destroy on stateful resources; protect production applies with approvals.
  • Pin provider and Terraform versions (required_version, .terraform.lock.hcl committed).
  • Never commit *.tfstate, *.tfvars with secrets, or credentials.
Real output
$ cd ~/lab/tf6
$ cat > versions.tf <<'EOF'
> terraform {
>   required_version = ">= 1.6.0, < 2.0.0"
> }
> EOF
$ terraform validate
Success! The configuration is valid.
$ terraform destroy -auto-approve | grep "Destroy complete"
Destroy complete! Resources: 2 destroyed.
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
terraform validate

What it does: Checks that the configuration is syntactically valid and consistent, without contacting any cloud.

When to use it: A fast check in CI and before committing.

Open the full command reference

In plain words

  • Save a plan (-out) and apply that exact file after review.
  • Workspaces give separate state per name; use separate directories for test and prod.
  • terraform test with assertions; add lint and security scanning in CI.
  • Safe teams: PR, CI plan, review the plan, remote locked state, no laptop applies to production.

Terraform · Lesson 7

Cloud patterns, providers and the bigger picture

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • recognise a typical cloud network and server configuration
  • explain provider authentication safely
  • use data sources, import and terraform_remote_state
  • decide what belongs in Terraform and what in Ansible or Kubernetes

This lesson is mostly reading real-world Terraform. The lab environment cannot reach cloud APIs or the Terraform registry, so the cloud blocks are Example (not run here). The one thing we can run is the language machinery that these examples use, at the end.

A typical AWS network and server

network.tf (Example, not run here)
provider "aws" {
  region = var.region
}

resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block           = "10.0.0.0/16"
  enable_dns_hostnames = true
  tags = { Name = "ev-${var.environment}" }
}

resource "aws_subnet" "private" {
  for_each          = { a = "10.0.1.0/24", b = "10.0.2.0/24" }
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id          # implicit dependency
  cidr_block        = each.value
  availability_zone = "${var.region}${each.key}"
}

resource "aws_security_group" "ev" {
  name   = "ev-servers"
  vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id

  ingress {
    description = "HTTPS from the corporate network only"
    from_port   = 443
    to_port     = 443
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = ["10.20.0.0/16"]
  }
  egress {
    from_port   = 0
    to_port     = 0
    protocol    = "-1"
    cidr_blocks = ["0.0.0.0/0"]
  }
}

data "aws_ami" "ubuntu" {                       # data source: look up, do not create
  most_recent = true
  owners      = ["099720109477"]
  filter {
    name   = "name"
    values = ["ubuntu/images/hvm-ssd/ubuntu-noble-24.04-amd64-server-*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_instance" "ev" {
  for_each               = var.servers
  ami                    = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type          = each.value.size
  subnet_id              = aws_subnet.private["a"].id
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.ev.id]
  user_data              = templatefile("${path.module}/bootstrap.sh.tftpl", { name = each.key })
  tags                   = { Name = each.key }
}

Every idea in this example appeared in the previous lessons. Also notice how the networking track shows up: a VPC and its subnets are the CIDR blocks and routes you built by hand, the security group is a firewall rule list, and the route to the internet is a default route to a gateway. Knowing Linux networking makes cloud networking easy.

Authentication: never put credentials in code

MethodNotes
Environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID...)simplest for local use; never commit them
Shared config / SSO login (aws sso login, az login)short-lived, tied to a person
Instance or workload identity (IAM role, managed identity)best for servers and CI: no stored secrets
OIDC federation (GitHub Actions, GitLab, Jenkins plugins)CI gets a temporary role without stored keys

Rule: the Terraform code names what to build; who is allowed is decided outside it, with the least privilege needed.

Data sources, import and remote state

  • Data sources read existing things (an AMI, a DNS zone, a secret's metadata) without managing them.
  • import adopts something created by hand into Terraform:
import.tf (Example, not run here)
import {
  to = aws_instance.legacy
  id = "i-0abc123def456"
}
# then: terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf  (drafts the resource block for you)
  • terraform_remote_state reads another configuration's outputs (a network stack publishing subnet IDs for an application stack). It is a built-in data source, so we can run it:
Real output
$ mkdir -p ~/lab/tf7/network ~/lab/tf7/app && cd ~/lab/tf7/network
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> resource "terraform_data" "net" {
>   input = "10.0.0.0/16"
> }
> output "cidr" {
>   value = terraform_data.net.output
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep "Apply complete"
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
$ cd ~/lab/tf7/app
$ cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
> data "terraform_remote_state" "network" {
>   backend = "local"
>   config = {
>     path = "../network/terraform.tfstate"
>   }
> }
> 
> output "app_sees_network" {
>   value = "app subnet will live inside ${data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.cidr}"
> }
> EOF
$ terraform init > /dev/null 2>&1
$ terraform apply -auto-approve | grep -E "app_sees_network"
  + app_sees_network = "app subnet will live inside 10.0.0.0/16"
app_sees_network = "app subnet will live inside 10.0.0.0/16"
$ cd ~/lab/tf7/app && terraform destroy -auto-approve > /dev/null
$ cd ~/lab/tf7/network && terraform destroy -auto-approve > /dev/null
What do these 7 commands do, and when would I use them?

What it does: Creates a folder.

When to use it: Setting up folders for projects, logs or backups.

-p create parent folders too and do not complain if it exists

What it does: Changes the current folder.

When to use it: Moving around the file system. cd alone goes home, cd - goes back to the previous folder, cd .. goes up one level.

cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

terraform init

What it does: Prepares a Terraform folder: downloads providers and modules and sets up the backend for state.

When to use it: The first command in a new folder, and again after adding a provider, module or backend.

terraform apply

What it does: Makes the changes shown in the plan, then updates the state.

When to use it: After reviewing the plan. Without -auto-approve it asks you to confirm.

-auto-approve skip the confirmation (for pipelines)PLANFILE apply a saved plan-var-file=F variable values from a file
grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

terraform destroy

What it does: Deletes everything the configuration manages.

When to use it: Tearing down a test environment.

Careful: In production this removes real infrastructure. Check the plan; use prevent_destroy for critical resources.

Open the full command reference

This layered approach (network first, application on top) gives small, fast states and limits the blast radius of mistakes.

Terraform and the other tools

LayerToolNote
Cloud and platform resources (networks, VMs, databases, DNS, IAM, clusters)Terraformthe "what exists" layer
Configuring the inside of servers (packages, files, users, services)Ansiblethe "how it is set up" layer. Terraform can output the host list for Ansible's inventory
Packaging appsDockerbuilt in CI, stored in a registry
Running apps at scaleKubernetesTerraform can create the cluster; deployments use Kubernetes manifests, Helm or GitOps
Running it allJenkins / GitHub Actionspipelines call plan, apply, build, deploy

Terraform can also manage Kubernetes objects and Docker containers via providers (kubernetes, helm, docker), but most teams keep cluster creation in Terraform and application deployment in a dedicated deploy tool.

Immutable infrastructure

A common modern approach: instead of logging in to patch a server, build a new image (with Packer, or a container image), have Terraform replace the old servers with new ones, and throw the old ones away. Nothing is ever hand-edited, so servers do not drift. create_before_destroy makes the replacement seamless.

Costs and cleanup

Cloud resources cost money while they exist. Habits that save you:

  • tag everything (Owner, Env, ExpiresOn), and use Infracost in PRs
  • terraform destroy lab environments when finished
  • set budget alerts in the cloud account
  • never leave test databases or GPU machines running overnight

Terraform or OpenTofu?

In 2023 HashiCorp changed Terraform's license. The community forked it as OpenTofu (Linux Foundation). The language, providers and workflow are the same, and the commands are tofu init/plan/apply. Everything in this track applies to both.

In plain words

  • Real configurations: networks, security groups, servers, data sources, templated bootstrap scripts.
  • Authenticate with short-lived identities (SSO, roles, OIDC), never keys in code.
  • import adopts existing resources; terraform_remote_state shares outputs between layered stacks.
  • Terraform creates the platform; Ansible configures servers; Docker/Kubernetes run applications; pipelines glue it together.

Kubernetes · Lesson 1

Why Kubernetes, and how a cluster is built

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what an orchestrator does that Docker alone does not
  • name the control plane and node components and what each does
  • explain the declarative model and the reconciliation loop
  • use kubectl to look around a real cluster

The problem

With Docker on one machine you can run a few containers. At real scale new questions appear:

  • Which of my 50 machines should run this container?
  • A machine died at 3 am. Who restarts its containers elsewhere?
  • How do I ship version 2 without downtime, and roll back if it is bad?
  • How do containers on different machines find each other?
  • How do I add more copies when traffic grows?
  • Where do configuration and secrets live, and who may change what?

Kubernetes (K8s; "K" + 8 letters + "s") is an orchestrator that answers these. You tell it the desired state ("run 3 copies of this image, reachable on port 80"), and it continuously works to make reality match, restarting, rescheduling and scaling as needed.

Declarative and reconciling

You do not tell Kubernetes "start a container". You declare objects (in YAML) describing what you want, and store them in the cluster. Controllers are loops that compare desired state with actual state and act on the difference:

  1. You say: replicas: 3.
  2. The controller sees only 2 running. It creates one more.
  3. A node dies, so one drops. The controller notices and creates another elsewhere.

This reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes. It is the same idea as Terraform's plan/apply and Ansible's desired state, but running continuously.

The parts of a cluster

A cluster has a control plane (the brain) and worker nodes (the muscle).

ComponentWhereJob
kube-apiservercontrol planethe front door: every tool (and every other component) talks to the cluster through this REST API. Authenticates, authorises, validates, stores
etcdcontrol planethe cluster's database: a consistent key-value store holding all objects. Back it up!
kube-schedulercontrol planepicks a node for each new Pod (considering resources, rules, taints)
kube-controller-managercontrol planeruns the controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node, Job, ...)
cloud-controller-managercontrol plane (cloud only)talks to the cloud API (load balancers, disks, nodes)
kubeletevery nodethe node agent: makes sure the Pods assigned to its node are running and healthy, reports status
container runtimeevery nodeactually runs containers (containerd or CRI-O). Docker Engine is not needed
kube-proxyevery nodeimplements Services: network rules that send traffic for a Service address to its Pods
CNI pluginevery nodegives Pods IP addresses and connects them (Calico, Cilium, Flannel...)
CoreDNSin the clusterDNS names for Services

Managed services (EKS on AWS, AKS on Azure, GKE on Google) run the control plane for you; you manage worker nodes (or even none, in serverless modes).

Look at a real cluster

The course lab runs a small real single-node cluster (control plane and node on one machine) so every command in this track is real. A single-node cluster is unusual for production but identical in behaviour.

Real output

Server Version: v1.37.1
$ kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.conditions[-1].type,VERSION:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion

lab-node   Ready    v1.37.1
$ kubectl get --raw=/readyz

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

In this lab, the control plane processes run directly on the machine (like a kubeadm-less install) so they do not show as Pods. On a kubeadm cluster you would see etcd, kube-apiserver, kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager as "static Pods" here as well.

Everything is an API object

kubectl api-resources lists every kind of object the cluster understands:

Real output
$ kubectl api-resources --no-headers | awk '{print $1}' | grep -E "^(pods|services|deployments|replicasets|configmaps|secrets|namespaces|nodes|persistentvolumeclaims|ingresses|jobs|cronjobs|statefulsets|daemonsets)$" | sort | tr '\n' ' '; echo

What do these 8 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl api-resources

What it does: Lists every kind of object the cluster knows.

When to use it: Discovering names and short names for objects.

awk

What it does: A small programming language for text columns: it splits each line into fields ($1, $2, ...) and runs actions on lines that match.

When to use it: Printing or adding up a column, or filtering lines by the value in one column.

-F ',' set the field separator'{print $1}' print the first column'$3 > 100' select rows where column 3 is above 100
jobs

What it does: Lists the background jobs started from this shell.

When to use it: Seeing what you have running with & or paused with Ctrl+Z.

sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
tr

What it does: Translates or deletes single characters.

When to use it: Converting case (tr a-z A-Z), squeezing spaces, or turning separators into newlines.

-d delete the characters-s squeeze repeats into one
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

kubectl explain

What it does: Built-in documentation for any field of any object.

When to use it: What can I put in spec.containers? kubectl explain pod.spec.containers.

head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

kubectl explain is built-in documentation for any field. You will use it a lot. Every object has the same top-level shape:

shape.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1        # which API group and version
kind: Deployment           # what type of object
metadata:                  # identity
  name: web
  namespace: default
  labels: {app: web}
spec:                      # the DESIRED state (you write this)
  replicas: 3
status: {}                 # the ACTUAL state (Kubernetes writes this)

spec is what you want; status is what is true. Controllers close the gap between them.

Objects you will learn

ObjectPurposeLesson
Podone or more containers that run together2
Deployment / ReplicaSetkeep N Pods running; rolling updates3
Servicea stable address for a set of Pods4
ConfigMap / Secretconfiguration and sensitive data5
Volume, PV, PVCstorage6
Requests/limits, probes, schedulingresource control and health7
Namespace, RBAC, securitymulti-tenancy and access control8
Troubleshootingfinding what is wrong9
Jobs, DaemonSets, StatefulSets, Helmthe rest of the toolbox10

In plain words

  • Kubernetes keeps declared desired state true, through controllers running reconciliation loops.
  • Control plane: apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager. Node: kubelet, runtime, kube-proxy, CNI.
  • Everything is an API object with apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec (desired) and status (actual).
  • kubectl talks to the API server using a kubeconfig; explain and api-resources document the API.

Kubernetes · Lesson 2

Pods

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain what a Pod is and why it is not the same as a container
  • create Pods with kubectl run and with YAML
  • read status, logs, events; run commands inside a Pod
  • understand multi-container Pods, init containers and restart behaviour

What a Pod is

A Pod is one or more containers that are scheduled together on one node and share the same network (one IP address) and storage volumes. Most Pods have one container; extra containers are sidecars (a log shipper, a proxy) that help the main one. Kubernetes never schedules a bare container, always a Pod.

Pods are ephemeral: they are created, they run, they are replaced, never repaired. Their IP changes each time. That is why you almost never create Pods directly (lesson 3 uses Deployments) but you must understand them.

Create a Pod

Real output
$ kubectl run hello --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh -c 'echo "hello from a pod"; sleep 3600'
pod/hello created
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/hello --timeout=60s
pod/hello condition met
$ kubectl get pod hello -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase,READY:.status.containerStatuses[0].ready,NODE:.spec.nodeName
NAME    STATUS    READY   NODE
hello   Running   true    lab-node
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl run

What it does: Starts a single pod from an image.

When to use it: Quick tests and debugging pods. Add --restart=Never for a one-shot pod.

--image=IMG the image--restart=Never do not restart--overrides tweak the spec as JSON
sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

kubectl wait

What it does: Blocks until an object reaches a condition.

When to use it: In scripts: wait for a pod to be Ready or a job to complete.

--for=condition=Ready --timeout=60s
kubectl get

What it does: Lists Kubernetes objects (pods, services, deployments, nodes...).

When to use it: The first command of any investigation. Add -o wide, -o yaml, or -o custom-columns for more.

-n NS namespace-A all namespaces-o wide/yaml/json output format-l key=value filter by label-w watch for changes

kubectl run is the quick, imperative way. Pending while scheduling and pulling, then Running. See what happened:

Real output
$ kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=hello --sort-by=.lastTimestamp -o custom-columns=REASON:.reason,FROM:.source.component --no-headers

dev

What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl logs

What it does: Shows the output of a container in a pod.

When to use it: Debugging applications. --previous shows the run before a crash.

-f follow--previous the crashed container-c NAME choose a container
hostname

What it does: Shows (or sets) the computer's name.

When to use it: Confirming which server you are on, especially when you have several terminals open.

id

What it does: Shows your numeric user ID (uid), primary group ID (gid) and all groups you belong to.

When to use it: Diagnosing "permission denied" problems: check whether the user is in the group that owns the file.

-un only the user name-gn only the primary group name-G all group IDs
kubectl exec

What it does: Runs a command inside a container of a pod.

When to use it: Looking inside a running pod: kubectl exec -it POD -- sh.

ls

What it does: Lists the files and folders in a directory.

When to use it: Seeing what is in a folder, checking sizes, dates and permissions.

-l long format (permissions, owner, size, date)-a include hidden files starting with a dot-h human-readable sizes-t newest first-R recurse into subfolders-d show the folder itself, not its contents
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes

Open the full command reference

The events show the whole story: Scheduled (by the scheduler), Pulled the image, Created, Started (kubelet and runtime). logs shows stdout/stderr; exec runs a command in the container; kubectl exec -it POD -- sh opens a shell.

The same Pod as YAML

Real work uses YAML files in Git (declarative):

Real output
$ cat > pod.yaml <<'EOF'
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: Pod
> metadata:
>   name: web
>   labels:
>     app: web
>     tier: frontend
> spec:
>   containers:
>   - name: nginx
>     image: nginx:1.27-alpine
>     ports:

pod/web created
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/web --timeout=60s

$ kubectl get pods -l app=web --no-headers -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,STATUS:.status.phase

What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

kubectl apply

What it does: Creates or updates objects from a YAML file, making the cluster match the file.

When to use it: Deploying declaratively. Running it twice is safe.

-f FILE the file or folder-k DIR use Kustomize--dry-run=server validate without creating

Reaching a Pod

The Pod has its own IP inside the cluster network. From another Pod you can fetch it directly; from your machine use kubectl port-forward, a tunnel for debugging:

Real output
$ ip=$(kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath='{.status.podIP}')
$ kubectl run client --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- sh -c "wget -qO- http://$ip | grep -o '<title>.*</title>'"
pod/client created
$ kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.phase}'=Succeeded pod/client --timeout=60s
pod/client condition met
$ kubectl logs client
<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>
$ kubectl port-forward pod/web 18080:80 > /dev/null 2>&1 &
$ sleep 3
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18080/ | grep -o "<title>.*</title>"
<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>
$ kill %1
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl port-forward

What it does: Opens a temporary tunnel from your machine to a pod or service.

When to use it: Testing a service that is not exposed, for example a database.

curl

What it does: Makes web requests from the command line and prints the response.

When to use it: Testing an API or web page, checking HTTP status codes, downloading files.

-s silent-I headers only-o FILE save to a file-w '%{http_code}' print the status code-v show the whole conversation-X POST set the method
kill

What it does: Sends a signal to a process (by default asks it to stop politely, SIGTERM).

When to use it: Stopping a process or job: kill PID. Use kill -9 PID only if it ignores the polite request.

-15 (default) please terminate-9 force kill, no cleanup-0 only check the process exists-l list signals

Open the full command reference

describe: the most useful debugging command

Real output
$ kubectl describe pod web | grep -E "^(Name|Namespace|Node|Status|Image|State|Ready|Restart Count|QoS Class|Labels)" | sed 's/  */ /g' | sed 's#Node: .*#Node: <node>#'
Name: web
Namespace: lab2
Node: <node>
Labels: app=web
Status: Running
QoS Class: BestEffort
Node-Selectors: <none>
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
kubectl describe

What it does: Shows an object's details and, at the bottom, its recent events.

When to use it: A pod is not starting: read the Events section.

Open the full command reference

describe combines spec, status and the Events at the bottom, which usually explain what is wrong.

Multi-container Pods

Containers in a Pod share the network (they reach each other on localhost) and can share volumes. An init container runs to completion first, then the app containers start:

Real output
$ cat > multi.yaml <<'EOF'
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: Pod
> metadata:
>   name: multi
> spec:
>   volumes:
>   - name: shared
>     emptyDir: {}
>   initContainers:
>   - name: prepare
>     image: busybox:1.37
>     command: ["sh", "-c", "echo 'prepared by init' > /data/note.txt"]
>     volumeMounts: [{name: shared, mountPath: /data}]
>   containers:
>   - name: app
>     image: busybox:1.37
>     command: ["sh", "-c", "cat /data/note.txt; echo app-sees-init-output; sleep 3600"]
>     volumeMounts: [{name: shared, mountPath: /data}]
>   - name: sidecar
>     image: busybox:1.37
>     command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo sidecar-tick >> /data/side.log; sleep 1; done"]
>     volumeMounts: [{name: shared, mountPath: /data}]
> EOF
$ kubectl apply -f multi.yaml
pod/multi created
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/multi --timeout=60s
pod/multi condition met
$ kubectl get pod multi -o jsonpath='ready containers: {.status.containerStatuses[*].name}{"\n"}'
ready containers: app sidecar
$ kubectl logs multi -c app
prepared by init
app-sees-init-output
$ sleep 3
$ kubectl exec multi -c app -- sh -c 'grep -c sidecar-tick /data/side.log > /dev/null && echo "app can read the sidecar log through the shared volume"'
app can read the sidecar log through the shared volume
What does this command do, and when would I use it?
echo

What it does: Prints text (and the values of variables) to the screen.

When to use it: Showing messages in scripts, checking what a variable contains (echo "$PATH"), or writing a line into a file with a redirect.

-n no trailing newline-e interpret escapes like \n

Careful: Quote variables ("$name") so spaces in the value do not split it into several words.

Open the full command reference

An emptyDir volume lives as long as the Pod and is shared by its containers. Typical sidecar jobs: ship logs, refresh certificates, proxy traffic (service meshes inject a proxy sidecar).

Restarts and failure

restartPolicy (default Always) tells the kubelet what to do when a container exits. A container that keeps crashing goes into CrashLoopBackOff: restarts with growing delay.

Real output
$ kubectl run crasher --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh -c 'echo "starting"; exit 1'
pod/crasher created
$ for i in $(seq 1 30); do kubectl get pod crasher -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}' 2>/dev/null | grep -qE '^[1-9]' && break; sleep 2; done
$ kubectl get pod crasher -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,RESTARTS:.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount,LAST_EXIT:.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState.terminated.exitCode
NAME      RESTARTS   LAST_EXIT
crasher   1          1
$ kubectl logs crasher --previous
starting
What do these 3 commands do, and when would I use them?
exit

What it does: Ends the shell or script and returns a status code (0 means success, anything else means failure).

When to use it: In scripts, to tell the caller that something failed: exit 1.

seq

What it does: Prints a sequence of numbers.

When to use it: Loops: for i in $(seq 1 10).

for

What it does: A loop that repeats commands once for each item in a list.

When to use it: Doing the same thing to several files, servers or numbers: for h in ev01 sql01; do ...; done.

Open the full command reference

logs --previous shows the output of the container before the last restart, which is exactly what you need when a container will not stay up. Exit code 1 is the application's own failure; 137 means killed (often out of memory); 127 command not found.

Pods are not self-healing

Real output
$ kubectl delete pod web --wait=true
pod "web" deleted from lab2 namespace
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web --no-headers | wc -l
No resources found in lab2 namespace.
0
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl delete

What it does: Deletes objects.

When to use it: Removing a pod (a controller will recreate it), a deployment or a whole namespace.

-f FILE delete what a file defines--wait=false do not wait--all every object of that type
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Open the full command reference

Nobody recreated it. A bare Pod that is deleted (or whose node dies) is gone. That is the job of a controller, which is the next lesson.

In plain words

  • A Pod is one or more containers sharing one IP and volumes, scheduled together. Pods are disposable.
  • kubectl run/apply -f, get, describe, logs (--previous), exec, port-forward.
  • Labels identify Pods; selectors find them.
  • Init containers run first; sidecars share network and volumes. CrashLoopBackOff = repeated failure with backoff.
  • Bare Pods do not heal. Use a Deployment.
Your turn

Write a Pod YAML with two containers that talk over localhost (one runs nginx, the other wgets http://localhost in a loop). Read the second container's logs with -c.

Kubernetes · Lesson 3

Deployments, ReplicaSets and rolling updates

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pod and how they relate
  • scale and watch self-healing
  • do a rolling update and a rollback
  • read what happens when an update goes wrong

Three layers

ObjectRole
Podthe running containers
ReplicaSetkeeps exactly N identical Pods running (replaces any that die)
Deploymentmanages ReplicaSets to give you rolling updates and rollbacks

You create a Deployment; it creates a ReplicaSet; that creates Pods. Each Pod name shows the chain: web-<replicaset-hash>-<random>.

Your first Deployment

Real output
$ cat > deploy.yaml <<'EOF'
> apiVersion: apps/v1
> kind: Deployment
> metadata:
>   name: web
> spec:
>   replicas: 3
>   selector:
>     matchLabels:
>       app: web
>   template:
>     metadata:
>       labels:
>         app: web
>     spec:
>       containers:
>       - name: nginx
>         image: nginx:1.27-alpine
>         ports:
>         - containerPort: 80
> EOF
$ kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
deployment.apps/web created
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=90s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ kubectl get deployment web -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,DESIRED:.spec.replicas,READY:.status.readyReplicas,UP-TO-DATE:.status.updatedReplicas
NAME   DESIRED   READY   UP-TO-DATE
web    3         3       3
$ kubectl get rs -o custom-columns=KIND:.kind,DESIRED:.spec.replicas,READY:.status.readyReplicas
KIND         DESIRED   READY
ReplicaSet   3         3
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web --no-headers | wc -l
3
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?
cat

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).

When to use it: Reading short files, or creating a file from a heredoc (cat > file <<'EOF').

-n number the lines

Careful: For huge files use head, tail or less instead.

kubectl apply

What it does: Creates or updates objects from a YAML file, making the cluster match the file.

When to use it: Deploying declaratively. Running it twice is safe.

-f FILE the file or folder-k DIR use Kustomize--dry-run=server validate without creating
kubectl rollout

What it does: Manages Deployment rollouts: status, history, undo, restart.

When to use it: Watching an update finish, or rolling back a bad release.

status wait for completionundo go back one versionhistory restart recreate pods gradually
tail

What it does: Prints the last lines of a file.

When to use it: Reading the newest log entries; tail -f follows the file as it grows.

-n N last N lines-f keep watching for new lines
kubectl get

What it does: Lists Kubernetes objects (pods, services, deployments, nodes...).

When to use it: The first command of any investigation. Add -o wide, -o yaml, or -o custom-columns for more.

-n NS namespace-A all namespaces-o wide/yaml/json output format-l key=value filter by label-w watch for changes
wc

What it does: Counts lines, words and bytes.

When to use it: How many lines did grep find? command | wc -l.

-l lines-w words-c bytes

Important: the selector.matchLabels must match the template.metadata.labels: that is how the ReplicaSet knows which Pods are its own.

Self-healing

Delete one Pod and watch Kubernetes notice the difference between desired (3) and actual (2):

Real output
$ victim=$(kubectl get pods -l app=web -o name | head -1)
$ kubectl delete $victim --wait=true > /dev/null
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=60s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web --no-headers | wc -l
3
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
head

What it does: Prints the first lines of a file or of piped output.

When to use it: Peeking at the start of a file, or limiting output (command | head -5).

-n N first N lines-c N first N bytes
kubectl delete

What it does: Deletes objects.

When to use it: Removing a pod (a controller will recreate it), a deployment or a whole namespace.

-f FILE delete what a file defines--wait=false do not wait--all every object of that type

Open the full command reference

Three Pods again, with a new one replacing the deleted one. Node failure works the same: Pods on a lost node are recreated elsewhere. This is the reconciliation loop from the architecture lesson.

Scaling

Real output
$ kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=5
deployment.apps/web scaled
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=90s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='ready={.status.readyReplicas}{"\n"}'
ready=5
$ kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=3
deployment.apps/web scaled
$ kubectl wait --for=jsonpath='{.status.replicas}'=3 deployment/web --timeout=60s
deployment.apps/web condition met
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl scale

What it does: Changes the number of replicas of a deployment.

When to use it: Handling more load, or scaling to zero.

kubectl wait

What it does: Blocks until an object reaches a condition.

When to use it: In scripts: wait for a pod to be Ready or a job to complete.

--for=condition=Ready --timeout=60s

Open the full command reference

For automatic scaling, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler adjusts replicas based on CPU or custom metrics (it needs the metrics-server add-on, which this lab does not run, so here it is only an example):

hpa.yaml (Example, not run here)
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: web}
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70}}

Rolling update

Change the image version. Kubernetes starts a new ReplicaSet and gradually moves Pods from the old one to the new one, keeping the service available throughout:

Real output
$ kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.28-alpine
deployment.apps/web image updated
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ sleep 5
$ kubectl get rs -o custom-columns=IMAGE:.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image,DESIRED:.spec.replicas,READY:.status.readyReplicas --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp
IMAGE               DESIRED   READY
nginx:1.27-alpine   0         <none>
nginx:1.28-alpine   3         3
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web -o custom-columns=IMAGE:.spec.containers[0].image --no-headers | sort | uniq -c
      3 nginx:1.28-alpine
What do these 4 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl set

What it does: Changes parts of an object, such as the container image of a deployment.

When to use it: Starting a rolling update: kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.28.

sleep

What it does: Pauses for a number of seconds.

When to use it: Waiting for a service to start, or spacing out retries in a script.

sort

What it does: Sorts lines of text.

When to use it: Ordering output, or preparing for uniq (which needs sorted input).

-n numeric sort-r reverse-u remove duplicates-k N sort by column N-h sort human-readable sizes like 2K, 1G
uniq

What it does: Collapses repeated adjacent lines; with -c it counts them.

When to use it: Counting how often something occurs: sort | uniq -c | sort -rn.

-c prefix lines with counts-d show only duplicated lines

Open the full command reference

Two ReplicaSets exist: the old one scaled to 0 (kept for rollback) and the new one with 3 Pods. The pace is set by the update strategy:

Real output
$ kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='{.spec.strategy}{"\n"}'
{"rollingUpdate":{"maxSurge":"25%","maxUnavailable":"25%"},"type":"RollingUpdate"}

maxSurge: 25% (how many extra Pods may exist during the update) and maxUnavailable: 25% (how many may be missing). With 3 replicas that rounds to one extra and zero unavailable, so capacity never drops. Combined with readiness probes (lesson 7), a new Pod receives traffic only when ready: a zero-downtime release.

History and rollback

Real output
$ kubectl annotate deployment web kubernetes.io/change-cause="upgrade nginx to 1.28" --overwrite > /dev/null
$ kubectl rollout history deployment/web
deployment.apps/web 
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         upgrade nginx to 1.28
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/web 2>&1 | grep -v Warning
deployment.apps/web rolled back
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ kubectl get deployment web -o jsonpath='image now: {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
image now: nginx:1.27-alpine
What do these 2 commands do, and when would I use them?
kubectl annotate

What it does: Adds notes (annotations) to objects.

When to use it: Storing metadata such as the change cause of a rollout.

grep

What it does: Searches text for lines that match a pattern and prints those lines.

When to use it: Finding errors in a log, filtering the output of another command, or checking whether a setting exists in a file.

-i ignore upper/lower case-n show line numbers-r search a whole folder-v show lines that do NOT match-c count matching lines-E extended regular expressions

Careful: grep treats the pattern as a regular expression: characters like . and * are special. Use grep -F for plain text.

Open the full command reference

rollout undo goes back to the previous ReplicaSet; --to-revision=N picks a specific one. In GitOps practice you roll back by reverting the commit instead; the effect is the same.

A bad release

What if the new image does not exist? The rolling update stalls safely and the old Pods keep serving:

Real output
$ kubectl set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:does-not-exist
deployment.apps/web image updated
$ sleep 10
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=10s 2>&1 | tail -1
error: timed out waiting for the condition
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web -o custom-columns=IMAGE:.spec.containers[0].image,STATUS:.status.containerStatuses[0].state.waiting.reason --no-headers | sort | uniq -c
      3 nginx:1.27-alpine      <none>
      1 nginx:does-not-exist   ImagePullBackOff

Some Pods show ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff (the new ones), but because maxUnavailable protects capacity the old working Pods are still running. The fix is to roll back:

Real output
$ kubectl rollout undo deployment/web 2>&1 | grep -v Warning
deployment.apps/web rolled back
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ sleep 8
$ kubectl get pods -l app=web --no-headers -o custom-columns=STATUS:.status.phase | sort | uniq -c
      3 Running

This is why rolling updates are safe: a bad version never takes over fully. Set progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) so a stuck rollout is reported as failed, and make your pipeline run kubectl rollout status so a failing deploy fails the build.

Other update strategies

StrategyHow
RollingUpdate (default)gradual replacement
Recreatekill all old Pods, then start new ones (downtime; used when two versions cannot coexist)
Blue/greenrun both versions as separate Deployments, switch the Service selector
Canarysend a small share of traffic to the new version first (labels, ingress weights, or Argo Rollouts / Flagger)

In plain words

  • Deployment -> ReplicaSet -> Pods. The selector must match the Pod template labels.
  • Controllers heal: delete a Pod and it returns. kubectl scale changes replicas; HPA automates it.
  • Rolling updates replace Pods gradually (maxSurge, maxUnavailable). rollout status/history/undo.
  • A bad image stalls the rollout without taking the service down.
Your turn

Set maxSurge: 0 and maxUnavailable: 1 in the Deployment, update the image, and describe how the Pod counts differ compared to the default.

Kubernetes · Lesson 4

Services, DNS and networking

By the end of this lesson you can:
  • explain why Services exist and how selectors build endpoints
  • create ClusterIP and NodePort Services and reach them
  • use cluster DNS names
  • understand Ingress and LoadBalancer at a conceptual level

Pods come and go, so we need Services

Pod IPs change every time a Pod is recreated. A Service gives a set of Pods one stable virtual IP and DNS name, and load-balances across the healthy ones. Which Pods? Those whose labels match the Service's selector. The matching Pods are tracked as EndpointSlices.

Real output
$ cat > app.yaml <<'EOF'
> apiVersion: apps/v1
> kind: Deployment
> metadata:
>   name: web
> spec:
>   replicas: 3
>   selector:
>     matchLabels: {app: web}
>   template:
>     metadata:
>       labels: {app: web}
>     spec:
>       containers:
>       - name: nginx
>         image: nginx:1.27-alpine
>         ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
> ---
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: Service
> metadata:
>   name: web
> spec:
>   selector:
>     app: web
>   ports:
>   - port: 80          # the Service port
>     targetPort: 80    # the container port
> EOF
$ kubectl apply -f app.yaml
deployment.apps/web created
service/web created
$ kubectl rollout status deployment/web --timeout=90s | tail -1
deployment "web" successfully rolled out
$ kubectl get service web -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TYPE:.spec.type,PORT:.spec.ports[0].port
NAME   TYPE        PORT
web    ClusterIP   80
$ kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web -o jsonpath='endpoints: {.items[0].endpoints[*].addresses[0]}{"\n"}' | sed 's/[0-9]*\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*\.[0-9]*/<podip>/g'
endpoints: <podip> <podip> <podip>
What do these 6 commands do, and when would I use them?

What it does: Prints the contents of one or more files (and joins them together).
